items.summary: Filed 2026-08-12 from NR-163. Neither NATION_GENERATION.md nor GENERATION_STRATEGY.md fixed a corporation count; the premise (player + major AI as lean specialists against a saturated economy) implies many background firms but never said how many.
items.design:
SETTLED (Ben, 2026-08-12, review-queue Q&A): **~22 private corporations per nation** is the density target - above the midpoint of the 10-20 he originally floated, so read it as a crowded market rather than a cast of named rivals.

Two things this is not. It is not yet a measurement: the generator currently opens far leaner, so reaching 22/nation is a generation change, and at that density the per-tick cost of corp_ai's scored-utility evaluation over every background corp becomes the binding constraint (NR-162, the unmeasured hardware question, is the sibling - measure before scaling). And it is not a hard floor: a nation whose provinces cannot support that many firms should open leaner and say so, consistent with the NR-118 answer that focus - and by extension presence - follows the ground.

Sequencing note: this interacts with BL-365's saturation calibration. Saturation is a calibrated generation invariant, not an authored building count (NR-151), and this density target must be expressed the same way - a target the calibration aims at, not a literal per-nation loop count.

items.title: Pacing target - a skilled player reaches space in 20-40 years
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-12 from NR-168, and answers NR-166. Ben wanted assurance that base-game international trade reliably clears and that a player can plausibly beat Era 1 on trade alone; there was no stated invariant for this in MARKETS.md or FINANCE.md, only an implicit hope.
items.design:
SETTLED (Ben, 2026-08-12, review-queue Q&A): **a skilled player should reach space industry in about 20-40 years of game time.**

This is stronger than the question asked for, in the useful direction: it is bounded on both sides. Under ~20 years the base game is too easy and Era 0 has no weight; over ~40 it stalls, which is the failure NR-168 was actually worried about. So it is a checkable pacing target, not a reassurance.

Three pieces of work follow.

1. **Write it down.** ERAS.md is the natural home - it owns the Era 0 -> Era 1 transition and already carries the not-implemented banner. MARKETS.md and FINANCE.md should cite it rather than restate it, since what they own is the clearing behaviour that has to make the target reachable.

2. **Measure it.** This wants a headless harness (tools/verify/) that runs a competent-play approximation forward and reports the year at which Rocketry + launchpad + propellant first become affordable - the same shape as pregame_balance_harness. Beware the trap NR-156 records there: an assertion that passes off a band peg measures nothing.

3. **Only then tune.** Do not reshape prices to hit the number before the number has been measured once. Measure, then decide whether the economy or the target is wrong.

Blocked in practice on Era 1 gating being implemented at all (ERAS.md: designed, not implemented); until then a harness can measure affordability, not the actual transition.

items.title: Continent lens key floats above the always-open Selection band
The mercenary contract seam — a polity pays the player's company to make a fact about the world true
items.summary: The sell side of the mercenary company, and the player's income under the 0 CE refocus (NR-177). A contract is a condition_set (BL-342, shipped) that a client polity will pay to have become true by a deadline; the player chooses what force to commit, which is what keeps it a strategy rather than a mission list. Offers are derived from history_sim's existing campaign scorer — a polity that wants a province but cannot take it alone offers it as a contract — so offers are deterministic and their fees track a value the sim already computes. Reuses BL-350's command seam, split-payment pacing and (buyer, supplier) reputation scalar, but needs its own record: procurement's resource+quantity deliverable and countdown completion cannot express 'hold this province through the season', and it needs a third terminal state (failed) distinct from cancelled.
items.design:
**Status:** designed 2026-08-12, at Ben's request, as the first design work of the 0 CE refocus
(NR-177). This is the item NR-177 names as *"the mercenary SELL side (who contracts you, on what
terms, win/lose consequences) has no item at all, where procurement.cpp is only the buy side."*

### What this item owns

The player's **income**. Under the refocus the player is a mercenary company — the militia ancestor
— and a mercenary company's core loop is not extraction and it is not trade. It is: **be
contracted, field force, be paid.** Every other system in the game is either what you spend that
money on or what makes fielding force expensive.

That makes this the item the refocused product stands on. BL-350 shipped the seam by which the
player **buys**; nothing yet describes the seam by which it **earns**.

### The claim to reuse — stated precisely, because the loose version is wrong

The tempting one-liner is *"a mercenary contract is BL-350's procurement contract with the player as
the supplier."* **That is wrong in the part that matters**, and stating why is what shapes the
design.

`procurement_contract` (components.hpp:499, a 40-byte save-format record) carries
`resource + quantity` as its deliverable and completes when `ticks_elapsed` reaches
`lead_time_ticks`. Both are wrong here:

- **The deliverable is not fungible.** `resource + quantity` cannot express *"hold the river
  province through the campaign season"*. There is no resource whose quantity means that.
- **Completion is not a countdown.** A procurement contract finishes when enough ticks pass. A
  mercenary contract finishes when a **fact about the world** becomes true — or fails when the
  deadline passes and it is still false.
- **Failure is a distinct outcome from cancellation.** BL-350 has cancel (you walked away, you
  forfeit the deposit). This needs *lost* (you fought, you were beaten) — the same money outcome,
  a very different reputation and narrative outcome, and the one that makes contracts risky.

So: **a sibling record, not the same record.** What genuinely transfers is three shipped things,
and they are worth having:

1. **The command seam.** Three more `corp_verb`s appended to the same enum BL-350 extended to 14
   (append-only, BL-293's convention), so the player's press and an AI's command stay one
   implementation.
2. **The split-payment pacing.** Deposit on acceptance, remainder across the term — BL-350's Q1
   answer, already tuned, already legible, already reusing BL-095's construction model.
3. **The reputation scalar.** `world::corp_reputation`, a (buyer, supplier) map, already
   serialised. A mercenary's standing with a client is exactly that object.

### The spine

> **A contract is a condition_set the client will pay to have become true, by a deadline.**

That is the design, and it is short because `condition_set` (BL-342, shipped v0.1.3) is already
generic, pure, deterministic predicate machinery — and BL-350 already evaluates one for its
embargo decline, so the precedent for using it as *contract terms* is set rather than invented.

A contract record therefore carries: the client, the company, a **success `condition_set`**, a
**deadline in ticks**, a fee, a deposit fraction, and the accrued state (`ticks_elapsed`,
`deposit_paid`). The whole variety of contract types — take this province, hold that one, break a
siege, escort a convoy, deny a road — is **authored data in the predicate**, not a type enum in
C++. Adding a contract kind is a Lua change.

This is the design's main claim to legibility and it is the same claim BL-350 made: reuse a shipped,
understood mechanism rather than invent a parallel one.

### Where offers come from — the second reuse, and the stronger one

Contracts must be *offered* by someone, and the offers must be deterministic (io-standing-rules
§ Determinism). The answer is already in the tree.

`history_sim.cpp` scores four verbs per polity per year, and one of them is **campaign** — a pure,
integer, argmax-over-bounded-candidates scorer that already decides *which neighbouring province a
polity wants and how badly* (`w_farm`, `w_ore`, `w_port`, `w_ring`, `w_dist`, `w_def`,
`w_cult`). It also already computes the **stall**: a campaign whose arriving force falls under
`stalled_supply_q` because the objective is too far or the defender too strong.

> **A contract offer is a campaign the polity wants and cannot win alone.**

Take the existing candidate scoring; where the polity's own projected force is insufficient but the
objective's value is high, it does not launch — it **offers the objective as a contract**, at a fee
derived from the value it scored. Where it can win alone, it campaigns and offers nothing.

Three things this buys, none of which needs new machinery:
- **Offers are deterministic and replayable**, because the scorer already is.
- **Offers are legible**, because the fee tracks a value the sim actually computed rather than a
  designer's table.
- **The contract market has a natural rhythm** — offers appear when the political map is under
  tension and dry up when it is settled, which is a *reason* for boom and drought rather than a
  spawn timer.

The architecture transfers; the constants do not. That is BL-271's own transfer contract, applied.

### The four questions this design has to answer

**Q1 — Does the player choose the force, or does the contract specify it?**
**The player chooses.** The contract names the *outcome* and the *fee*, never the force. This is the
single decision that keeps the item a strategy game rather than a mission list: the whole skill is
reading whether the fee covers the force the objective actually needs, and a contract that specifies
its own force has pre-solved that.

It also makes underbidding a real failure mode — take a cheap contract, send too little, lose the
fight, lose the fee *and* the standing. That is the loop's teeth.

**Q2 — What happens on failure?**
Three distinct terminal states, deliberately, against BL-350's two:
- **completed** — the predicate held before the deadline. Balance of fee paid, reputation up.
- **failed** — the deadline passed with the predicate false. Deposit forfeit, no balance, reputation
  down *harder* than cancellation. You are not paid for trying.
- **cancelled** — the player withdrew before the deadline. Deposit forfeit, reputation down, but
  less than failure. An honest early exit costs less than a rout.

Failure must be survivable, per CONCEPT.md § Stagnation as loss: there is no lose screen, and losing
a contract is a *progressive* setback. The loss vector is the spiral — reputation falls, fees on
offer fall with it, and the company can no longer afford the force that would win the contracts that
would restore it. That is bankruptcy-by-reputation, and it is the mercenary reading of CONCEPT.md's
two existing loss vectors rather than a third one.

**Q3 — Can the player hold contracts from opposed clients?**
**Yes, and nothing prevents it mechanically — but standing prices it.** Accepting a contract against
a client you also serve is legal, resolves normally, and costs reputation with the injured party on
completion. Making it *illegal* would need a faction-alignment model the game does not have and the
refocus does not want; making it *free* would delete the only interesting thing about being a
mercenary.

This is the one answer here taken on design judgement rather than derived from a shipped mechanism.
It is recorded in NR-177's family as reversible.

**Q4 — Is the contract offer public or private?**
**Private per client, visible to the player only where the activity fog already reaches** — the
existing `body_activity_visibility` tiers (BL-089, DISCOVERY.md). A polity you have never dealt
with and cannot see does not offer you work. This gives the discovery layer a second job for free
and gives reputation a *reach* dimension: standing opens the map, not just the price.

### Serialisation

A **fifth flat-binary stream** after history_log, order_book and procurement, following procurement
exactly: leading magic (`IOMC`) + version, count-prefixed records, rejection rather than
reinterpretation, a `static_assert` on the record size as the tripwire. See procurement.hpp; this
item does not restate the rationale.

The `condition_set` in the record is the one novel serialisation question — it is a structured
predicate, not a scalar. Two options at promotion: store the predicate inline, or store an index
into an authored contract-template table and keep the predicate in Lua. **Recommend the template
index**: it keeps the binary record fixed-size, it makes contract kinds data, and a save that
outlives a template-table change should reject rather than reinterpret, which the version bump
already gives.

### Scope explicitly excluded

The combat that resolves a contract (**BL-315**, conflict spine — this item states what is *at
stake*, never how a fight resolves). Unit materiel draw per tick. Multi-round fee haggling — a
contract is take-it-or-leave-it in this cut, matching BL-350's Q4 exclusion. Contracts between the
player and *another corporation* rather than a polity. Any narrative or dialogue layer.

### Requirement sketch (owed at promotion)

`headless`, a new contract_harness: one contract offered by the objective scorer, accepted, paced
and completed with the fee paid in the split shape; plus one observed instance of **each** of the
three terminal states, and one determinism assertion (same seed, same offers). Written this way
because Sprint 9's `hire_unit` shipped correct and was never observed firing across five seeds
(NR-121), and BL-350's own requirement was written to stop that recurring.

## REOPENED 2026-08-22 — this item was closed in error and was never built

Status was flipped to `complete` by commit `bb4f612`, *"Close BL-377 and BL-378 - two more
landed items still listed as open"*. BL-378 (minimap base render) genuinely had landed. This
item had not, and four independent checks say so:

1. The `files` list names `src/world/contracts.hpp`, `src/world/contracts.cpp` and
   `scripts/contracts.lua`. `git log --all --diff-filter=A` finds **no creation commit** for any
   of the three, on any branch.
2. A grep of `src/` for `BL-377` returns nothing.
3. `corp_verb` carries no contract verb. The design above calls for three appended verbs.
4. `world.hpp` holds `procurement_quotes` and `procurement_contracts` only — BL-350's **buy**
   side. No mercenary contract record exists in `components.hpp`.

`docs/MANUAL.md` § 4.10 independently marks Contracts `[DESIGNED]` and was right throughout.
ROADMAP § The near sequence still names Sprint 16 as *"BL-377 (contract seam) playable
end-to-end"*, and SPRINTS.md § Sprint 16 is open — so the item was closed inside the sprint
that would deliver it.

The design below is unchanged and was never the problem. Found by the phantom-feature scan
(`docs/development/PHANTOMS.md` § Class 0, NR-510).


## RULED 2026-08-22 (Ben, design register)

**Q1 — a fee comes FROM THE BUDGET.** A nation cannot offer what it cannot pay, and offers dry up
when treasuries do. This couples offer generation to BL-537 and preserves NATIONS.md's conservation
rule without an exception.

**Q2 — TEMPLATE INDEX.** The record stays fixed-size, contract kinds stay data, and a save that
outlives a template-table change rejects rather than reinterprets.

**Q3 — RIVALS COMPETE.** *"Losing a bid is a real outcome."* This is a widening: an offer is no
longer addressed to the player, it is **contested**, and the scorer needs a bid. It also removes
the BL-446 defect before it can repeat — a mechanism no AI uses is a mechanism that ships
unexercised.

**Q4 — a LEDGER and the MAP**, and Ben added a third thing neither option named:

> *"Contracts consume resources, I believe we should be able to render moving contracts
> (convoys)."*

So a contract is not only an agreement, it is **materiel in motion**. Its fulfilment draws goods
and those goods move on the logistics network as convoys — which means the contract layer and the
supply layer share a surface, and a player watching a convoy is watching a contract being
delivered. **That couples this item to `docs/economy/LOGISTICS.md` far more tightly than the
original design assumed**, and it is the strongest argument yet that a contract is a *logistics*
object rather than only a financial one.

items.title: Retire the circumplanetary minimap — the inset becomes a fixed max-zoom render of the player's starting base
Corp AI candidate enumeration should use the same placement budget as the seam that applies it
A rival's sell order permanently caps its throughput on that resource, because listing suppresses the auto-surplus path and the order never updates
items.summary: Three separately-reasonable rules compose into a trap. A standing sell order makes clear_markets' auto-surplus path YIELD for that (corp, body, resource); the AI's trade candidate freezes quantity at 0.5 x (pool - 50) as measured on the listing tick; and the anti-duplicate rule blocks any replacement while the scorer never emits remove_sell_order. So a rival that lists once trades that resource through a frozen snapshot forever, having given up the perfect counterparty that cleared its whole surplus.
items.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, found working through NR-137/NR-144.

## The composition

Each rule is defensible alone.

1. `market_clearing.cpp`'s `order_controls` lambda: a (corp, body, resource) carrying a standing sell order is 'under manual control', so the auto-surplus path yields and the floor-priced order governs the sale. Reasonable — an explicit order should not be second-guessed by a greedy auto path.
2. `corp_ai.cpp`'s trade candidate lists `trade_release_fraction x (pool - trade_hold_threshold)` — a quantity measured ON THE LISTING TICK and frozen into the order. Reasonable — metering the release beats emptying the pool into one clearing.
3. The anti-duplicate rule refuses a second order on a triple that already has one, on the grounds that 'the pool is the cap' so a second order would only grow the book. Reasonable — and it is the ONLY anti-thrash rule the trade path has, since a trade command's subject is a body and records no building cooldown.

Together: the corp gives up a counterparty that cleared its entire surplus at the reference price, in exchange for one that clears at most a number sampled once, and it can never revise or withdraw that number because the scorer emits no `remove_sell_order` and nothing expires an order. AI_OPPONENT.md section 2C already warns that 'can trade is not trades well'; the mechanism it anticipated was price-dumping. This is a different and worse one — not a bad price, a permanently throttled pipe.

## What is NOT yet established

How much this actually costs, and it could be little. If a corp's steady-state production on that resource is below the frozen quantity, the order drains it fine and nothing is lost. The harm scales with how far the pool grows past the snapshot, which depends on production rate versus `trade_release_fraction`. MEASURE BEFORE FIXING: instrument a rollout for per-(corp, resource) pool trajectories after a listing, and compare a listed resource against an unlisted one on the same corp. If pools with orders grow monotonically while pools without do not, the trap is real and sized.

## PROPOSED FIX (was: candidate fixes, cheapest first)

**RECOMMENDED — re-list on drift.** Allow a replacement when the pool has grown past the listed quantity by a margin, emitting `remove_sell_order` then `place_sell_order`. Both verbs already exist and are already reachable on the seam, so this is scoring work rather than new mechanism, it stays inside `corp_ai.cpp`, and it needs one new `corp_ai_params` field (the drift margin) so tuning remains a data change. It also gives the scorer its first use of `remove_sell_order`, which is currently emitted by nothing. Guard it with the existing `max_trades` budget so a drifting pool cannot spend every evaluation re-listing.
**Alternative 1 — expire orders.** Give a sell order a lifetime, after which the auto path resumes. Changes save-format state and affects the player's orders too, so it is a design call rather than a tuning one.
**Alternative 2 — cap rather than suppress.** Let the auto-surplus path handle the excess ABOVE the standing order's quantity instead of yielding entirely. Arguably the most honest of the three — the order expresses a floor on price, not a ceiling on trade — but it changes market behaviour for the player as well and wants Ben's call.

## Note on scope

This is a rival-AI problem in practice because the player can see the Market Ledger and withdraw an order by hand. It is filed under AI for that reason, but fix 2 and fix 3 are economy changes and would need MARKETS.md updating.

items.title: Re-point the AI's glut forecast at the resolved price, which is already public, already smoothed, and already means what the gate needs
items.summary: BL-203's predictive spending -- the Victoria-3 import AI_OPPONENT.md calls 'the single most important design import' -- vetoes a build at supply/demand >= 2.0. Measured on a real rollout the gate is NON-DISCRIMINATING and silent exactly where it is needed: roughly 45% of supply-bearing slots carry no demand signal at all, where the function returns 1.0 and applies no penalty, while every slot that does carry one sits at 78-339 and is vetoed outright. The taper band 1.0-2.0 has zero occupancy. The cause is not tuning.
items.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, from the NR-180 investigation. Read the whole brief before touching a threshold.

## What was ruled out

NOT a stock-versus-flow blunder at the field level. `market_component.supply` and `.demand` are zeroed together at the top of every `clear_markets` (market_clearing.cpp, the only reset site in the codebase) and both nominally count units passing through the market this tick. The obvious hypothesis is wrong.

## Why the ratio is still a non-measure, in order of size

**0. A correction to how this was first written, kept because it matters.** The first draft of this item said the gate was 'firing on nonsense' and 'non-functional', and quoted '81% of slots carry supply against demand == 0'. Both were overstated and the figure was mis-derived — 81% is the share of ALL demand facts that are zero; the share of SUPPLY-BEARING slots with no demand is about 45% (5 of 11 in the sampled rival). And glut is not wholly unpenalised even today: resolve_price floors at 0.25x base and the observed slots are pegged there, so oversupply already reaches the AI through the profit estimate. The accurate charge is that the gate is NON-DISCRIMINATING (every demand-bearing slot is past veto, so it cannot rank candidates) and SILENT EXACTLY WHERE NO CONSUMER EXISTS. That is still worth fixing; it is not the same claim.

**1. Supply is unbounded by demand BY CONSTRUCTION.** `clear_markets` makes the market an unconditional buyer of last resort: every listed unit sells at the reference price regardless of what demand says. Meanwhile three of the five demand writers (`inject_population_demand`, `inject_background_demand`, `inject_interbody_demand`) are NOTIONAL — they record appetite and buy nothing. So the two arrays are not two sides of one book, and their ratio is not an excess-supply measure. It cannot be made into one by tuning.

**2. Only 12 of 42 resources have any standing consumer, and no raw ore has one.** The population basket names six goods, the background basket a few more. A glut of iron ore is therefore structurally invisible to this gate — which is precisely the glut a build candidate is most likely to create, since the scorer only ever proposes extraction sites.

**3. The two sides are authored on unrelated scales.** Supply: extraction `base_rate = 20.0` per workforce point, times richness, across every corp's every site. Demand: the POPULATION injector gives a centre at most `scale (<= 5) x weight (<= 0.60) x elasticity (<= 2.50) = 7.5`, and the measured maximum demand fact across a whole world was **8.25** — demand sitting at its structural ceiling rather than at a level the economy chose. (The BACKGROUND injector is different and the first draft misdescribed it: it sums EVERY centre's scale on the body and multiplies that body total by the basket weight, so it is not per-centre-capped. The order-of-magnitude gap survives, since a body carries few centres, but the neat arithmetic match to 8.25 is established for the population side only.)

**4. A vertically-integrated corp's real consumption is invisible.** `run_processing` draws inputs pool-first and records only the market-inventory remainder into `report.purchases`, so the demand a corp genuinely exerts on its own chain never reaches `mc.demand`.

**5. A THIRD saturated consumer, and it is the strongest argument here.** `dispatch_convoys` gates inter-body hauls on `dest_market.demand[r] - dest_market.supply[r] > 0`. With demand three orders below supply that difference is essentially never positive, so the same mismatch SUPPRESSES INTER-BODY CONVOY DISPATCH — not merely an AI gate and a dead injector, but the logistics layer itself. Corroborated independently: data_creep_harness's coverage section reports that `dispatch_convoys` auto-dispatch never fires in a 3000-tick rollout, which had been attributed to the launchpad gate alone.

## The inversion, stated plainly

`if (demand <= 0.0f) return 1.0f;` — 'no public demand signal to forecast against; do not guess.' That reads as humility and is in fact the bug: the slots with no demand signal are the REAL gluts, and they are exactly the ones that get no penalty. The gate fires only where a token signal happens to exist.

## The candidate denominator already exists

`market_component.inventory` (BL-130) is genuinely persistent, genuinely drains against production and construction, and genuinely grows when nothing consumes. **A rising inventory is what a glut actually looks like in this economy.** Re-pointing the forecast at inventory level or inventory TREND is the cheapest change with real meaning behind it.

The alternative is to make demand real — give the offstage economy a consumption model that scales with production rather than with population scale. That is a bigger and more interesting change, and it is an ECONOMY decision rather than an AI one.

## Scope, and what to commit to

(a) **Mechanical, small:** `projected_supply = m.supply[r] + added_rate_per_tick * horizon` compares ONE tick of existing supply against HORIZON ticks of added supply (horizon = build_duration + 1, so roughly 3x). Both should be per-tick. DELIBERATELY NOT FIXED in isolation on 2026-08-13 — see the note below.
(b) **The proposed fix above:** re-point at the resolved price, forecasting the candidate's own contribution through
`resolve_price` rather than by adding raw quantities. Self-contained in `corp_ai.cpp` plus two new `corp_ai_params` fields, so tuning
stays a data change.
(c) **The harness is complicit and must be re-based:** `corp_ai_predictive_harness` asserts the taper band against hand-set fixtures (`demand = 1000, supply = 0` and `demand = 10, supply = 0`) that no generated world can reach. It is green against a shape the game does not produce, which is why this went unnoticed. Any fix must add an assertion driven by the REAL generated world.

## Why (a) was not just fixed

It is a genuine defect and a small edit, and fixing it would move every blessed golden (it changes build scoring, hence world evolution). Paying that cost to correct the numerator of a gate whose denominator is not a constraint buys nothing but a different set of wrong vetoes. Fix it WITH (b), in one re-bless, or not yet.

items.title: One market write only the AI can see, and one demand pull that can never fire
Remove the dormant buy side of the order book, and the unreachable matching pass it alone feeds
items.summary: Resolves NR-125. The buy side is read-but-never-written: no corp_verb authors a buy_order, no UI does, and clear_markets' explicit matching pass therefore iterates an always-empty vector. It is also semantically STALE rather than merely unused -- a matched trade debits the seller's pool and charges the buyer's expenditure but never credits the buyer's pool and never decrements market inventory, so reviving it as-is would take money and deliver nothing.
items.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, from the NR-125 investigation.

## Why remove rather than finish

The buy-side ROLE has already shipped, in a better shape. BL-350's procurement seam is a named-counterparty buy side with quotes, contracts, paced delivery, reputation and four typed declines — and crucially it DOES deliver goods (`pool_for(c.buyer, c.body).quantities[...] += c.quantity`), which is exactly the step the order book's buy path lacks. The 2026-08-12 mercenary refocus (NR-177) makes 'procure force and supply' the player's core loop, and procurement-by-named-supplier is the right shape for that, not an anonymous price-time book.

The dormant code is not neutral. A matched buy would charge `flows[t.buyer].expenditure` and debit the seller's pool without ever crediting the buyer's — under BL-130's real-inventory model that is goods vanishing and money spent for nothing. So this is not 'harmless dead weight we may want later': it is a trap for whoever revives it, and if it is ever wanted it should be re-derived against the inventory model rather than switched back on.

## Cut list

NARROW (~106 lines): `buy_order` + its static_assert (components.hpp); `world::buy_orders` (world.hpp); the buy legs of write/read_order_book (order_book.cpp) and of the world hash (world.cpp); the buy ingestion in clear_markets. Harness fixtures in order_book_harness.cpp and econ_harness.cpp. Header/doc prose.

CASCADE, deletable because nothing else can reach it (~173 lines): `ob_buy_entry` and `matched_trade`; the explicit matching pass including its preferred-seller two-pass and both sorts; matched-trade settlement; the VWAP branch collapsing to a plain `mc.price[r] = ref_price[mid][r]`; `ob_sell_entry::rem` folding back into `qty`.

TOTAL about 280 lines, roughly a third of market_clearing.cpp.

## What survives, untouched

`sell_orders`, both sell verbs, the Market Ledger's sell tab, auto-surplus listing, auto-demand billing, BL-130 real inventory, BL-351's per-order pool reservation, the auto-clear-at-max(ref, floor) path, and price resolution. `clear_markets` reduces to: accumulate supply/demand, resolve price, clear everything at the reference price.

## Acceptance test, and it is a strong one

Every econ_harness expectation EXCEPT the three explicit-matching assertions (BL351.4/.5/.6) must be bit-identical afterwards — because those paths never fired. If anything else moves, the cut removed something live and the diff is wrong. The three matching assertions are retired with the feature.

## Sequencing

Its OWN commit, not folded into anything. Two reasons: the world hash changes (buy_orders is folded into it) and `order_book_version` must go to 2, with `read_order_book` REJECTING v1 rather than reinterpreting a stream whose shape moved. Amend BL-160's design prose with a supersession note.

## One open dependency, stated rather than assumed

Whether the 0 CE product keeps a resource market at all is owed by the refocus items and cannot be answered from source. It cuts the same way though: a market that may not survive the refocus is the last place to invest in a dormant feature.

## THIS ITEM MUST LAND FIRST IN ITS CLUSTER (2026-08-22, hotspot audit)

It removes `buy_orders` from `world::state_hash` (`world.cpp`:174-184), **so every pinned golden
moves when it lands.** Any item in the components.hpp cluster that blesses a golden ahead of it
blesses twice, and the second bless hides whatever the first one actually changed.

Recorded here because the backlog had no way to say it: an ordering constraint with no shared line
of code behind it is invisible to a file-collision map.

items.title: A quarter of generated worlds fight no war at all (was: the Era -1 sim conquers nothing)
items.summary: RESTATED 2026-08-21 ON MEASUREMENT, and the original framing was wrong. The item was filed against a single seed reading '267 battles and ZERO conquests' and read that as a global property. Measured over 8 real 0->1960 runs with tools/verify/history_conquest_gap.cpp: the sim conquers heavily - 1199 conquests over 1226 battles, 43 to 435 per world on six of eight seeds. What is actually broken is narrower and stranger: seeds 0 and 4 fight ZERO battles. Not few. None. The outcome is close to binary - a world is either warlike or perfectly peaceful - and BL-384 was written against one of the peaceful ones.
items.design:
> **RESTATED 2026-08-21.** The original text below the line is kept because its METHOD was right
> and its conclusion was wrong, which is worth having on the record. It said: confirm the mechanism
> before changing a constant, and if the hypothesis fails, 'tuning combat constants would be tuning
> the wrong thing'. That instruction is what stopped this sprint from being spent on the wrong fix.

## What the measurement actually says

`tools/verify/history_conquest_gap.cpp`, 8 worlds, real terrain, real tuning:

| Seed | Battles | Conquests |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | **0** | **0** |
| 1 | 236 | 210 |
| 2 | 435 | 435 |
| 3 | 163 | 163 |
| 4 | **0** | **0** |
| 5 | 164 | 164 |
| 6 | 44 | 43 |
| 7 | 184 | 184 |

**All three candidate mechanisms this item named are refuted by measurement**, not argued away:

1. **The scorer is not systematically optimistic.** Bucketed against realised outcomes it is off by
   **−0.0pp** in the bucket holding 1215 of 1226 battles — calibrated to the measurement's own
   resolution. Terrain defence is live in 488/1226 battles (40%), so this is not the scorer being
   spared a term that rarely fires; it sees the term's absence and is right anyway.
2. **The scored hub and the levying hub never differ** — 0 of 1226.
3. **The transfer bar is not the constraint** — 99.8% of victories convert to a conquest.

> **These are the CORRECTED figures.** The first run of this harness hardcoded a 312×145 grid — the
> homeworld's size before BL-424 took it to 70% area — against a real 261×121. `build_sim_terrain`
> fills an oversized grid with defaults, so anchors outside the real bounds read as flat grassland
> and `region_distance`'s cylinder wrapped at the wrong width. The tell was terrain defence firing in
> only 20% of battles, which read as a finding about the sim and was a finding about the fixture. The
> zero-war result and every refutation survived the correction; two magnitudes moved.

## The real question, which is Ben's and not a tuning decision

**Is a peaceful world a bug?** A world with room left to expand choosing Settle over Campaign is
arguably correct behaviour, and BL-224's non-hegemony invariant positively wants some worlds to stay
multipolar. But 25% of worlds generating an entire era with no war at all is a strange distribution
for a game whose Era −1 premise is a hegemon that rises and falls, and Sprint 30's done-when asks
for a fragmentation rate 'inside a stated band across N seeds'. A quarter of worlds at zero is
either the tail of that band or evidence the band cannot be met.

## Sequencing note

This blocks Sprint 28 as written ('a province changes hands, and a large polity keeps campaigning') —
provinces change hands 1185 times, so half that sprint is already done and the other half is aimed
at the wrong target. Re-scope before building. See NR-474. (A companion claim that BL-321's defence works appear in zero battles was WITHDRAWN the same
day — it was an artifact of the harness passing no works registry, NR-475. The underlying question is
reopened honestly as NR-563.)

---

DESIGNED 2026-08-13, from the tier-triage investigation.

## The observation

The harness run line reads: `82 provinces -> 1755, 267 battles, 0 conquests, 1673 foundings, 0 winter`. Not one province changes hands in 1960 simulated years. Every new province is a Settle. The political map is therefore produced entirely by expansion into empty space, and war contributes nothing to it.

The code's own comment knows this shape: history_sim.cpp records that the pre-BL-308 state was 'centuries of fighting over the same ground moved nothing — battles outnumbered conquests by up to 1000:1', and names the contest_q relief mechanism as the fix. 267:0 is that failure returned, and it is worse than the ratio the comment describes, because it is not a ratio at all.

## Likely mechanism, to be confirmed rather than assumed

The scorer and the resolver appear to disagree systematically in the DEFENDER's favour. The objective scorer estimates the odds of winning from attacker manpower x supply x cohesion against the defender's raw manpower_stock, with **no terrain term at all**. `resolve_battle` then compares a symmetric levy on each side and applies `terrain_defence()` to the defender only. So the scorer picks fights on odds the resolver does not honour, and the defender's terrain advantage is invisible at selection time and decisive at resolution time.

That is a HYPOTHESIS from reading, not a measurement. Confirm it before changing a constant: instrument one run to log, per battle, the scorer's estimated p_win against the realised outcome. If the estimate is systematically optimistic by roughly the terrain factor, the mechanism is established and the fix is to give the scorer the same terrain term the resolver uses. If it is not, the cause is elsewhere and tuning combat constants would be guessing.

## Why this is priority A rather than an Era -1 curiosity

NR-177's refocus rules that history_sim STAYS as the generator, with its stop_year moved from 1960 to ~0 CE, and that the ancient product is built on what it produces. A generator whose war layer cannot move a border produces a world whose borders were drawn entirely by settlement — which is a substantive claim about the generated history, made by accident rather than by design, and one the ancient product would inherit wholesale.

## The harness is complicit, and fixing it is part of this

Six assertions in history_sim_harness are red and NONE of them covers conquest count, so the defect sat under the reds rather than being one of them. Worse, R3b2 ('the far target is never chosen') currently passes VACUOUSLY — the far target is never chosen because NOTHING is ever chosen in its two-polity fixture. Add a conquest-count assertion to the full run, and re-author the R3a/R3a2/R3a3/R3b block against a fixture where a campaign can actually be scored: hand-arithmetic on the current symmetric 1v1 shows the score never clears its threshold, so those four are testing an empty world.

## Separately, R7's premise is stale and should not be carried

R7 asserts a 3000 ms budget for the full run — itself already relaxed from 1000 ms. Measured 67,721 ms in the cloud session and 165,737 ms on Ben's machine (NR-122). A 23-55x overshoot across two different machines is not a tuning miss; the bound describes a sim that no longer exists. Re-measure and re-author it against reality, or drop it and let BL-320 own sim performance — but do not leave a number nobody can plan against.

## PROPOSED FIX, conditional on the measurement above

If the instrumented run confirms the scorer is systematically optimistic by roughly the terrain factor, the fix is to give the SCORER the same terrain term the RESOLVER already applies — i.e. fold `terrain_defence()` into the `def_est` the objective scorer compares against, so a polity stops picking fights whose odds it has mis-estimated. That is a change to one estimate rather than to combat tuning, it leaves `resolve_battle` untouched, and it is the smallest change consistent with the observed symptom.

Two guards on that fix. First, it will make polities campaign LESS, not more, in the short run — they will correctly decline fights they were previously taking and losing — so 'battles went down' is the expected first result and is not a regression. What must go UP is conquests-per-battle. Second, add the conquest-count assertion BEFORE the fix, not after: a fix landed against a harness that cannot see conquests is a fix nobody can verify, and this defect survived four days precisely because no assertion covered the number that matters.

## FINDING 2026-08-19 — hypothesis instrumented and REFUTED

Per the item's own prescribed order (confirm before fix), the scorer's per-campaign p_win_q was
logged against the realised outcome for a full 4000 BCE -> 0 CE run over the real Kepler world
(seed 9001, current main HEAD f384ce5). Result: **the hypothesis does not hold**, because no
campaign is ever launched in the first place — there is no battle for a terrain-blind p_win_q to
lose.

Instrumented counts, one full run:
- 524,800 campaign candidates scored across the run.
- 372,660 of them (71%) cleared the Campaign verb's own threshold (campaign_threshold_q=40),
  mean qualifying score 120.8, max 373.
- 0 of them ever became the polity-year's FINAL best_verb. Final verb tally over the same run:
  settle=1188, invest=12, campaign=0, consolidate/none=0, build_work=0.
- Consequently: 0 campaigns executed, 0 battles, 0 conquests — matching BL384a/b's measured RED.

**The terrain asymmetry the hypothesis named is real** (resolve_battle applies terrain_defence()
to the defender via combat.cpp; the scorer's def_est at history_sim.cpp's campaign-scoring block
carries no terrain term) but it cannot be the cause of a zero-battle run, because the scorer never
reaches battle at all in this run. That asymmetry may still matter once Campaign is reachable
again (B318c's synthetic two-polity fixture, which does not compete against Settle, still shows
conquest > 0), but it is not this defect's proximate cause and should not be fixed as if it were.

**The real, now-established cause: a scorer-magnitude mismatch between two verbs sharing one
comparison axis (BL-309's 'one common currency').** Settle's score is close to a direct fraction
of region_value_q (daughter_value = 0.8 x region_value_q, times a pressure ratio up to 1.0, no
risk discount) — so a polity with population pressure scores it in the 400-800 range essentially
every year. Campaign's score starts from the same kind of region-value term but is then run
through FIVE separate discounts before it competes on the same best_score axis: campaign_gain_q
(0.7x), p_win_q (the odds ratio, often well under 1.0), a distance factor (0.2x-1.0x), a
foreign-culture factor (0.85x when the target is foreign), and two subtractive terms (def_eff,
supply cost). The measured ceiling this produces (max 373, mean-when-qualifying 120.8) sits below
Settle's typical winning score, so Settle wins the comparison in effectively every polity-year —
1188/1200 in the measured run, with Invest taking the rest.

**No fix applied.** This is a different and larger-scoped problem than the item as filed —
rebalancing a four-verb shared-currency scorer (touching campaign_gain_q, the discount chain, or
Settle's own formula) is exactly the kind of tuning the item's own text warns against doing blind
('tuning combat constants would be guessing'). It also risks moving B318c and the R3/R5/B299
assertions that currently pass against synthetic fixtures. Recommend this becomes its own scoped
follow-up (a shared-currency rebalance pass with its own before/after measurement), rather than a
same-session patch on top of this confirmation. Logged to NEEDS_REVIEW.json.

**R7 (harness perf budget) — dropped, not re-measured.** Attempted to re-measure the full-suite
runtime directly (per the item's instruction to re-measure or drop it). Three single-run
timings against the real Kepler world came back internally-timed at ~0 ms of actual sim compute
(steady_clock around run_history_sim, matching R7's own measurement method) but ~90-96s of wall
time with near-zero user/sys CPU each — consistent with this sandboxed Windows environment's
per-exe-launch scan overhead (the same class of issue as the project's own
'io-use-wsl-for-blocked-tooling' / Smart App Control note), not sim cost. The full harness suite
(12+ full-span runs including the 8-seed B384 outcome sweep) could not be walltime-measured
cleanly in this session — every attempt was killed by the sandbox's own background-task duration
cap before finishing. Rather than author a number from a confounded measurement, R7's fixed
budget is dropped in favour of BL-320 (Era -1 sim performance) owning this, per the item's own
stated fallback.

items.title: The blackboard exports a price with no reference value, so an agent cannot tell cheap from dear
items.summary: export_corp_blackboard emits price, supply and demand per (market, resource) but not base_price. A price of 3.2 is therefore uninterpretable to an out-of-process agent: it cannot tell whether that is a glut, a shortage, or ordinary. Found while checking BL-381's own premise -- the in-process scorer has base_price in hand and an external policy does not, so the two cannot reason alike.
items.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, found checking whether BL-381's proposed fix was computable by the audience it is meant to serve.

## The gap

`export_corp_blackboard`'s market section emits three facts per priced resource: `price`, `supply`, `demand`. It skips any resource whose `base_price` is zero (correctly — an untraded good has no public quote) and then never emits the base price it just tested.

So an agent reads `price:steel = 3.2` and has no way to know whether steel is cheap, dear or ordinary. Every price-based judgement an external policy might make — is this glutted, is this worth producing, is this a good moment to sell — needs a reference, and the reference is present in the market component and withheld from the export.

It is worse than a missing convenience: the two aggregates that ARE exported, supply and demand, are exactly the pair BL-381 establishes cannot be divided meaningfully. So the blackboard currently gives an agent two numbers it should not use and withholds the one it should.

## Not a visibility question

Worth stating so it is not re-litigated: `base_price` is a rarity-derived property of the market and the resource, not of any corporation. Exporting it reveals nothing about a rival, so BL-068 is not engaged. This is an omission, not a policy.

## The fix

Emit `base_price:<r>` alongside the existing three, with `public_market` provenance, in the same loop that already reads it. Two lines. Bump the blackboard `_v` and re-bless `blackboard_harness`'s fact counts, which is the only real cost.

## Do it with BL-381, not before

Landing this alone adds facts to every export for no consumer. Landing it WITH BL-381 means the scorer's new price-based gate and an external policy's view of the same decision are computed from the same public numbers — which is the property that makes the AI's reasoning reproducible from outside, and the one AI_OPPONENT.md section 6 claims for the export in the first place.

items.title: A sell order's floor price is paid in full by nobody — unbounded money printing, and it is what tripled the AI's net worth
apply_corp_command never checks that the caller may act AS the corporation it names, and BLACKBOARD never checks which corp it may read
The build verb silently discards its recipe argument — every processor built through the seam is a steel smelter
--serve never loads world_gen.lua, so the AI seam plays a materially different economy than the GUI
items.summary: run_serve loads recipes.lua and economy.lua and never constructs a world_gen_config, so make_hard_coded_world falls back to built-in defaults. Only 16 of 42 resources carry a price on any market; coal, silica, copper ore, rare earths and the rest are unpriced and unbuyable. Every conclusion drawn from the seam is a conclusion about a different game.
items.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, found by AI play.

## The defect

`run_serve` loads `scripts/recipes.lua` and `scripts/economy.lua`. It never builds a `world_gen_config` from `scripts/world_gen.lua`, so world generation falls back to its built-in defaults. A player enumerated every `price:<r>` fact across all four markets and found 16 of 42 resources priced. Missing: coal, silica, copper ore, rare-earth ore, iron-nickel ore, platinum-group metals, and the rest.

## Why it is the most quietly expensive of today's findings

Every other defect found by play is a defect in the game. This one means **the seam is not playing the game**. Any measurement taken through `--serve` — the trace corpus BL-279 wants, a skill benchmark, an agent's learned policy — describes a world the player never sees. It also silently explains the processing dead end: steel's coal reagent has no price and no stock, so a steel smelter cannot run, which is every processor the seam builds (BL-388).

`--export-blackboard` shares `run_serve`'s setup and inherits the same divergence, so BL-206's exports have the same problem.

## PROPOSED FIX

Factor the world setup that `app::setup_world` performs into one function and call it from all three entry points — the GUI, `--serve` and `--export-blackboard`. The duplication is the bug: three call sites each assembling the world slightly differently is how one of them came to skip a config file. This session already collapsed the same shape once inside `run_serve` (the tick sequence was duplicated between the warm-up loop and the TICK opcode, which is how `advance_surveys` came to be missing from both).

Add an assertion that the served world prices the same resource set as the GUI world — a count comparison is enough and it would have caught this immediately.

## Independently verified 2026-08-13

Triaged as a real defect at high confidence. The triage pins the three call sites exactly: only `app.cpp` loads `scripts/world_gen.lua`, builds a `world_gen_config` and passes it to `make_hard_coded_world`; `run_serve` and `run_blackboard_export` both call the no-config overload. The market template reads `gen_cfg.kepler_base_price`, so under `--serve` markets open with the built-in defaults instead of the authored table — which is the whole divergence in one line.

items.title: The seam mints ids and prices it never discloses, and exports no state for orders, quotes, contracts or units — a player cannot see what it has done
items.summary: Three players independently hit the same wall. place_sell_order and request_quote allocate ids and return `building=0`; request_quote also withholds the PRICE, which is the one thing a quote exists to communicate. No opcode and no blackboard predicate lists a corp's own orders, quotes, contracts, units or reputation. One player recovered an order id by sweeping 600 values; another counted commands for forty turns, miscounted once, and silently corrupted every id afterwards.
items.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, from three independent play sessions that each stalled on it.

## The write channel answers, and then forgets

`apply_corp_command`'s out-param is written by exactly two verbs: `build` and `hire_unit`. `place_sell_order`, `request_quote` and `accept_quote` all allocate ids and return `building=0`. Yet `remove_sell_order`, `accept_quote` and `cancel_contract` all REQUIRE those ids. The seam hands out handles through a channel it does not have.

Observed consequences, all from real sessions: one player swept `order=1..600` reading rejection codes to locate their own order. Another derived ids from `next_procurement_id` by reading the source, counted `applied` results for forty commands, forgot one, and every id after that was silently wrong — `rejected_invalid` cannot distinguish 'wrong id' from 'already gone'.

## And request_quote withholds the price

This is the sharpest instance. A quote's entire purpose is to communicate a price and a lead time so a buyer can COMPARE. The response is `RESULT result=applied building=0`. A player swept 26 suppliers, got 20 willing on iron ore, and had no way to tell them apart; they accepted arbitrarily and learned the price afterwards by differencing their cash balance. 'Sweep suppliers, compare, accept the best' is not expressible.

## The read channel has no vocabulary for any of it

`export_corp_blackboard`'s predicates are cash, building_type/tile/recipe/workforce/decommissioned, pool, price, supply, demand, rival_building_*, tile_deposit, body_activity, route, survey. There is NO predicate for sell orders, buy orders, quotes, contracts, reputation or units. A corp cannot see its own commitments.

Three further gaps in the same vocabulary, each independently reported: a corp cannot see its own extraction sites' TARGET RESOURCE (so it cannot tell what it produces — one player reverse-engineered it from tile deposits); pools are emitted only when non-zero, and auto-sell drains them every tick, so a player sees no inventory ever; and 66,995 tile_deposit facts carry no body, no coordinate and no terrain, so they can be ranked but not located.

## PROPOSED FIX, in two halves

**Half 1, cheap and immediate — return what you mint.** Widen the RESULT line beyond `building=`: report the allocated id for `place_sell_order` / `request_quote` / `accept_quote`, and report `unit_price` and `lead_time_ticks` for `request_quote`. The out-param is already threaded; this is a wider response record, not new mechanism. It removes the brute-force sweep and makes quotes comparable.

**Half 2 — give the blackboard a self-state section.** Own orders, quotes, contracts (with ticks_elapsed), units, reputation, and the extraction target on own buildings, all `own_asset` provenance. This is strictly a corp reading ITS OWN state, so BL-068 is not engaged. Emit pools unconditionally including zeroes, since 'I have none' is information and its absence is currently indistinguishable from 'not exported'. Bump the schema version and re-bless blackboard_harness.

Fold BL-385 (the missing reference price) in here if both land together — it is the same defect one aisle over.

items.title: Falling below the procurement reputation floor is permanent — the only way to raise reputation requires a contract you can no longer get
items.summary: Reputation rises only via reputation_on_complete, which fires when a contract completes. A contract requires accept_quote, which requires a quote, which request_quote refuses below the reputation floor. So a corp that cancels its way past the floor with one supplier is blacklisted by that supplier forever, with no mechanic anywhere that can undo it.
items.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, found by a player who cancelled contracts until a supplier refused them and then looked for the way back.

## The deadlock

There are exactly two writers to `w.corp_reputation`: `+reputation_on_complete` when a contract completes, and `reputation_on_cancel` (negative) when one is cancelled. `request_quote` refuses below `reputation_floor`.

So the recovery path from below the floor runs: raise reputation -> complete a contract -> accept a quote -> obtain a quote -> be above the floor. It is a cycle with no entry. The player measured it at reputation -6 against a floor of -5 and found no mechanic anywhere that could move it back up.

## Why it is a design fault rather than harsh balance

A permanent, unrecoverable, per-counterparty blacklist earned by an ordinary in-game action is not a difficulty setting; it is a state the player cannot reason about, because nothing tells them the floor exists until they hit it and nothing tells them it is final. It is also invisible: no blackboard predicate exports reputation (BL-390), so a corp cannot see its standing with anyone either before or after.

The mercenary refocus (NR-177) makes this worse rather than academic — BL-377's contract loop is built on exactly this reputation axis, and a loss-spiral that cannot be exited is a much bigger problem for a company whose whole livelihood is being hired.

## PROPOSED FIX — decay toward neutral

Reputation drifts back toward 0 by a small amount per tick, so a burned relationship heals with time rather than never. That is one line in the tick, it needs no new verb, it makes the floor a TEMPORARY consequence with a natural duration, and it gives 'wait' a legitimate strategic use. Author the rate in economy.lua so it is a data change.

Alternatives, both worse: a reparations verb (new mechanism, and a player below the floor has no way to learn it exists), or flooring reputation at the refusal threshold so it can never go below (removes the consequence rather than bounding it).

Whichever is chosen, the floor and the current standing must be VISIBLE — pair this with BL-390's blackboard section, or the player is still reasoning about a number they cannot see.

## REPOINTED 2026-08-22 — the fix is now a property of the substrate, not a patch on procurement

This item proposed decay toward neutral, and Ben's NR-520 ruling makes that the **substrate's own
behaviour** rather than a line added to the procurement tick. Under BL-545, reputation is a view of
a continuous derived quantity that decays; **a quantity that decays has no permanent floor by
construction.**

So the deadlock does not need fixing here — it stops existing when BL-546 lands the migration. Land
this item **through** BL-546 rather than beside it, and keep this item's two demands, which the
substrate does not supply on its own:

1. **The floor and the current standing must be VISIBLE** (pair with BL-390's blackboard section).
   A player reasoning about a number they cannot see is the defect's other half, and decay does not
   touch it.
2. **The decay rate needs a reason.** *How long should a burned relationship take to heal?* is a
   question a player can answer, and it deserves the treatment BL-543 gave value — an anchor, not
   a guess.

## RULED 2026-08-22 — decay is anchored, and the factor list widens

Ben's answer to the decay question (design register, RELATIONS Q3) chose **an anchor rather than a
number**, and widened it to the factor list — see BL-545. This item's two remaining demands are
unchanged and neither is supplied by the substrate: the floor and current standing must be
**visible** (pair with BL-390), and the rate needs a **reason**.

## RE-VERSIONED 2026-08-22 — v0.1.15 → v0.1.24, and this inversion was created THIS SESSION

The sentiment ruling (Ben, NR-520) made this item `require` **BL-546**, which is **v0.1.24** — so
a v0.1.15 item was left waiting on a v0.1.24 one. The dependency is right and the version goal was
the thing that had to move.

**Why the dependency rather than the version is right.** This item's fix — decay toward neutral —
is no longer a line added to the procurement tick; it is a **property of the substrate**. A quantity
that decays has no permanent floor by construction, so implementing it separately at v0.1.15 would
be building the same behaviour twice and then deleting one of them.

**The cost, stated rather than buried:** this is a **priority-A live defect** — a player measured
reputation −6 against a floor of −5 with no mechanic anywhere that could move it back — and it now
ships two minors later than it did this morning. If that is the wrong trade, the alternative is to
land decay standalone at v0.1.15 and migrate it in BL-546, which is the double-build this ruling
was meant to avoid. **Ben's call, and it is recorded rather than assumed.**

---

The seam's response says `building=` for units and orders, and returns rejected_invalid for failures that need different fixes
items.summary: Every COMMAND answers `building=<n>`, but a hire returns a UNIT id there and a sell order returns 0 (a valid entity id, not an absence). Separately, rejected_invalid covers four distinct causes on place_sell_order, three on hire_unit, and on the order= verbs cannot distinguish 'never existed' from 'already gone' from 'that id is a quote not a contract'. Every player independently reported navigating by trial and error as a result.
items.design:
DESIGNED 2026-08-13, from four play sessions that each hit it.

## Two faults in the same channel

**The out-param is untyped.** `RESULT ... building=<n>` is the whole return surface. A `hire_unit` puts a UNIT entity id in that field; `place_sell_order` and `request_quote` put nothing and it reads 0, which is a syntactically valid entity id rather than a recognisable absence. An agent parsing this cannot tell what kind of thing it just made, or whether it made one.

**The rejection is under-resolved.** `rejected_invalid` covers, on `place_sell_order` alone: no such body, that body has no market, that market does not price the resource, and malformed quantity/floor. On `hire_unit`: bad roster index, row not currently available, and non-existent tile — three different fixes, one code. On `accept_quote`/`cancel_contract`: the id never existed, the id names the other kind of record, and the contract completed and was erased.

That last one is the worst in practice. A player's id bookkeeping drifted by one, and the seam could not tell them the difference between 'wrong id' and 'already finished' — which are opposite situations calling for opposite responses.

## Why it matters more here than in a UI

AI_OPPONENT.md section 10a names typed, enumerated failure as the property that lets an out-of-process policy correct itself. A UI can render four different messages from one code because a human reads the surrounding screen; an agent has only the code. This session already fixed one instance of exactly this (the four BL-350 declines collapsed into rejected_invalid) and these are the remainder.

## PROPOSED FIX

* Replace `building=` with a typed pair — `result=applied kind=unit id=34912` / `kind=order id=42` / `kind=none` — so the response says what it made. This changes the wire format, so bump whatever the protocol's version marker becomes and update smoke.js and the dictionary together.
* Split `rejected_invalid` where the causes call for different responses. `rejected_no_market`, `rejected_unpriced`, `rejected_not_found` and `rejected_unavailable` would cover every case reported above, and `corp_command_result` is append-only so adding them is safe.
* Fold in the three smaller legibility findings while in here: `survey` accepts and CHARGES FOR the star (three players hit it; `dispatch_survey` never checks `body_type::star`), `set_workforce` is accepted on a military base that staffs at zero by design, and `request_quote`'s `subject` is accepted and never read.

items.summary: Split out of BL-315 (conflict spine) on Ben's 2026-08-13 ruling. BL-315 owns how force reaches an outcome; this owns what the company is ANSWERABLE TO while using it. The same law classes the militia framing named - embargo, basing rights, conscription - but with the direction of agency inverted: terms the company is subject to and must route around, not instruments it wields.
items.design:
## Why it is its own item

It was BL-315's third strand, and it was blocking a buildable item behind an unbuilt one:
at 0 CE there is no live law system to be subject to. Splitting it lets the conflict spine
be built now, and lets answerability arrive when there is law for it to read.

## What it owns

The terms an armed trading house operates under, and the consequence of breaking them.
The direction of agency is the whole point - an embargo is something procurement must be
routed around, basing rights are granted rather than granted BY, a levy applies TO the
company's recruitment pool.

It is also where BL-315's identity ruling cashes out. Ben, 2026-08-13: the same company
reads as army, mercenary or pirate depending on policy - so the reading is a function of
whose terms it operates under, and which it has broken. That derivation belongs here, not
in the conflict spine.

## Design owed

Which law classes bind a company rather than a nation; what a breach costs (standing?
contract access? interdiction?); and whether the army/mercenary/pirate reading is
per-polity (one nation's privateer is another's pirate) or global. The per-polity reading
is the richer one and is probably right, but it is not settled.

Spectator god view - lift the survey mask, the activity fog and the rival-internals redaction, in the UI layer only
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-14. A spectator currently sees LESS than the AI it is watching. The planetary canvas is survey-masked (survey_tile_visible, body_surface_canvas.cpp), the comms feed is deliberately redacted to one nation-level aggregate event per tick (session_history.cpp, honouring the BL-068 competitor-visibility rule), and selecting a rival corp yields name / nation / starting capital / asset count and nothing else (entity_summary.cpp draw_corporation_summary). Spectator mode needs a god view that lifts all three - and needs to lift them WITHOUT touching world/* or the blackboard export, because those are what keep the AI honest. [LANDED 2026-08-19 @ merge 57e596f, awaiting R1's live click-through (needs a spectate entry path — the toggle is spectate-only by construction). 7 captures eyeballed; off-path byte-identity by construction + determinism harnesses green. Comms-redaction lift deliberately deferred (post-time store, needs read-time-filter design — DISCOVERY.md carries the note).]
items.design:
## The rule this breaks, and why that is legitimate

DISCOVERY.md's competitor-visibility rule (BL-068) and the two fogs exist to make the
player earn information. **In spectator mode there is no player** (BL-409), so there is
nobody being cheated. The rule protects a competitive relationship that spectating does
not instantiate.

That argument only holds if the lift is **strictly presentational**. The hard line:

- **May change:** what `src/ui/*` draws and what the comms feed prints.
- **May NOT change:** `world/*` state, `survey_tile_visible`, the activity-fog store, or
  `export_corp_blackboard`. The blackboard's whole value is that it is visibility-honest
  (corp_ai.hpp: rival buildings existence/type/tile ONLY, never cash, pools, recipes or
  workforce). A god view that reached into the export would silently give a future agent
  player telepathy, and STRATEGIES.md § Resolutions already settled that question - Ben,
  2026-08-06: *"No additional information for the AI."*

So the flag is read at the draw call, never at the source. Enforce it by construction:
the spectator flag lives in `ui_state`, and `world/*` never sees it.

## The three lifts

1. **Survey mask.** `body_surface_canvas.cpp` gates per-tile detail on
   `survey_tile_visible(body.survey, ...)`. Under spectate, treat every region as
   revealed. The `UNSURVEYED` / `Surveying n/m` header suffix stays - it is now
   *information about the AI's own blindness*, which is exactly what a spectator wants to
   read, and it becomes far more interesting once you can see what it is missing.
2. **Comms redaction.** `post_nation_agency_comms` posts one nation-voiced line per nation
   per tick, the heaviest event only, by design. Under spectate, post per-corp and
   unthrottled. Keep the nation voice as an option rather than deleting it - the redacted
   feed is the one a player will ship with, so it must stay exercised.
3. **Rival internals.** `draw_corporation_summary` gains the full readout under spectate:
   cash, per-body pools, running recipes, workforce targets, reserve floor, and the
   should-have buffer. All of it is already computable from public functions
   (`corp_reserve_floor`, `corp_should_have_buffer`, `estimate_building_profit`).

## The tell to design for

When the mask is lifted, a spectator should still be able to see **where the AI's own
fog is**. A build the scorer never considered because the tile was unsurveyed is one of
the most legible strategy signals in the game, and it is invisible if god view simply
erases the distinction. Render revealed-but-unsurveyed tiles with a marker rather than
as ordinary revealed ground.

## Obligations

DISCOVERY.md gains a section on the spectator exemption when this lands (not before -
the authority doc time-slices). `question_log.json` entries for the changed surfaces.

items.title: Spectator mode has no human seat - every corp is scored, and player_entity becomes a viewpoint rather than an ownership claim
Attention director - follow the tick's heaviest decision, and jump to any decision from the feed
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-14. Nothing moves the camera on its own, so a spectator stares at one body while the interesting build happens two bodies away. Two affordances: click a decision-feed row to select its subject and navigate the zoom ladder to it, and an opt-in auto-follow that each econ tick moves to that tick's heaviest decision. The severity ordering already exists - session_history.cpp's severity_of ranks idled/demolished (4) above built/hired (3) above recipe_switch/resumed (2) above road/workforce/survey/order traffic (1).
items.design:
## Two modes, one mechanism

**Jump-to (manual).** A decision-feed row knows its `corp_decision.command`, which
carries the target entity. Clicking it sets `selected_entity` and drives the zoom
ladder to the owning body - the same descend-by-click path CANVASES.md already
defines, invoked programmatically rather than by a press.

**Auto-follow (opt-in, off by default).** Each econ tick, pick the heaviest decision
by the existing `severity_of` ordering, break ties by lowest corp id (determinism),
and navigate there. Reuse `severity_of` rather than authoring a second ranking - a
second ordering that disagrees with the comms feed's would be a bug generator.

## The pacing problem, which is the real design work

At speed 5 an econ tick resolves every ~11 real seconds (16x multiplier, 2 s/day at
1x, 90-day quarter). Auto-follow that snaps the camera every 11 seconds is unwatchable,
and at lower speeds it is dead air. Three things make it read:

1. **Ease, never snap.** Route through `interp.cpp`, over roughly a second. The
   transition is what tells the eye *where it went*, which is most of the value.
2. **Hold a minimum dwell.** Never retarget within ~4 real seconds of the last move,
   even if a heavier decision lands. A camera that twitches shows nothing.
3. **Ignore the noise floor.** Do not follow severity-1 traffic (roads, workforce
   nudges, order-book churn) at all. Follow builds, demolitions, idles and hires -
   the decisions that change the industrial landscape.

## Determinism

The director is presentation and must not touch the sim. Camera state lives in
`ui_state`; nothing in `world/*` learns that it exists.

## Obligations

CANVASES.md gains the programmatic-navigation note when this lands. `question_log.json`
for the follow toggle; `ACTIONS.json` for the new controls.

> ⟳ 2026-08-19: FIRST TASK (verdict O4): the spectate initial viewpoint fix folds in here — spectate currently inherits the would-be player corp, which on seed 0 is insolvent and asset-less (NR-231). Opening camera = heaviest-decision corp of the first evaluated tick, a natural special case of auto-follow.

items.title: Emergent-strategy readout - per-corp run summary of verb mix, spend by priority bucket, and reason-code tally
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-14. The literal answer to the question that prompted the spectator session - Ben, 2026-08-14: watch AI play "and discover what strategies emerge from the current game", to have "a better way to describe and explain our main aims". The decision feed (BL-407) shows the moves; this shows the SHAPE across a run. Aggregates the same two stores into a per-corp profile: verb mix, spend split across the must-have / should-have / nice-to-have buckets (corp_ai.hpp bucket_for_reason), reason-code tally, and how those shift over the run. [LANDED 2026-08-19 @ merge d3d9e6e, awaiting R1's live click (nav slot 12). Recorder-pattern aggregation (O(new decisions)/tick), 64-quarter window, counts-not-credits, score fields excluded per the NR-226 fence; 3 captures eyeballed; question_log pair drafted.]
items.design:
## What a strategy looks like in this engine

The scorer has no strategy object - `corp_strategy` is a direct read of
`industrial_focus`, kept as its own name precisely so it can diverge later
(corp_ai.hpp). So an emergent strategy is not a thing to read out of a field; it is a
**distribution over decisions**. Three distributions carry almost all of it:

1. **Verb mix.** What fraction of this corp's decisions were builds, dials, surveys,
   roads, hires, orders. An expander and a consolidator have visibly different mixes.
2. **Spend by priority bucket.** `bucket_for_reason` already classifies every reason
   into must-have (solvency defence) / should-have (feed the running assets) /
   nice-to-have (expansion). A corp spending most of its run in must-have is drowning;
   one that stays in nice-to-have is running unopposed. This is the single most
   legible health signal available, and it is free - the mapping is a pure function
   that already exists.
3. **Reason-code tally.** Which reasons actually fired. § 10h's idle/resume
   oscillation would have shown here as two reciprocal codes dominating the tally.

## Over the run, not just at the end

Each quarter, plot the bucket split as a stacked band per corp. The interesting
artifact is the *transition* - the quarter a corp falls out of nice-to-have and never
recovers is the quarter it lost, and being able to point at that quarter is exactly
the "describe and explain our main aims" the session asked for. Use `charts.cpp` and
the existing per-tick history recorder pattern in `session_history.cpp` rather than a
new store.

## Feeds two things beyond spectating

- **STRATEGIES.md's invention loop.** The deck is AI-invented and the schema authored
  (Ben, 2026-08-06), and a card earns its slot by same-seed comparison. This readout is
  the measuring instrument that comparison needs; without it "the card worked" is an
  assertion.
- **BL-279 (trace corpus).** The same aggregation labels a run, which is what a
  fine-tuning corpus needs alongside the traces.

## Honesty constraint

Report the distribution; do not name the strategy. A label like "aggressive expander"
rendered from three thresholds is a fiction the reader will trust more than it earns,
and naming it would also pre-empt STRATEGIES.md's settled position that the deck is
discovered rather than authored. Show the mix and let the shape speak.

> ⟳ 2026-08-19: FENCE (NR-226 / verdict O1): decision-ring score fields are EXCLUDED from aggregation — runner_up can legitimately exceed winning_score because candidate_before sorts by priority bucket before score (AI_OPPONENT.md § 10i). If margins are ever wanted, normalise within priority bucket first. The readout aggregates verb mix, spend buckets and reason codes only, as designed.

items.title: Live agent control seam - let an external agent play a rendered session, not just a headless one
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-14. --serve (BL-278) is headless-only: main.cpp branches to the line-protocol server INSTEAD of app::run, so an agent playing through the MCP seam is invisible while it plays. Spectating the deterministic scorer (BL-407 to BL-411) and spectating a language model are therefore different jobs, and this is the second one. Deliberately filed as its own item so the first five do not silently acquire its cost. [LANDED 2026-08-19 @ merge e88636b, awaiting R3's canvas-eyeball half (Ben; app left open with --host-agent). Everything else green: 22/22 harness incl. transcript-replay determinism over a real socket; R4 listen-only confirmed by verifier-review; the actor gate ALSO proven live when the first watch session read as the wrong corp and was refused. First watch session ran this date: qwen2.5:3b-instruct attached, ticks released 1..8 through the gated clock.]
items.design:
## The structural gap

`main.cpp` dispatches on argv: `--serve` runs the line-protocol loop, `--verify` runs
the headless capture harness, `--autostart` runs the GUI. They are exclusive branches.
The seam an agent drives and the loop that draws pixels never coexist, so the only way
to observe an agent's play today is to read a transcript after the fact.

## Shape

The honest version is: `app::run`'s frame loop gains a non-blocking drain of pending
protocol requests, serviced at a tick boundary rather than mid-frame. Requests apply
through `apply_corp_command` - the same seam the presses and the scorer already use, so
no third code path appears. `ADVANCE_TICK` under a live session means *release the clock
for one econ tick*, which is a different contract from the headless one and is the part
that needs designing rather than coding.

## The three real problems

1. **Clock ownership.** Headless, the agent drives the clock. Live, the wall clock does.
   Either the agent gates the clock (and the session stalls whenever the model is
   thinking - honest, and probably right for watching) or the clock free-runs (and the
   agent plays a moving target). Pick deliberately; do not let it fall out of the
   implementation.
2. **Determinism.** A wall-clock-paced session where commands land on whichever tick
   they happen to arrive is **not replayable**, which forfeits the property AI_OPPONENT.md
   § 10h leans on hardest (*"a play transcript is a replay artifact"*). Applying commands
   only at tick boundaries, in arrival order, recorded, preserves it. This is the reason
   to gate the clock.
3. **Transport.** stdio is taken by the app's own console. Needs a socket, and the
   engine still ships no HTTP client, no API key, no cloud dependency - the hard
   invariant of AI_OPPONENT.md § 10. A local socket the agent connects TO is inside
   that line; anything the engine dials out to is not.

## Relation to the rest

Composes with BL-407 (the feed shows the agent's moves alongside the scorer's) and
BL-408 (god view). It does NOT need BL-409 - an agent playing a corp is the opposite
of the no-seat mode; the seat is occupied, just not by a human. Both configurations
should be reachable.

## Research use, not the shipped rival

The § 10g ruling stands: the deterministic scorer remains the action generator for the
shipped rival. This is the research and diagnostics seam § 10h argues already pays.

items.title: resource_type name lookup is hand-implemented three times with no check that they agree, and it has already caused one startup crash
Plain `ctest` still runs the harnesses labelled `sweep` and documented as excluded from the routine gate - a label excludes nothing on its own
