The build candidate score is quadratic in net margin - `net / payback` collapses to net squared over capex, and the tuning was calibrated against that curve without anyone deciding it should be there
items.summary: Filed from NR-230 (2026-08-14 housekeeping), found by running the new AI decision feed against real data. corp_ai.cpp computes `payback = capex / net` then scores `net / payback`, which is algebraically `net^2 / capex` - reads as capital efficiency, behaves as a margin bias (doubling margin quadruples the score; doubling cost only halves it). Real 144-tick runs score in the ~1.2 billion range. focus_weight/jitter/glut were tuned against this curve, so changing it silently retunes every rival's build behaviour and every blessed golden.
items.design:
Two steps, deliberately not one commit. (1) Rewrite the expression to say what it does - `c.score = (net * net / capex) * ...` - a no-op refactor, zero behavioural change, that stops the code lying to the next reader. (2) Separately and deliberately, decide whether the quadratic bias is wanted: keep it and comment why, or replace it with an explicit linear metric and re-tune the multipliers against the new curve (accepting the golden reshuffle that follows). Do not do (2) as a drive-by inside (1).

> ⟳ 2026-08-19 (N1 audit): HELD, not open. Step 1 landed+verified at 56bcb86 (score = net²/capex, corp_ai.cpp:694-713); req group quadratic-build-score-honest R1–R4 complete, R5 pending. Step 2 is Ben's call (NR-265 re-scope, NR-268) and should sequence AFTER BL-439's golden re-bless. Consider splitting step 2 to its own item at next triage.
items.step_1_landed:
Landed 2026-08-17, Sprint 19 — THE HONEST REWRITE ONLY. corp_ai.cpp's extraction build candidate now scores `(net * net / capex) * focus_weight * jitter * glut` directly; the intermediate `payback = capex / net` is gone. A comment states the quadratic bias, why it is retained (focus_weight/jitter/glut were tuned against this curve, and every blessed golden records a world evolved under it), and that replacing it is step 2.

THE "ZERO BEHAVIOURAL CHANGE" CLAIM IN THIS ITEM'S DESIGN WAS NOT ESTABLISHED WHEN IT WAS WRITTEN. `net / (capex / net)` and `(net * net) / capex` round differently in float, so the rewrite could have moved every candidate score, hence world evolution, hence every blessed golden — which would have made step 1 exactly the thing the item says it is not. Measured rather than assumed, A/B on the pinned MSVC 14.44 build against this branch's base: ai_skill_harness byte-identical across all 5 seeds (ALL PASS, 0 failures, both sides); spectator_determinism byte-identical, played=855E07DE529684EC / spectated=5AC90B4ACE717FCF unchanged. It IS free on this toolchain — by rounding luck, not by algebra. Had it moved, the golden re-bless would have been part of step 1 and reported as such rather than smuggled in. Recorded as NR-268. Full local CTest logic tier green — the gate the remote session could not run at all.

Corrected in passing: the military_base candidate's comment claimed it must never out-bid "a genuine extraction/processing net-positive candidate". There is no processing_facility build candidate in this scorer at all — see BL-439.

items.title: Chain depth is the growth track — how far down the production graph a corp can reach is what gates its next building
The building roster is 7 types and half of them are space-era — the ancient arc needs 20+ buildings that consume the resources it already has
items.summary: RULING 2026-08-15 (Ben): take the roster past 20 building types, as a content sprint of its own. Measured today: scripts/economy.lua carries SEVEN building_type entries (extraction_site, processing_facility, port, launchpad, inland_logistics_hub, military_base, research_institute) and scripts/recipes.lua carries 17 recipes, one per output. Named buildings like the Hydroponics Bay and Fishing Wharf are not types at all - they are the generic processing_facility distinguished by recipe and placement rule, which is the pattern the expansion should follow rather than minting enum values.
items.design:
FILED 2026-08-15 from Ben's sprint-planning ruling ("20+ types, content sprint of its own").

## What is actually there today

  * building_type entries in `economy.lua` : 7
  * recipes in `recipes.lua`               : 17, one per output, no alternates
  * of the 7 types, LAUNCHPAD is space-era and the refinery chain runs on PETROLEUM

The arc is the ancient product at 0 CE (NR-177). A roster expansion that adds to the current
set without confronting that would double the space-era debt inside the live product - see
BL-433, filed alongside this, which owns the misplacement question.

## The pattern to follow, and the one to avoid

BL-166/BL-168 established it and `economy.lua` records it: the Hydroponics Bay and the Fishing
Wharf are the SAME `processing_facility` / `extraction_site` types as everything else,
distinguished by recipe and by placement rule, not by a new enum value. That is how a roster
reaches 20+ named buildings without a 20-value enum, without touching the serialised width,
and without a glyph explosion.

**Mint a new `building_type` only where BL-325's test is met** - it earns the enum value with a
distinct placement rule AND a distinct glyph AND behaviour no recipe can express. The
military_base passed that test. A tannery does not.

## What the roster should cover, against the resources that already exist

The enum already holds the ancient substrate: stone, timber, sand, clay, peat, charcoal,
iron_blooms, grain, fodder, salt, bullion, plus the endemic four (tobacco, spices, coffee,
furs). Most are BL-286 orphans - in the enum, unconsumed by any recipe, several unpriced in
`world_gen.lua`. The roster's job is to give every one of them a consumer, which is BL-340's
admission rule applied to the ancient tier:

  * **Extraction** - quarry (stone), clay pit, sand pit, woodcutter (timber), peat cutting,
    salt pan, grain farm, pasture (fodder), mine (iron ore, copper ore)
  * **Primary processing** - charcoal burner (timber -> charcoal), bloomery (iron ore +
    charcoal -> iron_blooms), kiln (clay -> ceramics), glassworks (sand -> glass),
    sawmill (timber -> timber goods), mill (grain -> flour/rations)
  * **Secondary** - smithy (blooms -> tools/arms), tannery, weaver, potter, shipwright,
    stonemason
  * **Terminal / mercantile** - mint (bullion), warehouse, market stall

That is comfortably past 20 named buildings on ~3 building_type values. Exact list, recipes
and magnitudes are the sprint's content work; the ADMISSION RULE is the invariant - no
building whose output nothing consumes, no resource no building consumes.

## Depth, and how this item relates to BL-428

Every entry above declares its minimum chain depth (BL-428). The roster IS the depth ladder
made concrete: quarry at depth 0, bloomery at 1, smithy at 2, and so on. Build the ladder and
the roster in the same pass or the numbers will not agree.

## UI consequence, which is half the work

20+ buildings will not fit the Build door's current shape, and ICONS.md gains a glyph per
named building. Both are in scope: a roster the player cannot browse is not content, it is a
data file. Its question_log entry must be written with it (BL-260).

## SLICE 1 LANDED 2026-08-15 — the chains, not yet the named buildings

What landed: the ancient production chains and the prices that make them tradeable. What did NOT:
the named building identities (quarry, woodcutter, kiln, smithy...), their placement rules and
glyphs, and a Build door that can present 20+ entries. Requirements `ancient-chain-roster` R1-R4
complete, R5-R6 pending.

**The measurement that justified doing it this way round.** Before this slice the ancient arc's max
chain depth was **1** — one layer above raws and nothing beyond. Named buildings on top of a flat
economy would have been 20 ways to do the same shallow thing. Depth first, identities second.

**The load-bearing edit was a RETAG, not the five additions.** Tagging the coal-fired `steel` recipe
`industrial` is what gave the ancient arc depth. With the shallow coal route still available (coal is
a raw), BL-428's min-across-recipes rule correctly collapsed steel back to depth 1 — the new chain
would have existed and meant nothing. Ancient max depth went 1 -> 3 on exactly that change. Worth
remembering as a general shape: adding a deep chain does not deepen an economy while a shallow route
to the same good remains open.

**A trap this slice created and closed in the same pass.** Three call sites defaulted an
unconfigured processing facility to `recipe_id("steel")`. That still RESOLVES after the retag — the
storage path is band-independent by design (BL-433) — so an ancient campaign would have silently
seeded its processors with an industrial recipe, and nothing would have refused it, because the era
gates browsing and placement rather than execution. Now `default_recipe_id()`. The general rule, and
it is worth stating because the next author will hit it: **ask the registry for a sensible default;
do not name a recipe and hope.**

**A latent defect found on the way** (NR-237): `resource_from_name` was missing eight BL-286 enum
values despite its own comment claiming full-enum coverage, so any recipe naming one threw at load.
Invisible until now because BL-286 shipped those goods with their behaviours "unfiled", so nothing
ever authored against them.

**Still orphaned**, and recorded rather than glossed: `sand` and `peat` are priced by this slice but
consumed by nothing. BL-432 is where that becomes a mechanical assertion.

## SLICE 2 LANDED 2026-08-15 — named identities, sand/peat closed, peat_cutting gap fixed

Built: a `recipe::display_name` field (recipe_registry.hpp/.cpp), authored for the five slice-1
ancient recipes (Charcoal Burner, Bloomery, Smithy, Potter & Weaver, Miller) and shown by both the
Build door (selection_panel.cpp) and the live-building method selector (construction_panel.cpp) in
place of the raw recipe key / the old "Processing: X" prefix. An `extraction_building_name()` lookup
does the same for extraction rows (Quarry/stone, Woodcutter's Camp/timber, Sand Pit, Clay Pit, Peat
Cutting, Iron/Copper Mine, Water Extractor, Coal Mine, Oil Field, Silica Quarry, Rare-Earth Mine),
plus Farm vs Fishing Wharf now read as distinct names rather than sharing one "Extraction:
Agricultural Produce" label. `display_name` defaults to a title-cased recipe name when unauthored, so
every recipe (industrial included) has a legible label with nothing new to author.

**R6 closed**: sand and peat, "still orphaned" per slice 1, now each have a consumer — Glassworks
(sand -> trade_goods_misc) and Peat Kiln (peat -> charcoal), recipes 22/23. Both are a second producer
of an existing output from a different raw, the same multi-producer shape `steel` already has
(coal-smelter / iron-nickel / bloomery), not BL-430's alternate-method feature.

**A real pre-existing gap found and fixed on the way**: `placement_rules::k_extractable` never
listed `resource_type::peat`, despite tile_generation.cpp authoring peat deposits on wetland tiles —
no extraction_site could ever have targeted it. Fixed by adding it to the array; `buildings_rework_harness`'s R1 (`n >= 15`) still holds at 16.

**Ancient-band Build-door count**: with the additions, an ancient campaign on a resource-rich tile
can show up to ~9 named extraction rows + 9 named processing rows (2 any-era + 7 ancient recipes) +
4 infrastructure rows (Port/Hub/Military Base/Research Institute, all any-era) — comfortably past the
R5 threshold of 20+.

**Deliberately NOT done this slice, and recorded rather than glossed** (the remainder of R5):
**per-building glyphs.** Icons still render per `building_type` (`icons::building` switches on
`extraction_site`/`processing_facility`/...), so every named extraction building shares one ore-chunk
glyph and every named processing building shares one square — exactly how Farm/Smelter/Hydroponics
Bay already render today, not a regression. Giving 16 ancient buildings each a silhouette-distinct
hand-drawn glyph (ICONS.md's own "Adding a new glyph" process, one at a time) is real asset-authoring
work this slice did not attempt; a follow-on item should own it explicitly rather than R5 quietly
passing without it. See NEEDS_REVIEW.json for the decision record.

**Also recorded**: this slice's C++ changes (recipe_registry.hpp/.cpp, placement_rules.hpp,
selection_panel.cpp, construction_panel.cpp) were authored and manually re-reviewed but NOT
compiled — the remote session's network policy denies `codeload.github.com` (SDL3/sol2/ImGui
FetchContent sources), a 403 confirmed as an organization policy denial, not a transient fault. Lua
changes (recipes.lua) were syntax-checked with `luac5.4 -p` and pass. A compile + the existing
headless/visual harnesses are owed at the next session with real toolchain network access.

## SLICE 3 LANDED 2026-08-15 — R5's glyph clause closed (NR-239)

`icons::building()` gained a fourth parameter, `resource_type identity`: an extraction
site's target resource, or a processing facility's PRIMARY OUTPUT (the new shared
`primary_output_resource()`, moved from construction_panel.cpp into recipe_registry.hpp so
every UI file draws the same identity). 14 new hand-drawn glyphs cover the 9 extraction +
5 processing resource keys the ancient roster reaches — Quarry, Woodcutter's Camp, Sand Pit,
Clay Pit, Peat Cutting, Iron Mine, Copper Mine, Water Extractor, Farm/Fishing Wharf, and (for
processing) the charcoal-kiln, bloomery, ingot, goods-bundle and ration-pack shapes. Two or
more named buildings reaching the same resource share one glyph BY DESIGN (documented in
ICONS.md § 1c): the glyph says what a building makes, not which recipe, so Charcoal Burner/
Peat Kiln (both -> charcoal) and Potter & Weaver/Glassworks (both -> trade_goods_misc) read
the same — exactly as two Iron Mines on different tiles already share a glyph.

All four `icons::building()` call sites updated: the Build door (selection_panel.cpp), the
Buildings-tab identity plate (construction_panel.cpp), the on-canvas marker
(body_surface_canvas.cpp — the target/recipe lookup was hoisted OUT of the wrap-copy k-loop,
since the pre-existing under_construction pattern it was modelled on only resolves at k==0
and would have shown the wrong glyph on every wrap copy of a non-default-resource building),
and the placement ghost preview (extraction-only — armed placement mode carries no recipe
field to key a processing ghost on).

requirements.json's `ancient-chain-roster` group is now ALL SIX rows complete (R1-R6).
BL-429's own status stays `designed` rather than flipping to `complete`, deliberately: see
NR-241 below.

**Not done, and this is the real caveat on all of the above (NR-240, NR-241).** None of this
was ever compiled or rendered. This session ran remote with `codeload.github.com` blocked
(SDL3/sol2/ImGui FetchContent sources — confirmed an organization policy denial), so
`icons.cpp`'s 14 new vertex lists were hand-checked for angular ordering (a simple perimeter,
not self-intersecting) but never actually seen on screen. "Silhouette distinct" is reasoned
by shape family, not verified the way ICONS.md's own process asks for ("a glance should
disambiguate"). The next session with a real GUI build owes: compile, open the Build door on
an ancient-band tile, the Buildings tab, and a built ancient building on the Planetary canvas
— fix proportions on sight, then promote BL-429 to `complete`.

> ⟳ 2026-08-19 (N1 audit): HELD on verification only — all six req rows complete (e822070, 6e563fa, 45a7886), no code owed. The hold is "never compiled, never seen" (NR-240/NR-241), a remote-session constraint that no longer exists on this machine. items.title: A building has a recipe, not a choice of one — alternate production methods with real trade-offs
items.summary: RULING 2026-08-15 (Ben): yes, alternates with real trade-offs - not tier upgrades. Today recipes.lua is one recipe per output and a building stores a single recipe id, so choosing a building IS choosing its method. An alternate is a different input basket for the same output, each honestly better under different conditions (local abundance, chain depth, wage cost, throughput), so the player is choosing rather than upgrading.
items.design:
FILED 2026-08-15 from Ben's sprint-planning ruling ("yes, alternates with real trade-offs" -
chosen over "only as tier upgrades" and over keeping one recipe per output).

## The distinction the ruling turns on

A **tier upgrade** is strictly better and therefore not a decision - it is a delay. An
**alternate** must be genuinely better under some conditions and worse under others, or the
player will find the dominant one once and never look again. That is the design bar, and it
is testable: if any alternate dominates its sibling on every axis, it is a tier, not a method,
and the pair should be re-authored or merged.

## The trade-off axes available today

Real ones the engine already has, so no new machinery is needed to make the choice bite:

  * **Input basket** - charcoal vs peat vs coal as smelting fuel: what is locally abundant
    differs by body and region, so the same method is not best everywhere.
  * **Labour intensity** - `base_wage` and workforce against `base_rate`: a hand method is
    cheap to build and dear to run; a water-powered one inverts that.
  * **Chain depth** - a deeper method needs a good you may not reach yet (BL-428), so the
    shallow method stays correct early and stays available late.
  * **Throughput vs yield** - batches per tick against output per batch.

## Shape

`recipes.lua` entries gain a `produces` / method grouping so several recipes can declare the
same output and be presented as siblings. The recipe id stays the 0-based index and ORDER
MUST STAY STABLE - authored ids are stored in `building_component.recipe` and a reorder would
silently repoint every existing building. Append new methods; never insert.

Switching method on a running building is the existing recipe-switch path (BL-079's reflex
already switches a floored recipe), so the mechanism exists - what is new is that the choice
becomes the player's, with a cost or a cooldown to switch so it is a commitment rather than a
per-tick optimisation. That cost is a first-cut constant in `economy.lua`, tuned by playtest.

## Guard

A headless harness assertion that no method DOMINATES a sibling on every axis
(inputs cost, wage, rate, depth) - the mechanical form of the design bar above. It will need
a price snapshot to compare input baskets, so it belongs next to the existing economy harness.

## Interaction with the AI

`corp_ai.cpp` scores build/demolish/survey/road/hire. Method choice is a NEW decision surface
and the scorer will pick badly by default (it has no notion of local abundance). Either the
alternates are scored - a small, deterministic addition in the same scored-utility layer - or
background corps are pinned to the shallow method explicitly. Pinning silently is the failure
mode: it would make every rival look strategically identical. Decide at promotion; either way
it is a stated call, not a default.

items.title: The production choice and the chain that leads to it have no surface — method selector, chain trace, and the depth readout
items.summary: The UI half of the economy-breadth sprint. Three surfaces the player needs the moment BL-429 and BL-430 land: a production-method selector on the building panel (with the trade-off legible at the point of choice, not after), a chain trace answering "what do I need to make this", and a depth readout answering "how far down the graph have I actually got". Without these the content is invisible: 20+ buildings and a choice of method are a data file the player cannot see.
items.design:
FILED 2026-08-15 with the economy-breadth sprint. This is the "pad out the UI" half of
Ben's ask, applied to the economy side; BL-393's unit surfaces are its military twin.

## Three questions, three surfaces (BL-260 discipline - each declares the question it answers)

1. **"Which way should this building make its output?"** - a method selector on the Selection
   panel's building view. Shows each alternate's input basket, wage and rate SIDE BY SIDE, so
   the trade-off (BL-430) is legible at the point of choice. A selector that shows only names
   pushes the player to a wiki. Switching cost shown before committing, like the Build door
   shows a credit total.
2. **"What do I need in order to make this?"** - a chain trace from any good back to its raws,
   reachable from the good itself (resource pip, market row, recipe line). Read off the same
   registry graph BL-428 computes depth from, so it cannot disagree with the simulation.
3. **"How far down the graph have I actually got?"** - the depth readout: the corp's reached
   depth, what the next depth would open, and what is missing to get there. This is the growth
   track made visible, and without it chain depth is an invisible gate that reads as a bug.

## Constraints

The Selection panel is already dense; the method selector must not push the workforce dial or
profitability off screen. Rule 0b applies at build time - state the current measurements
before reshaping the panel, and open the live app before asking Ben to judge the layout.

Toggle rule applies to any ledger slot this earns.

## Owed alongside the code

  * `docs/ui/question_log.json` entries for all three surfaces, written WITH them, not after.
  * `docs/ai/ACTIONS.json` - method switching is a new control and therefore a new dictionary
    entry. Transcribed from the seam verb once it exists (BL-270 discipline), never authored
    ahead of it.
  * A user story per surface in `user_stories.json`: the intent axis has nothing on "choose how
    I produce" today.

items.title: The live ancient product still ships a Launchpad and a petroleum refinery — the roster contradicts the arc
processing_facility does the job of every kind of processing — split it into recognisable sub-facility groups
One harness for the roster invariants — no orphan resources, no unplaceable buildings, no dominant method, no cyclic graph
Let the player choose their starting corporation, instead of being assigned one by the seed
A processing facility earns less than the extraction site it replaces — the whole refining chain is a net income loss
items.summary: Measured 2026-08-16 while landing BL-435: swapping ONE extraction site for ONE processing facility on the same corp, same seed, halves its balance (55,179 -> 28,288 cr), and the same swap across the generated economy moves ai_skill_harness's five seeds by -71/-37/-9/-20/-38% on final net worth. Refining is supposed to be the value-add step the whole economy is built around; today it is a way to earn less. Filed as its own item on Ben's call so BL-435 is not blocked by an economy rebalance.
items.design:
FILED 2026-08-16 (Ben's call on NR-260, option B), out of BL-435's generation fix.

## The measurement, and why it is trustworthy

This is an unusually clean natural experiment, which is why it is worth acting on
rather than filing as a hunch. BL-435 moved the processor in `focus_asset_pattern`
from a slot the holdings draw rarely reached to one it always reaches. Nothing
else changed: same seeds, same tiles, same corps, same recipes, same prices. The
ONLY difference is that some corps now open with 2 extraction + 1 processing where
they previously opened with 3 extraction + 0 processing.

  * Player corp, seed 0: 55,178.8 -> 28,288.2 cr after 12 warm ticks. Halved.
  * ai_skill_harness final net worth, all five seeds, 30-tick rollouts:
      seed 0  181,559 -> 51,950   (-71%)
      seed 1  110,289 -> 69,804   (-37%)
      seed 2  173,754 -> 157,314  ( -9%)
      seed 3  621,950 -> 500,635  (-20%)
      seed 4  205,193 -> 126,637  (-38%)

Every seed moved the same direction. A single-building swap is not supposed to be
worth 20-70% of an economy.

## Why this is a design problem and not just a number

RESOURCES.md's whole tier model says margin WIDENS up the tiers - Tier 3 promises
the "widest price divergence", and BL-340 priced the chain that way on purpose
(spacecraft_components at 56x iron ore). PRODUCTION.md's processing chain is the
value-add step the trade pillar rests on. If a mine outearns the refinery fed by
it, then:

  * the chain-depth growth track (BL-428) asks the player to climb a ladder that
    costs money at every rung;
  * BL-430's alternate methods are a choice between ways of losing income;
  * BL-435's selection screen would present a corp with a processor as the better
    opening while it is in fact the poorer one;
  * and `corp_ai`'s build scorer is being asked to prefer processors on a payback
    curve that does not reward them (read alongside BL-417, which already flags
    the score as quadratic in net margin).

## What is NOT yet known, and should be measured before tuning

The cause is unidentified and there are at least four candidates. Measure first -
the standing lesson from Sprint 11 and Sprint 18 is that the plausible story loses
to the measurement about half the time:

  1. **Input cost vs output price.** Steel at 8.0 against 2 iron ore (2.5) + 1 coal
     (2.0) = 7.0 is a margin of 1.0 per unit, ~14%. An extraction site sells its
     raw output with no input cost at all. Check the whole recipe table this way -
     `chain_depth`'s R2 row already computes input-basket cost and could report it.
  2. **Wages and maintenance.** BL-049 split these; a processing facility may
     simply carry a heavier fixed cost per unit of output than a mine.
  3. **Market depth.** A processor must BUY its inputs from a market that may not
     carry them, so it idles or runs starved while a mine always has its deposit.
     If so the defect is availability, not price, and the fix is different.
  4. **Throughput.** Rates may differ enough that per-tick output value diverges
     regardless of per-unit margin.

## Done when

A processing facility fed by its own inputs earns MORE than the extraction site it
replaced, over a representative rollout - or there is a written, deliberate reason
why it should not, propagated into PRODUCTION.md. Either outcome closes it; the
current state, where the arrangement is accidental and undocumented, does not.

Guarded by a headless row so it cannot regress silently: the natural home is
`econ_harness` or a new margin-by-tier check, asserting the tier ordering the docs
already promise.
items.measurement:
MEASURED 2026-08-16 by the new tools/verify/tier_margin.cpp (3 seeds x 20 ticks, real generated world, real Lua economy, reading estimate_building_profit - the same per-building breakdown the Profitability page shows a player). Per building-tick, mean:
  extraction_site      revenue 1954.62  input 0.00   maint 5.84  wage 1.28  NET +1947.50  earning 85%
  processing_facility  revenue    4.62  input 14.18  maint 7.53  wage 1.08  NET   -18.18  earning 22%
Extraction out-earns processing ~107x on net, and processing is outright LOSS-MAKING: capex payback is 0 ticks against NEVER.

THE CAUSE IS NOT PRICING, and that rules out the item's first candidate. It is a structural asymmetry in how the two rates are computed (economy_system.cpp):
  extraction: base_rate 20 x RICHNESS x workforce x (1 - hazard)
  processing: base_rate 8 x workforce                     <- no comparable multiplier exists
components.hpp documents resource_deposit as 'deposit richness (the extraction rate multiplier)' and tile_generation rolls it at 20-50, so an extraction site produces on the order of 780 units/tick while a processor makes 8 batches. The revenue gap is 423x; the per-unit recipe margin (steel 8.0 against inputs 7.0, ~14%) is almost irrelevant beside it.

SECOND CAUSE, independent and additive: a processor produces NOTHING on 78% of its building-ticks (earning 22% vs extraction's 85%) while still paying wages and maintenance. That is the item's market-depth candidate confirmed - it cannot buy its inputs - and it means even a rate fix alone would leave most processors idle.

So of the four candidates filed: throughput (4) is the dominant cause but at a STRUCTURAL level rather than a tuning one; market depth (3) is a real and separate contributor; input-cost-vs-price (1) and wages/maintenance (2) are both rounding errors at this magnitude - fixed costs are ~8.6/tick against a 1947/tick gap.
items.starvation_measurement:
MEASURED 2026-08-16 (Ben's call: measure the starvation before choosing a rate fix). tier_margin R3 classifies every processing building-tick by the reason the ECONOMY ITSELF recorded in building_report, rather than by inference. Over 3 seeds x 20 ticks, 1279 processing building-ticks:
  produced output           38.9%
  STARVED (input missing)   34.9%
  no recipe set             11.3%
  idle, no reason recorded  14.9%
  unstaffed                  0.0%

So 'processors do nothing 78% of the time' decomposes into THREE independent problems, not one, and only the first is the market-depth cause the item guessed:
  1. STARVATION, 34.9% - the largest. Binding input when starved is dominated by COAL (resource id 1) at 38.5% of starved ticks, far ahead of silica 11.6%, rare_earth_ore 10.7% and ree_alloy 10.7%. Coal is a raw with deposits and a price; it is the steel recipe's reagent, and steel is the era-aware DEFAULT recipe, so most processors want coal and cannot get it. Worth checking whether anything actually mines coal at scale before assuming a market-routing fault.
  2. NO RECIPE SET, 11.3% - a straight defect, and these buildings can never produce while still paying wages and maintenance. app::load_economy assigns a default to every unconfigured processor, but it runs BEFORE generate_background_firms, so processors created by the background-firm pass that its own gap-relief chooser did not assign a recipe to are left at no_recipe permanently. Likely a cheap fix with a disproportionate effect.
  3. IDLE, NO REASON RECORDED, 14.9% - unexplained. Not starved, not unstaffed, has a recipe. Needs its own look; the report has no field that explains these.

METHOD NOTE, because it inverted the answer once. Measuring WITHOUT load_economy's default-recipe pass reports no-recipe at 26.5% and starvation at 20.9% - i.e. it reverses which cause is largest. That pass is a real startup stage, not a harness convenience (recipe ids are registry indices that do not exist at generation time), and it runs before background firms. tier_margin now performs it by default and documents why; the opt-out remains only to isolate how much the pass is carrying.
items.rate_fix_progress:
RATE ASYMMETRY FIXED 2026-08-16 (Ben's call). Framed as a RESTORATION, not a rebalance: building_economics::base_rate has always documented itself as 'units/tick AT RICHNESS 1', while tile_component::resource_deposit is generated as a QUANTITY (measured mean 53.3, max 72,321) and was multiplied in raw. Mine effective rate ~1067 against a processor's flat 8 - a 133:1 structural gap (tier_margin R6).

Richness is now divided by a measured reference and clamped to a band, all three authored in scripts/economy.lua (richness_reference 53.3, min 0.25, max 2.0). A reference of 0 disables the conversion and restores raw behaviour, so an un-migrated economy.lua is unchanged. The design statement behind the clamp: richness decides how LONG a deposit lasts, not how fast you can pull it out - reserve still scales with raw richness, so a rich tile is still worth far more over its life.

Applied at ALL FOUR sites that compute a rate from richness, via one shared free function (richness_rate_scalar) so a preview cannot drift from the tick: extraction_nominal (the live tick), the BL-181 workforce solver, building_profit's expected-output estimate (shown on the Build door), and corp_ai's build-candidate revenue estimate (which gates on net <= 0, so a raw richness had the scorer expecting ~50x the revenue a site delivers).

RESULT: extraction revenue 1942.80 -> 11.07/tick, net 1935.85 -> 4.75, capex payback 0 ticks -> 21. Extraction is a real business rather than a money fountain, and the two tiers are finally the same order of magnitude. Processing is still -19.95/tick, so R2 still FAILS - but what remains is a genuine balance question at comparable scale rather than a structural absurdity, which is what this step was for.

CRITICAL CAVEAT ON THE GREEN SUITE, and it must not be read as safety: ai_skill_harness and spectator_determinism both PASSED unchanged, and that is because they HAND-BUILD their recipe registry and never load scripts/economy.lua. richness_reference therefore defaults to 0.0 in both, the conversion is disabled, and they measured the OLD rate model. Their goldens are vacuous with respect to this change - exactly the hand-built-fixture trap the verifier-headless skill documents (BL-404 is the precedent). The AI's real behaviour under the new rates is UNMEASURED.
items.harness_gap_closed:
HARNESS GAP CLOSED 2026-08-16 (Ben's call: close it before playtesting), AND IT IMMEDIATELY FOUND WHAT IT WAS HIDING.

ai_skill_harness and spectator_determinism hand-build a recipe_registry that CLAIMS to mirror scripts/economy.lua. It had fallen out of date: neither set richness_reference, so it defaulted to 0, the BL-436 conversion was disabled, and both harnesses measured the PRE-BL-436 rate model while reporting ALL PASS. The three fields are now mirrored in both, with a comment saying why leaving them unset is not a harmless omission.

WITH THE MIRROR RESTORED, THE AI ECONOMY COLLAPSES. Final net worth across the five benchmark seeds, previously all positive:
  seed 0  +51,950 -> -22,787   solvency 10/30 -> 18/30 below zero, survival 0.86 -> 0.71
  seed 1  +69,804 ->  -8,282   solvency  0/30 -> 12/30,             survival 0.86 -> 0.43
  seed 2 +157,314 -> -56,070   solvency  5/30 -> 20/30,             survival 1.00
  seed 3 +500,635 -> -75,806   solvency  0/30 -> 24/30,             survival 0.71
  seed 4 +126,637 ->  -6,194   solvency  7/30 -> 11/30,             survival 0.57
17 assertions fail. Every rival corporation goes insolvent.

WHAT THIS MEANS. The rate fix is directionally right - it removed a 133:1 structural absurdity - but the CALIBRATION is wrong, and the reason is now obvious in hindsight: the entire cost side of the economy (maintenance 5, wage 8, build_cost 100, starting capital) was tuned against extraction earning ~1947/tick, where costs were effectively free. Cutting extraction income ~410x to 4.75/tick leaves costs dominating everything, so no corp can fund its own operation.

The band cannot fix this on its own: with richness_max 2.0 the best possible site earns ~22/tick revenue, so raising the reference or widening the band only moves a ceiling that is already far below the cost base. The levers that actually reach it are extraction base_rate, the maintenance/wage/build_cost scale, or starting capital - i.e. a deliberate re-tune of the cost side to match the corrected income side. THAT IS A DESIGN DECISION AND IS BEN'S; nothing is being tuned on his behalf.

GOLDENS DELIBERATELY NOT RE-BLESSED. Blessing a set of numbers in which every AI corporation is bankrupt would record economic collapse as the expected state. They stay red until the calibration is settled.

This is the whole argument for closing a harness gap before playtesting: the previous run of this same harness reported ALL PASS on exactly this code.
items.calibration_sweep:
CALIBRATION ATTEMPTED AND NOT SETTLED 2026-08-16 (Ben's call: settle it before playtesting). The conversion is LANDED BUT DISABLED - scripts/economy.lua sets richness_reference = 0.0, which is the documented off switch; set it to 53.3 to enable. Everything else about the fix is in place.

THE SWEEP. Hypothesis: normalising richness fixed the 133:1 RATIO but also cut absolute SCALE ~53x, and the cost side (maintenance 5, wage 8, build_cost 100, starting capital) was tuned against the old inflated income - so restore scale by multiplying BOTH producer base_rates together, holding the 2.5:1 ratio. Measured at three points (tier_margin, per building-tick):

  scale   extraction net   processing net   processing earning%   AI net worth (5 seeds)
  x1      +4.75            -19.95           18%                   all 5 bankrupt, -6k to -76k
  x4      +27.95           -61.86            4%                   4 of 5 bankrupt, to -250k
  x10     +75.25           -58.16            4%                   (not run; x4 already worse)

THE HYPOTHESIS IS WRONG AND THE SWEEP KILLED IT. Scale is not the lever. Raising extraction income makes the collapse WORSE, not better, because corps spend the extra income building processors that lose MORE per tick at higher scale - and processing's 'earning' share FALLS from 18% to 4% as scale rises, because scaling multiplies a processor's input demand against a supply that does not scale with it. Seeds 1 and 3 reach -225k and -250k at x4 against -8k and -76k at x1.

WHAT THAT LEAVES. The AI collapse is driven by PROCESSING LOSSES, not by extraction income, so the calibration cannot be settled by any number on the extraction side. The open half of BL-436 is therefore processing profitability itself, and it has two identified components already measured: (a) starvation - processors earn on 18% of ticks at best, and BL-437's co-extraction only lifted coal to ~98 units/tick against roughly 5x that in demand; (b) the per-batch margin against fixed costs - steel clears 1.0/batch at 8 batches/tick = 8 gross against 22 in maintenance + wages, so steel processing loses ~14/tick EVEN AT 100% UPTIME. (b) is arithmetic and can be settled without a sweep; (a) needs supply work.

LEFT DISABLED RATHER THAN HALF-TUNED so the tree is green and playable: with the conversion off, ai_skill_harness and every other golden pass unchanged. tier_margin still fails R2 and R4 by design - those two rows ARE the open work.
items.harness_price_gap:
MEASUREMENT INSTRUMENT WAS WRONG, CORRECTED 2026-08-16. Going after the processing margin, R7 (authored base_price vs live market price) showed only 14 resources priced in any market - COAL among the missing - which read as 'processors starve because coal has no market'. That was the HARNESS, not the game: tier_margin loaded recipes.lua and economy.lua but NOT world_gen.lua, which carries the market base_price table, so markets fell back to world_gen_config.hpp's built-in defaults. This is exactly BL-389's defect (--serve never loads world_gen.lua either), reproduced by omission in a brand-new harness written to diagnose the economy. A harness that loads two of the three economy scripts measures an economy the game never runs. Fixed: world_gen.lua is loaded and world_gen_config.cpp linked; 36 resources now price.

THE CORRECTED NUMBERS MOVE MATERIALLY, so earlier figures on this item should be read as suspect wherever they involve prices or input cost:
                       broken harness   corrected
  processing net       -19.95           -9.32
  processing earning    18%              50%
  starved               34.9%            30.1%
  no recipe set         11.1%             9.4%

WHAT THE CORRECTED MEASUREMENT SAYS. Processing revenue 12.84 against input cost 13.15 - a GROSS margin of about -0.31 per building-tick, i.e. the recipes are roughly value-NEUTRAL at live prices before a single fixed cost. Maintenance 7.85 and wages 1.16 then carry it to -9.32. So both halves are real and neither alone explains it: the chain adds no value at market prices, AND fixed costs are unfunded. Note this is measured with the richness conversion DISABLED (the calibration is still open), so extraction still reads 1695/tick.

NOT FIXED. The margin work stopped here deliberately rather than tuning on top of numbers that had just moved under it.

items.title: Eight raw resources with deposits are mined by NOTHING - a site takes only the richest deposit on its tile, and iron ore always wins
A mine now yields a basket and every UI surface still shows one resource - and one of them multiplies the basket by the wrong price
items.summary: BL-437 made an extraction site work every deposit on its tile, but every UI surface still reads only building_component::target_resource - entity_summary's 'Target:', hover_content's 'Extracting:', the corporation dashboard and the selection panel all name one resource for a building that now produces several. Worse, body_surface_canvas.cpp:1239 values a site as output_quantity x price[target_resource]: since BL-437 output_quantity is the WHOLE BASKET while the price is the primary's, so the on-canvas value figure is now arithmetically wrong whenever a tile carries more than one deposit.
items.design:
FILED 2026-08-16 during the Sprint 19 playtest, from reading the surfaces rather than
from playing them - the gap is unambiguous in the code.

## Two problems, one cause

BL-437 changed what an extraction site DOES without changing what any surface SAYS.

1. **Presentation.** Four surfaces name exactly one resource for a site that now
   produces a basket: `entity_summary.cpp:173` ("Target: %s"), `hover_content.cpp:116`
   ("Extracting: %s"), `corporation_dashboard.cpp:28`, `selection_panel.cpp:1543`.
   A player watching coal accumulate with no building anywhere claiming to mine coal
   has no way to understand their own economy.

2. **A REAL ARITHMETIC BUG**, and it is the urgent half. `body_surface_canvas.cpp:1239`:
       value = br.output_quantity * price[br.target_resource]
   `output_quantity` is the sum over every deposit worked (economy_system.cpp's
   co-extraction block sets it to `produced_total`), while the price is the PRIMARY's.
   On a tile whose secondary deposits are worth more or less than its primary, this
   figure is simply wrong, and it was correct before BL-437.

## What it needs

`building_report` carries one `target_resource` and one total, so the per-resource
breakdown is not currently recoverable by any reader - the same limitation that made
tier_margin misreport coal as unmined (it had to switch to measuring reserve depletion
instead). The honest fix is for the report to carry the basket, which then serves the
valuation AND every presentation surface from one source.

Smaller alternative if that is too heavy: value the site by summing over the tile's
deposits at their own prices, and have the surfaces render the tile's worked deposits
rather than the stored primary. That fixes the output without touching the report, at
the cost of each reader re-deriving the split.

## Note

The presentation half is BL-437's own follow-on and was foreseeable when it landed;
the valuation bug was not noticed and is a genuine regression introduced by it.

items.title: The AI build scorer cannot build a processing facility - it enumerates extraction sites and one military base, and nothing else, so no rival can ever climb the production chain
items.summary: Found 2026-08-17 while verifying BL-417 (AI build score is quadratic). corp_ai.cpp emits corp_verb::build from exactly two places: the ranked_sites loop, hard-coded to building_type::extraction_site, and the single military_base candidate. There is no processing_facility build candidate anywhere in the scorer. The seam is fine - corp_command.cpp handles a build command naming a processor, recipe and all (BL-388), so a player or an MCP agent can build one; the deterministic scorer simply never asks. A rival corp therefore only ever owns the processors it was GENERATED with, for the whole campaign.
items.design:
Add a processing_facility build candidate to run_corp_strategic_step's enumeration, scored on the same curve as the extraction candidate and subject to the same solvency, glut and reserve-floor gates. Three things the extraction candidate does not have to solve, and this one does: (a) SITING - a processor is not sited by a deposit, so the ranked_sites list gives no candidate tiles; it needs its own siting rule (near the corp's own input supply / near a market / within logistics reach of both). (b) RECIPE CHOICE - the command must name one (corp_command rejects a recipe that does not match the type, and construct_building silently substitutes steel for no_recipe, which is exactly the trap BL-388 closed); recipe_margin already exists in this file and is the natural scorer. (c) INPUT ACCESS - a processor with no reachable input is an immediate loss-maker, and the BL-203 should-have buffer already prices feeding running processors, so the candidate must be gated on the corp being able to source its recipe's inputs at all.

This is NOT a tuning change and must not be folded into one. It changes which buildings exist in every evolved world, so it reshuffles every blessed golden and every ai_skill_harness band - that reshuffle is the item's cost, paid once, deliberately, and re-blessed as part of landing it. Guard: extend ai_skill_harness with an assertion that at least one rival corp builds at least one processing_facility over the run, which today would fail by construction.

> ⟳ 2026-08-19 (N1 audit): HELD on task C only (golden re-bless, Ben's NR-269 pick). A/B/D landed at debfa87 — corp_ai.cpp:736-905 processing candidate + ai_skill_harness guard; req R6 failed = the bands FELL and blessing would record bankruptcy as expected. Sequencing insight from the audit: BL-443's interest finding (98.8% of deficit) means landing the debt lever first may make C's bands legible without tuning. Order: BL-443 → re-run → C.
items.consequences_for_shipped_claims:
Three shipped claims are wrong because of this, corrected 2026-08-17 (see NR-265, NR-266, NR-267):

1. BL-436's design says corp_ai's build scorer 'is being asked to prefer processors on a payback curve that does not reward them'. It is not being asked anything of the sort - processors are not candidates. 'The AI prefers mines' is STRUCTURAL, not a scoring-curve artefact. This reassigns the blame BL-417 was filed to test: BL-417's quadratic curve is real and worth writing out honestly, but it was never the reason rivals do not build processors.

2. BL-436's calibration_sweep narrative explains the x4 collapse as corps 'spending the extra income building processors that lose MORE per tick at higher scale'. That mechanism is impossible - the AI cannot build a processor. Whatever the sweep measured, it was generated and warm-start processors only, and the conclusion needs re-deriving before any cost-side number moves. Do NOT re-tune on the old narrative.

3. BL-428 (chain depth) gates recipes on a corp's reached depth. A rival that cannot build a processor can never increase its depth, so the growth gate has no AI player. Ancient-only today, so it does not bite a 1960 campaign - but the ladder is currently single-player by construction.

items.title: An extraction site can only target the RICHEST resource on its tile, so a resource that is never the richest anywhere is never mined — coal has 1,671 tiles, 0 mines, and binds 54% of all starved processor ticks
items.summary: Found 2026-08-17, chasing why processing starves after BL-436 enabled the richness conversion and BL-439 fixed the no-recipe defect. Both the AI scorer (rank_extraction_sites) and world generation (author_building) pick an extraction target with placement_rules::richest_extractable(tile) — the single richest extractable deposit on that tile. A resource that is present on many tiles but rarely the richest on ANY of them is therefore structurally unmineable, whatever the demand for it. Coal is the worked example: 1,671 tiles carry it, it is the richest extractable on 1.1% of them, ZERO extraction sites target it, and it is the binding input on 54.0% of all starved processing building-ticks. The same shape appears in tier_margin R5 for resource ids 8/9/10, flagged as siting/reach by NR-266.
items.design:
The rule is a TILE-LOCAL heuristic making a decision that needs a WORLD-level fact. Richness answers "what is most abundant here"; siting needs "what is worth extracting here", and those differ exactly when a wanted good is common-but-never-dominant. Three parts, in order:

(a) ENUMERATE, do not pre-select. rank_extraction_sites emits at most one candidate per tile, at the richest target, so no scorer can ever see the alternative. It should emit a candidate per extractable target the tile carries (bounded by the existing top_m_sites cut), and let the existing net/glut/solvency scoring choose. This alone does not fix coal — coal loses on richness and would still be out-scored — but without it there is nothing for (b) to act on.

(b) LET UNMET INPUT DEMAND WEIGH. A resource that a loaded recipe names as an input and that nothing produces is a world fact, derivable deterministically from the registry plus current production, and it is exactly what tier_margin R4 already computes. Weight a candidate target by that shortfall. This is NOT a price signal and must not be routed through one: the price signal cannot work here by construction, because a processor has to be RUNNING to bid for coal, and it cannot run without coal. The deadlock is the defect.

(c) GENERATION uses the same rule, so a fresh world should not open with the shortage already baked in (author_building calls richest_extractable directly). Fix both or the AI spends the campaign digging out of a hole generation made.

Deliberately NOT in scope: repricing (NR-271), processing upkeep, and the richness band. Calibrating any of them against a chain whose second input is unobtainable would tune around the shortage and have to be undone once it is mined.

Guard: extend tier_margin R5 from a report into an assertion — no resource that a loaded recipe names as an input may have deposits on more than a threshold number of tiles and zero sites targeting it. That row fails today on coal by construction, and on ids 8/9/10 besides, so it must be run against the pre-change build first to prove it discriminates.

PROGRESS 2026-08-17. (a) and (b) are BUILT: rank_extraction_sites now emits a candidate per extractable deposit on a tile instead of one for its richest, weighted by input_demand_weights() — recipes-wanting-it over sites-already-named-for-it, so the pull is self-limiting and decays as the shortage is answered. corp_ai_params::input_demand_pull (default 4.0) makes it a data change; 0 restores the old behaviour.

(c) IS THE HALF THAT MOVES THE NUMBERS, and it is not done. tier_margin is BYTE-IDENTICAL across (a)+(b) — extraction 14.53/7.82, processing 12.37/-10.44, samples 2993/1916, and all seven UNSITEABLE rows still red. A 3-seed 20-tick run is dominated by GENERATED assets, and generation still sites by richest_extractable in author_building. The AI fix cannot show until generation stops digging the hole.

The blocker on (c) is structural and is the same one assign_default_recipes has: generate_corporations runs inside make_hard_coded_world, BEFORE the Lua economy layer loads, so it cannot see recipe demand any more than it can see recipe ids. Two shapes, and this is a DESIGN CALL rather than an implementation detail:
  (i) a post-registry retarget pass — a sibling of assign_default_recipes that walks generated extraction sites and re-points a site whose tile also carries a starved input. Cheap, consistent with the pattern already established, and needs no generation restructuring. It mutates a generated decision after the fact, which is only defensible because BL-437 made a site work its whole tile, so target_resource names what a site is FOR rather than all it extracts.
  (ii) hand generation a static demand hint so it sites correctly first time. Cleaner in principle, and it means the opening world is right rather than corrected, but it needs the recipe graph available at world-gen time, which is the ordering constraint the whole file is built around.

> ⟳ 2026-08-19 (N1 audit): HELD — 2/4. (a)+(b) landed (97fe33a: input_demand_weights/rank_extraction_sites, corp_ai.cpp:434-593); (c) SUPERSEDED by BL-441/BL-442 (both complete, 8cc2981) — do not build; (d) PRODUCTION.md propagation not started. Owed measurement first: re-run tier_margin R4b now that BL-441/442 are in — green means only (d) remains; red re-opens (c) in a new shape (NR-354 option A).
items.consequences_for_shipped_claims: It reassigns BL-436 one more time, and this is the third reassignment in two days. BL-436 was filed as "processing underearns extraction", diagnosed as a scoring-curve artefact (wrong — NR-265, it was structural), then as a richness rate ratio (right, and fixed by enabling richness_reference at the median), and now the residual is neither margin nor upkeep but SUPPLY: 46.3% of processing building-ticks starve, and over half of that is one resource nobody can mine. NR-271s sized price options (a/b/c) were all measured on a starved chain and must be re-derived after this lands, not applied before it.

items.title: The market demand register records FILLS, not WANTS — a starved processor that wanted 16 coal and got 2 registers demand of 2, so scarcity is invisible to the price signal
The price band is hard-coded as constexpr in TWO places and is far too narrow for scarcity to cross an inter-market margin
A corp that dips one quarter into the red compounds at 2%/tick forever, so a few thousand of operating loss reads as millions and every economy measurement downstream becomes unreadable
items.summary: Found 2026-08-17 while reading ai_skill_harness's -2M to -3.4M net worths (NR-269). k_debt_interest_per_quarter is 0.02 and the benchmark rollout is 300 ticks: 1.02^300 = 380x. Per-building extraction nets +5 to +11 on every seed, so a corp cannot lose millions by operating. It dips a few thousand negative on processor upkeep and compounding does the rest. The rate itself is defensible (~8%/yr); what is missing is any floor, recovery path or terminal state. An insolvent corp is not resolved, it just accelerates away from zero.
items.design:
MEASURE BEFORE CHANGING ANYTHING, and the measurement is the first deliverable: decompose a benchmark corp's final balance into operating flows versus accrued interest. The claim that the -3M is 'almost entirely compounding' is arithmetic inference from 1.02^300, not an observation, and it should be confirmed or overturned before a lever is chosen.

Note tools/verify/econ_bankruptcy.cpp ALREADY EXISTS and budget_system.hpp names it as a reader of the interest constant, yet budget_system.cpp contains no bankruptcy handling at all. Read that harness first: it may already pin the spiral as expected behaviour, in which case this item is partly a disagreement with an existing check rather than a new defect, and that has to be settled openly rather than by editing the check.

The design question is what insolvency MEANS, and it is a game-design call, not an arithmetic one. Candidates, deliberately not chosen here: (a) a debt ceiling past which no further interest accrues, cheapest and least meaningful; (b) forced liquidation - assets sold to clear debt, which gives 'survival' a real definition and makes the survival metric mean something it currently does not; (c) restructuring, where a corp idles or sheds buildings to return to solvency, which is the version that composes with the existing BL-079 reflex tier and the BL-202 scorer rather than sitting beside them.

(b) and (c) are the ones that feed Conflict and Trade; (a) only silences a number. Prefer whichever the measurement supports, and state the reason.

GUARD: a corp driven insolvent reaches a defined terminal or recovered state within a bounded number of ticks, rather than diverging. Must be shown to fail pre-change - today it diverges by construction.

> ⟳ 2026-08-19: Re-homed v0.1.16 -> v0.1.11: rides Lane D's first batch as its cheapest economy-truth unblock (Fall-arc amendment 5: interest is 98.8% of every benchmark deficit). Verify build state first — N1 lists this among the seven unaudited Sprint-26 items.

> ⟳ 2026-08-19 (N1 audit): CONFIRMED genuinely unbuilt by the N1 audit — the only code is the 2% charge itself (budget_system.cpp:218-226); zero floor/cap/reserve/terminal code in src/. items.title: No check asserts that a corp_verb is reachable from all three directions
Three procurement verbs are reachable by an agent and by no human
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-17 from the Sprint 22 audit. request_quote, accept_quote and cancel_contract landed with world state, serialisation and a harness, and no press. The dictionary already records all three as SEAM-ONLY in as many words.
items.design:
## The gap, in the dictionary own words

All three entries open identically: *No UI. SEAM-ONLY: this verb has NO player-facing
press.* BL-350 (procurement seam) landed the state, the serialisation and the harness and
stopped short of the surface. So an external agent can contract for goods and a human
cannot — the exact asymmetry the reachability argument exists to catch, and the largest
one on the board.

## Shape

A **Contracts** tab on the Market Ledger, beside Sell Orders, scoped to the ledger
selected body the way Sell Orders already is. Three regions:

- **Request** — supplier combo, resource combo, quantity, a Request button. The four
  decline results (`rejected_no_capacity`, `no_input_access`, `embargo`, `reputation`)
  are already distinguishable at the seam, so each gets its own message rather than a
  generic failure. That distinguishability was designed in and is currently unread by
  anything.
- **Live quotes** — one row per quote with price, lead time, deposit, and Accept.
- **Contracts in flight** — progress, remaining, and Cancel behind a confirm popup
  (irreversible and forfeits the deposit, so it follows the demolish precedent).

## What it must not do

It must not add a fourth code path. The presses issue `corp_command` records through
`apply_corp_command`, exactly as the Sell Orders tab does since BL-293, so the human and
the agent share one seam and one validation.

## Owed alongside

A `question_log.json` entry per region (the pair is required on every surface), and the
three `ACTIONS.json` entries rewritten — their `surface` and `press` fields currently
assert there is no UI, which is precisely the kind of stale entry BL-270 warns misleads
the AI player.

items.title: The rival scorer enumerates no procurement candidate
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-17 from the Sprint 22 audit. corp_ai.cpp assigns cmd.verb at ten sites and none of them is request_quote, accept_quote or cancel_contract. BL-350 gave rivals a procurement seam they never use.
items.design:
## The gap

BL-293 (order book on the seam) gave rivals the sell side. The buy side arrived with
BL-350 (procurement seam) and no scorer touched it. A rival whose local market cannot
supply a recipe input has exactly one remedy today — build differently — when the seam
offers a second.

## Shape, respecting the standing rules

One more candidate family on the existing deterministic scored-utility layer. No planner,
no new code path, legal verbs only:

- **Request.** For each completed building whose recipe is input-starved at its local
  market, score a `request_quote` against the highest-reputation supplier holding capacity.
  The supplier walk must be over a **sorted** corp id list — `w.corporations` is an
  unordered_map and iterating it directly is the nondeterminism BL-422 already caught once.
- **Accept.** Score each live quote against the counterfactual of buying the same goods on
  the open market over the lead time. Accept when the contract is cheaper *and* the
  deposit clears the solvency floor — the deposit is a spend and is subject to the reserve
  gate like every other, per the standing-rules ruling on NR-218.
- **Cancel.** Score only when the contracted good has become cheaper than the contract by
  more than the forfeited deposit. Deliberately conservative: cancellation moves
  reputation, and a scorer that churns contracts makes the reputation axis meaningless.

## Cap

One procurement command per evaluation, as `hire_unit` is capped. Contracts are durative
and a rival that opens six in a tick has committed cash it cannot see.

## APPEND-ONLY CONTENTION — recorded 2026-08-22 by the hotspot audit

This item appends to **`corp_decision_reason`** (`src/world/corp_command.hpp`), and so do: BL-447 (demolish/road), BL-450 (stance).

The enum is **serialised** and append-only: a value may be appended, never inserted or renumbered.
That is a **real ordering constraint between items that share no line of code**, which is exactly
what a file-collision map cannot see — and the backlog recorded it nowhere before now.

**Second-order, and easier to miss:** `corp_decision_reason_count` sizes two FIXED-SIZE ARRAYS in
UI code — `src/ui/strategy_readout.hpp`:64 and a filter loop in the decision feed. An append is
therefore not confined to the world layer, and any item appending here **under-declares its scope**
if it names only `corp_ai.cpp`.

**The batching rule that follows:** one appender per batch, in a stated order, exactly as the
Fall-arc convention already requires elsewhere.

items.title: Three verbs the docs say the scorer uses, it does not emit
items.summary: Filed 2026-08-17 from the Sprint 22 audit. The standing rules describe rivals scoring "build, demolish, survey and road decisions each tick". The scorer emits build, survey, the four dials and place_sell_order. Demolish, place_road and remove_sell_order have no candidate site.
items.design:
## The discrepancy

`.claude/rules/io-standing-rules.md` states the BL-202/BL-203 exception as *"build,
demolish, survey and road decisions scored each tick"*. Grepping `cmd.verb = corp_verb::`
in `corp_ai.cpp` returns ten sites covering eight verbs: build (x3), resume, idle,
set_workforce, set_recipe, survey, hire_unit, place_sell_order.

**Demolish and place_road are described and absent.** This is the backlog-prose-goes-stale
pattern applied to a standing rule, which is worse, because the rule is read as an
invariant rather than as a plan.

## Three separate calls, not one

1. **`demolish`** — a real gap. A rival with a persistently loss-making asset can idle it
   (and does) but never reclaims the tile. Idle is free and reversible, so the honest
   trigger is not "loss-making" but "the tile is worth more under a different building
   than this one is worth idled". That is a comparison against the build enumeration that
   already runs, so the candidate is cheap to site and easy to get wrong.
2. **`place_road`** — a real gap, and the one with a measurable payoff, since haulage is
   now instrumented (`haulage_measure`). Score a tier against the freight it would
   actually carry rather than against adjacency.
3. **`remove_sell_order`** — a real gap and the smallest. BL-293 gave rivals order
   placement and no withdrawal, so a floor priced for last quarter stands forever, and
   `max_sell_orders_per_corp` becomes a ceiling a long game will reach.

**`set_workforce_auto` is NOT in scope and is judged correctly absent.** It hands a dial
to an auto-solver; a scorer that already sets the dial has no use for it. Recorded so the
next audit does not re-file it.

## The doc half

Whichever of the three land, the standing-rules sentence and AI_OPPONENT.md are corrected
to the verbs actually emitted — and if one is deliberately not built, it is named as
deliberate rather than left reading as shipped.

## APPEND-ONLY CONTENTION — recorded 2026-08-22 by the hotspot audit

This item appends to **`corp_decision_reason`** (`src/world/corp_command.hpp`), and so do: BL-446 (procurement), BL-450 (stance).

The enum is **serialised** and append-only: a value may be appended, never inserted or renumbered.
That is a **real ordering constraint between items that share no line of code**, which is exactly
what a file-collision map cannot see — and the backlog recorded it nowhere before now.

**Second-order, and easier to miss:** `corp_decision_reason_count` sizes two FIXED-SIZE ARRAYS in
UI code — `src/ui/strategy_readout.hpp`:64 and a filter loop in the decision feed. An append is
therefore not confined to the world layer, and any item appending here **under-declares its scope**
if it names only `corp_ai.cpp`.

**The batching rule that follows:** one appender per batch, in a stated order, exactly as the
Fall-arc convention already requires elsewhere.

items.design:
## Why a separate item

BL-350 (procurement seam) landed a complete seam with no press, and nobody noticed for
weeks. The lesson is that the surface half must be its own tracked item, not a task inside
the model item where it is the first thing cut under pressure.

## Shape

The Corporation panel gains a stance column and the three presses, gated on visibility.
A stance toward a corp the player has not discovered is not shown — the BL-068
competitor-visibility rule applies, and *whether someone has declared war on you* is not
obviously public information. **That is a second question for Ben** and is smaller than the
symmetry one: does a declaration announce itself, or is it discovered on contact? It rides
naturally on the comms dock if it announces.

Presses issue `corp_command` records. Declaring hostility takes a confirm popup on the
demolish precedent — it is not literally irreversible, but under Reading A it is not
unilaterally reversible either, which is close enough to warrant the friction.
