Until then rate 0.0 is a deliberate, dated state, not an oversight; this item is the tripwire so it is not forgotten.
items.design: When the engagement trigger lands: pick small nonzero rates, run the BL-454 checks (N units debit exactly N x rate, empty pool decays at the authored scalar), measure how far rival balances move, re-bless the economy goldens. Makes BL-457's admission argument (ordnance has a consumer) true at runtime, which chain_depth's exemption currently asserts only structurally.

items.title: Delegate the corpus: saved agent roles and directory-scoped instruction files
One shared axis-to-candidates resource table behind the hire gate and the hire debit
items.summary: Code-review audit finding (2026-08-20): debit_hire_cost (corp_command.cpp:92-105) hand-mirrors unit_roster.cpp:143-154's campaign_gate_input preference lists, guarded only by a comment saying they must match. The BL-394 free-hire bug class recurs the day one side gains ordnance (BL-454/BL-457 work) and the other does not.
items.design: Lift the three axis preference lists into one table in unit_roster.hpp; both the gate and the debit consume it. Land BEFORE the military-milestone roster work touches either site. Assert with the existing hire harness: gate pass implies a matching debit for every axis.

items.title: Harness round-trips every corp_verb through the wire parser
items.summary: Code-review audit finding (2026-08-20): a new verb touches four surfaces (enum, apply_corp_command, corp_ai scorer, ACTIONS.json) and the pattern has already failed three times (main.cpp:391-401 - BL-324/BL-293/BL-350 each left verbs unreachable over the wire). Nothing machine-checks parser coverage; the AI-opponent milestone multiplies external callers.
items.design: Headless harness: enumerate corp_verb, serialise each through the wire encoding, parse back, assert a non-default verb and no silent degradation. Wire it into the standard verifier-headless set so a grown enum fails the same day.

items.title: Determinism harness widens from seed 0 to a real seed sweep
items.summary: Code-review audit finding (2026-08-20): determinism_harness.cpp:12-17 still says world-gen is not seedable and checks only the zero-seed world - but the seed IS threaded now (hard_coded_world.hpp:27-33). Nonzero-seed determinism, exactly what the Era -1 extension (BL-494) and nation behaviour lean on, has no guard.
items.design: Sweep a small fixed seed set (e.g. 5 seeds), assert byte-identical regeneration per seed and distinct state hashes across seeds. Update the stale header comment. Land before further history-sim work.

items.title: Lenses become a descriptor table instead of three inlined regions of the planetary canvas
items.summary: Code-review audit finding (2026-08-20): body_surface_canvas.cpp (2,906 lines) inlines the lens system across three non-adjacent regions - 12 draw_*_key functions (136-760), per-lens precompute (1162-1409), per-tile colour chain (1655-1736). Every new lens is a 3-4-touchpoint edit; nothing ties a lens's key legend to its colour rule, so they can drift invisibly.
items.design: Mechanical move, not redesign: a lens descriptor {key-draw fn, tile-colour fn, optional precompute} in a new lenses.cpp; the canvas iterates the table. Behaviour-identical - verify with the existing lens goldens at 0.0000%. Pays back on the next lens the roadmap adds.

items.title: Selection panel's ten private glyphs move into the icons catalogue
items.summary: Code-review audit finding (2026-08-20): ten glyph_* functions (selection_panel.cpp:985-1102) follow the (dl, centre, r, colour) contract but live outside icons.{hpp,cpp}, invisible to the catalogue - glyph_swap already exists twice in the same file. Violates the standing glyph invariant in src/ui/CLAUDE.md.
items.design: Move the ten into ui::icons, dedupe glyph_swap, catalogue each in ICONS.md per its recipe. Behaviour-identical; verify with the selection-panel goldens.

items.title: Selection panel, hover card and tile ledger converge on the shared per-entity builders
items.summary: Code-review audit finding (2026-08-20): SELECTION.md claims the Tile Ledger and hover card share the per-entity content builders, but entity_summary.cpp has effectively one consumer - selection_panel, hover_content and tile_inspector each build their own rendering of the same facts, three drifting paths. The cost triples when military/political entity kinds arrive.
items.design: Convergence onto the existing seam (entity_summary / selection_card), not new architecture: per entity kind, one builder both surfaces call, surface-specific framing kept at the call site. Verify with the selection and hover goldens; note any legitimate rendering differences in SELECTION.md as they surface.

items.title: A stateful strain accumulator: digestion retires strain, loss does not
items.summary: Sprint 30's NEW-6, filed. Replace the stateless burden (burden=(held-40)x4, recomputed from current holdings) with an accumulating pressure that can break. The adversarial pass's shape assertion is the acceptance test: the strain term must NOT decrease when holdings decrease - losing provinces must never make an empire logistically stronger.
items.design: Design in COLLAPSE.md section 'What the sim must grow' item 1 and the Pulse strategy: strain accumulates with expansion tempo and breadth-over-knee; Consolidate years retire it at an authored rate; province LOSS retires nothing (the grievance stays). Deterministic scalar per polity, serialised alongside cohesion_q. The Pulse strategy only exists once this lands - alternating Campaign/Consolidate must be arithmetically better than continuous Campaign at equal holdings.

items.title: The collapse itself: fragmentation into named successor polities
items.summary: Sprint 30's NEW-7, filed. When strain exceeds cohesion unmanaged, the polity fragments into successor polities along province/culture seams, emitting owner_none where nothing coheres and a real eliminated-polity event where alive=false is currently silent. COLLAPSE.md culmination E1.
items.design:
Successors route through the seeded phoneme generator - struct polity has no name field today and the naming rule is absolute (no placeholder). Each successor inherits a restoration-lean creed and a grudge toward whichever neighbour fed on the break (Sprint 29's payload). Break lines are a deterministic function of province adjacency + culture + local cohesion, never a roll.

## FILE SCOPE CORRECTED 2026-08-22 (hotspot audit)

Declared `src/world/name_generation.{hpp,cpp}`. **Neither has ever existed** — the same phantom-file
shape as BL-377, caught here before it cost anything. A successor polity's name comes from the
seeded phoneme generator in `src/world/tongue.{hpp,cpp}`, which is what the standing naming rule
requires anyway: every generated name is produced by the tongue banks and never drawn from an
Earth list.

items.title: Promote the hegemony measure from the sweep harness into the engine
items.summary: Sprint 30's NEW-8, filed. The sweep harness has a reporting threshold; the engine has nothing that can name, gate or narrate a great power. Promote it so polity::major means something and culminations/narration can key on it.
items.design: One function over holdings share + reach; the same number the sweep already computes, computed once and stored per polity per year. Consumers: the strain accumulator (BL-504, majors accumulate), the attractor sweep (BL-490), the history-tab narration (BL-489).

items.title: A Release verb: voluntary devolution into client polities
items.summary: The Hydra strategy's verb and culmination E2 (devolution - the managed release, the British-empire mechanism). A fifth scored polity verb: shed peripheral provinces into a client successor BEFORE strain chooses the break line. Second, voluntary trigger on BL-505's fragmentation machinery.
items.design: Scored like the other verbs (ruling: verb, not threshold rule - keeps it inside the nation-behaviour grant's shape). Value rises with strain and falls with cohesion headroom. The asymmetry is the point: released clients carry LOW grudge toward the core (devolution buys goodwill fragmentation never does); the core's creed shifts imperial->mercantile and keeps its reach.

items.title: Strained majors are readable prey: weakness as an observable, not telepathy
items.summary: Culmination E3 (absorption) needs rivals to score Campaign against a high-strain target - but no polity may read another's internal scalar. Expose weakness through observables: lost battles, stalled campaigns, supply shortfalls - the same tells the player sees.
items.design: A small derived 'apparent weakness' value per polity computed from public events only (battle outcomes, campaign stalls), consumed by rivals' Campaign scoring. Keeps the no-telepathy discipline STRATEGIES.md set at corp grain.

items.title: Conquering a strained polity imports its strain - absorption is never free
items.summary: COLLAPSE.md E3: without transfer, eating a strained major is a free lunch and absorption becomes the dominant exit. The conqueror inherits holdings AND a share of the victim's accumulated strain.
items.design: On province transfer from a polity above a strain band, a proportional strain quantum moves with it. One subtraction and one addition on BL-504's scalar; the absorbed culture persists as grudge+creed inside the new borders.

items.title: Reach feeds a second, slower strain inflow - the Metropole also breaks
items.summary: NR-356's hole: a reach-hegemon with few holdings never trips a holdings-fed accumulator, dodging Sprint 30's 'inevitable'. Recommended fix (option A): reach feeds the SAME accumulator at a slower rate, so the Metropole is the longest-lived shape and still breaks - usually via the Slow Fade (E6). CONFIRMED by Ben 2026-08-20 (NR-356 resolved, option A): 'logistics should be capable of determining reach... reach feeds strain' - the inflow reads the same logistics/reach substrate as everything else, per BL-325 ruling 3 (one reach field).
items.design: One additional inflow term on BL-504's accumulator scaled by reach-derived exposure (routes/dependencies held abroad). HISTORY.md Stage 5 (hegemony fails its final audition) later becomes a parameterisation of this, not a second system. RULED 2026-08-20 (Ben, NR-356 resolved, option A): reach feeds strain, and the inflow reads the same logistics/reach substrate as everything else per BL-325 ruling 3 (one reach field) - no longer pending; the filed shape stands as ruled.

items.title: Render the province, not the hex: province-grain canvas with softened borders
items.design:
## RULED 2026-08-21 (Ben, design form). Status: design-owed -> designed.

**Size: unchanged.** A province stays the ~4-tile 2x2 block BL-466 already builds
— 8,294 on the reference world. No repartition, so BL-466's id layout
(`body_rank | block_raster_index | component`), its history-log section and its
determinism rows all stand exactly as landed.

**What moves to province grain: rendering, selection, and unit position/movement.**
Building placement does NOT move.

**What the tile remains.** Ben: *"They are also the base element for storing
resource values, and buildings exist on tiles. So they are just going to be
rendered differently, but still instrumental unit values."* The tile is unchanged
as the data grain — deposits, terrain, buildings, richness. It stops being the
thing the player clicks and starts being the thing the Selection panel shows them
about what they clicked.

**Terrain reads as a blended gradient** across the province's real mixture — not a
dominant composition (which would discard the two-axis mixture TILES.md exists to
express) and not a texture pattern.

## The ruling this overturns, and why it is coherent

2026-08-13 (BL-315 ruling 2) put units as tokens on the TILE map, "not armies at
province grain". 2026-08-19 (BL-467) reconciled by splitting grains: command at
the tile, engagement at the province. **This ruling collapses that split** — units
now move and are selected at province grain, which is the same grain the battle
envelope already uses.

That is a simplification, not a complication: BL-467's engagement rule ("units of
two corps standing in the same province, at least one hostile") stops needing a
tile-to-province reduction, because a unit's position IS a province. The 4-tile
province keeps the change modest — positions quantise to a 2x2 cell, not to a
grand-strategy region.

## Costs this ruling carries — none of them blocking, all of them real

1. **`march_unit`'s payload changes from a tile to a province.** BL-470 landed
   `march_unit` / `halt_unit` / `disband_unit` on 2026-08-19 with `tile` as the
   target. The verb enum is serialised and append-only, so the VERB stays; the
   field it reads changes. The action dictionary entry (ACTIONS.json) and any
   `--serve` wire caller move with it.
2. **`unit_component` is tile-canonical** (MILITARY.md § the unit model). Whether
   the unit stores a province and derives a tile, or stores a tile and derives a
   province, is an implementation call — the second is cheaper and keeps every
   existing reader working, and is the recommendation unless Ben says otherwise.
3. **Every lens reduces per tile.** All eleven overlay modes key on tile fields.
   A blended province render needs a per-province reduction of each — decided lens
   by lens, and the blend means "mean" is available where "dominant" would lie.
4. **Convoys and logistics stay tile-pathed.** BL-458's interdiction reads
   `convoy_tile_at`; roads, catchments and the A* all remain tile-grain. Nothing
   in the logistics layer moves, because only UNIT position was ruled over.
5. **BL-471 (unit marker + command surface) and BL-469 (battle card)** should
   follow this work rather than precede it — they draw on the canvas it rewrites.

## The blend is the actual graphics work

No current surface draws anything but crisp hexes. Softening province borders
while keeping the interior mixture legible has no precedent in the codebase, and
it is the part of this item most likely to need a visual pass with Ben rather
than a specification.

## Companion item

The province building limit is **BL-513**, filed separately — it is economy and
generation, shares no file with this, and Ben's answer defines it independently.


## AMENDED 2026-08-21, after Ben saw it rendered

Three revisions, all made against the live result rather than against the spec —
which is the point of having built it before settling it.

**1. Size: 7-12 tiles, superseding the ~4-tile ruling above.** Ben: *"You were
right in that 3-5 tiles is too small for a province, we can use a range of 7-12
tiles."* The earlier ruling in this design (keep the 2x2 block) was made BEFORE
the render existed and is now history, not guidance. The repartition changes the
block from 2x2 to 3x3; the work is not the block resize but holding the 7-12 floor
when water cuts a block into fragments.

**2. One selection element, not two.** Ben: *"We do not need another selection
element, we can just use the same one as we used for tiles."* `draw_province_selection`
shipped as a separate function dispatched first and unconditionally, which reads as a
second element. SELECTION.md describes ONE pinned polymorphic panel; the province
becomes one more thing it can be showing. The CONTENT stays — the mixture bar is the
blend legend and is load-bearing — only the element rendering it changes.

**3. Global blend: HELD, not rejected.** Ben wants to see the larger provinces first.
Filed as BL-514 with the captures it needs, deliberately unbuilt.

Knock-ons of the size change, to be measured rather than assumed: BL-513 k=12.6468 should
survive (both sides of its ratio are sums over tiles, so the aggregate is size-independent)
but the per-province distribution changes completely; and BL-512 per_province_firm_cap=2,
measured as nearly inert against 4-tile provinces, may begin to bind against 9-tile ones.
items.landed_note: LANDED 2026-08-21, NOT COMPLETE. Rendering, province selection, the per-lens reduction table and the march_unit seam half are all in and verified. Requirement R1's LIVE half is owed: two agents in a row could not take it (no click injection in the verify API, no granted applications in a non-interactive session), so the hit-test resolution path is proven and the PRESS is not. See NR-416, NR-424.

items.title: Pin the two firm caps by measurement, and move them into economy.lua
items.design:
## Why this exists

`generate_background_firms` now shapes its firm budget with two caps
(commit b4b5b3e, 2026-08-20):

    constexpr int per_resource_firm_cap = 8;    // provisional
    constexpr int per_province_firm_cap = 2;    // provisional

Both are **unpinned numbers chosen to be measured**, not derived from anything.
Shipping an unpinned constant quietly is what BL-463's report-then-tune
discipline exists to stop, so they were flagged in the code comment and here
rather than left to be discovered later.

## What the work is

1. Move both to `scripts/economy.lua` as tunables, beside the existing
   `economy.substrate.clearing_fraction` (0.90) the coverage target already
   reads. Changing a generation shape becomes a data edit, not a recompile.
2. **Pin them by measurement**, the way BL-463 pinned the settlement divisor:
   sweep each across a range, read `province_capacity_probe`'s coverage column
   and firm counts, and choose from the measured spread.
3. While sweeping, answer the question the first cut could not: **what is the
   per-province cap actually for?** Measured 2026-08-20 it is nearly inert —
   provinces average ~4 tiles and the fullest holds 3 buildings, so a cap of 2
   firms rarely binds. It is correctly wired and it will matter as density
   rises, but today the per-resource cap carries the entire result. Either the
   province cap wants a different number, a different grain, or it is premature.

## The dependency worth naming

**BL-511 (province as render unit) may change what a province IS.** If the
partition gets coarser, the per-province cap changes meaning completely — a cap
of 2 against a 4-tile province is a different rule from a cap of 2 against a
40-tile one. Pin the per-RESOURCE cap now; consider holding the per-PROVINCE
number until BL-511's grain is ruled.

## Acceptance

`province_capacity_probe` shows every seed at or above the coverage target with
both values read from Lua, and the chosen numbers are justified in the item by
the measured spread rather than asserted.

items.title: A province limit on total buildings, from area, infrastructure, habitability and population
Blend all tiles, not only within provinces
Grow provinces from population centres, bounded by rivers, elevation and roads
Lake, coast and ocean as tile kinds; provinces drawn over water
Retain the generation heightmap as a per-tile field
The Era -1 sim redraws province borders as its wars resolve
items.design:
## Ben's brief (2026-08-21)

> "We can also use generation to edit province borders as wars are won."

Provinces are grown from settlement and terrain (BL-515). This item makes the
Era -1 history sim REDRAW them as its wars resolve, so the campaign opens on a
map whose borders carry the history that produced them — a province that changed
hands three times looks like it did.

## Why it belongs with the sim, not the partition

BL-515 is a generation pass: it runs once and derives shapes from terrain. This is
a consequence of simulated events across 4,000 years, and it reads the sim's
conquest record. Its natural home is beside the sim that produces that record
(`history_sim.cpp`), consuming the partition rather than computing it.

## The constraint that makes it buildable

Ben ruled that borders move **during generation only**, fixed once the campaign
starts. That keeps provinces generation output rather than live mutable state,
which is exactly what lets `world::provinces` stay outside `state_hash` — the
exclusion is documented on the field, and `determinism_harness` compares the
partition across two generations instead.

If this item ever grew into campaign-era border changes, that whole arrangement
would need revisiting. Worth remembering before anyone extends it.

## Open, and genuinely undecided

- **What a conquest does to a border.** Move it in the victor's favour by some
  margin? Transfer whole provinces? Split one?
- **Whether the sim's conquest record carries enough to act on.** BL-384's
  measurement (2026-08-20): 4 of 8 seeds conquer, at a near-1:1 conquest:battle
  ratio; the other 4 see no war at all. On a peaceful seed this item does nothing
  — correct behaviour, but it means the feature is invisible on half the worlds,
  and that should be expected rather than diagnosed as a bug later.
- **Interaction with the allocated id (BL-515).** If a province is split or
  absorbed, does its id die, survive, or fork? The allocated-id ruling makes the
  question answerable; it does not answer it.

## Prerequisite

BL-515 must land first. There is no point redrawing borders that are about to be
replaced by a different algorithm.

items.title: Split terrain_composition into substrate x cover, so a tile can be composite
Basic tile texturing: a substrate base plus a cover overlay
Click injection in the verify API, so an agent can satisfy a live check
One water tile reprices the whole haul — logistics_path::crosses_ocean is a route-wide boolean
items.summary: MEASURED 2026-08-21 (Sprint B2). `logistics_path::crosses_ocean` is one bit over an entire route, so a single water tile makes EVERY land tile on that route bill at the sea rate and travel at coastal_km_per_day (130) instead of caravan_km_per_day (25). It is not an edge case: 64.5% of market-pair routes are in sea mode today, and the shipped economy is mispricing them by 1.59x.
items.design:
## The measurement

`tools/verify/sea_leg_census.cpp`, 16 seeds, 1230 market-pair routes (stable against the 8-seed
default, which reports the same shape at 60.3% / 1.64x):

| | |
|---|---|
| Routes already in sea mode | **64.5%** — sea is the MAJORITY mode |
| Median water share of a sea-mode route | **12.9%** (p10 1.8%, p90 37.6%) |
| Sea-mode routes ≤5% water — a clip, not a voyage | **23.3%** |
| Sea-mode routes with **no open-ocean tile at all** | **23.3%** |
| Whole-route sea rate vs per-leg split | **1.59× overcharge** |

## Why this is its own item and not part of BL-188

BL-188 (coastal ports) is parked, and it should stay parked: its blocker is here, not in the road
raster. But this defect **bills wrongly today**, on two thirds of intra-body hauls, whether or not
a port is ever built. It is a live economy bug wearing a blocked feature's clothes.

It also makes BL-188 unbuildable as designed. Ruling 3 wants a mode **gated by a building at each
endpoint** — that cannot be built on a bit meaning "the cheapest path touched water somewhere".

## The shape of the fix

A **per-leg split** in `logistics_path` / `intra_body_path` / `price_convoy_leg`: a route carries
its water tiles and its land tiles separately and each bills at its own rate and travels at its own
speed. That is the prerequisite for everything BL-188 wants, and it is what makes the 1.59× go away
by construction rather than by tuning.

## The rate is ALSO backwards, and must NOT be flipped on its own

`scripts/economy.lua` has `land = 0.02, sea = 0.05` — sea is 2.5× **dearer**, contradicting
BL-188's own settled ruling 1 ("sea's advantage is a lower per-unit RATE").

**Do not flip it as a separate change.** `path.cost` does double duty: it is the A* routing weight
(`sea_leg_cost = 2.5` deliberately prices water above any landform so routes prefer land) AND the
haul price. Flipping the rate in that one number sends every convoy to sea. Untangling the routing
weight from the price is part of the per-leg split, not a tune that can precede it. Recorded because
a later reader will see the contradiction and reach for the one-line fix.

## A doc/reality gap comes with it

`docs/economy/SUPPLY.md` documents the mode as though the boolean were meaningful. It is firing on
two thirds of routes for the wrong reason, so the doc describes a mechanism the code does not have.

items.title: Not every corporation is a militia - a corporation KIND axis the scorer actually reads
items.summary: [RENUMBERED from BL-522 on merge — three lanes ran concurrently and two minted the same id; BL-522 (whole-route haul mispricing) was already pushed.] Filed 2026-08-21 from Sprint B3's NEW-11. The kind axis already exists in the data (corporation_component::is_background) and corp_ai.cpp does not read it - the file contains no reference to is_background at all, so every background firm evaluates the military_base and hire_unit candidates on the same terms as a named rival. The sprint's framing that only the player is seeded with a base is stale: BL-476 extended seeding to every named corp on 2026-08-19. Two designs offered (gate the existing axis vs a real corp_kind enum); both change what rivals decide and need a dated ruling from Ben.
items.design:
## The complaint, and what is actually in code

Ben, Sprint B3: **"not every corporation is a militia."** The sprint filed this as NEW-11 with
the claim that the situation is *inverted* — every rival converges on building a military base
while only the player is seeded with one.

**Measured 2026-08-21, and the claim needs correcting in both halves:**

* **Seeding is no longer player-only.** BL-476 (2026-08-19) extended `seed_starting_military`
  from the player alone to *every named corp in `corp_ids`* — one `military_base` plus one
  starting unit each. BL-365 background firms are deliberately excluded (they are not in
  `corp_ids`), which BL-476's own notes call a non-goal.
* **Convergence is real, and it is the scorer, not the seeding.** `src/world/corp_ai.cpp`
  contains **no reference to `is_background` at all**. The muster-building candidate
  (corp_ai.cpp ~1135-1290) and the `hire_unit` candidate are evaluated for *every* non-player
  corp on the same terms. `corporation_component::is_background`'s own doc comment states the
  position plainly: background firms are *"picked up by corp_ai.cpp's uniform non-player
  iteration like any rival."*

So the militia problem is precisely this: **a KIND axis already exists in the data and the
scorer does not read it.**

## What already exists

`corporation_component` carries a three-way kind today — `is_player` / `is_background` /
neither-i.e.-rival — and `GENERATION_STRATEGY.md`'s economic premise is built on it: the eight
named specialist corps are the space-interested minority; the BL-365 background firms are the
mundane, saturating industry that owns the base. That is a real kind axis and it is orthogonal
to `industrial_focus` exactly as NEW-11 wants.

What it is not is a kind axis with **behavioural meaning**. Nothing downstream branches on it.

## The two candidate designs, and the choice between them

**(A) The cheap one — teach the scorer the axis it already has.** Gate the military-base and
`hire_unit` candidates on `!is_background`. A background firm keeps every economic verb (build,
demolish, survey, road, trade, workforce) and loses only the military ones. The world's broad
industry stops raising private armies; the named specialists still can.

**(B) The designed one — a real `corp_kind` enum.** A generated axis with more than two values
(e.g. industrial / mercantile / security / prospecting), assigned at generation from the nation
and province it opens in, read by the scorer as a per-family weight rather than a hard gate. This
is the axis NEW-11 literally asks for, and it is a new persistent field: it needs the flat-binary
save/load path in the same change.

**(A) is a narrowing of an existing AI grant; (B) is a new generated axis.** Both change what
rivals decide, so both move generation and tick goldens, and neither should be built without a
ruling. **Recommend (A) first** — it is the smaller change, it is falsifiable against
`substrate_census`'s building-by-type row, and it makes (B) cheaper by proving the seam.

## Why this is not being built blind

`.claude/rules/io-standing-rules.md` § Determinism & data model lists every AI-agency grant as a
*dated, scoped* widening. (A) is a **narrowing** and so is the safer of the two, but it still
changes what a rival does, and the rule's whole shape is that these calls are Ben's and are
dated. (B) widens the axis the scorer reads and is unambiguously a ruling.

## Owed measurement

The corp-kind population cannot be measured in a Lua-free tree: background-firm counts come from
`generate_background_firms`, which sizes itself against `economy.lua`'s demand baskets and places
**zero** firms without live Lua (NR-338). Before either design is built, run
`substrate_census` and `province_capacity_probe` in a Lua tree and record: how many background
firms exist per nation, and how many military bases and units the scorer currently produces
across them. That is the "how militia is it, actually" number, and nothing has it yet.

items.title: Ownership divorced from identity — a SYNDICATE tier that holds, corporations that run themselves
items.summary: Parent framing item (Ben, 2026-08-21). Splits the two jobs corporation_component does at once. A CORPORATION keeps its current meaning — the operating firm (buildings, recipes, stockpiles, orders), ~88 of them, each already self-running on the full corp_ai scorer. A SYNDICATE is the new strategic tier (~8) that holds equity in corporations, allocates capital and decides. Ownership becomes a RELATION between the tiers rather than a property of the player. Three genuinely new mechanics: an equity relation, a public/private/closed ownership class, and valuation + the profit split; everything else is reuse of resolve_price, FINANCE profitability, BL-350 negotiation and BL-218 industrialisation timing. RULINGS: equity confers operating control above a >50% majority (NR-491, Ben overturning the earlier "never"); the holding tier is named SYNDICATE and "corporation" keeps the operating sense (Ben, 2026-08-21, resolving NR-492; the word is NR-497). Six children: BL-525..BL-530.
items.design:
**The idea, in Ben's words (2026-08-21):** *"not all companies are public... company ownership is completely divorced from player identity. As in the player can trade companies and invest in them, gaining profit as something like a corporation. The current focus we have on roughly 40 companies can be twisted so that instead we have 7 corporations, and each company has the ability to automatically run itself, trading and growing as a separate AI layer [under] the main decision making bodies."*

## Terminology — SETTLED 2026-08-21 (Ben, resolving NR-492)

Ben's framing used *corporation* for the holder and *company* for the operator. **That is inverted from the settled terms.** His ruling: **"corporation" keeps the operating sense; the holding tier gets a new word.**

The word is **syndicate** (NR-497 — chosen on Ben's behalf, overturnable).

| Tier | Term | Count | Who decides |
|---|---|---|---|
| Operating firm — buildings, recipes, stockpiles, orders | **corporation** *(unchanged)* | ~88 | its own `corp_ai` scorer, always |
| Strategic actor — holds equity, allocates capital, decides | **syndicate** *(new)* | **7** | player or `corp_ai` |

Why a new word rather than re-pointing an old one: "corporation" has ~483 items and the whole of `src/world/` behind it in the operating sense (`corporation_component`, `generate_corporations`, `corp_ai`, `corp_command`, the Corporation lens). Renaming the thing that already has a name, to free the name for the thing that does not, is the expensive direction. Why *syndicate* specifically: it means a body of pooled interests that **owns rather than operates**, which is exactly the object; it is grep-clean (zero hits in `src/`, zero real hits in `docs/`); and it reads in both arcs — a merchant syndicate at 0 CE and a corporate syndicate in near-future space. Runners-up and why they lost are in NR-497.

## What is already true — measured 2026-08-21, not assumed

Stated first, because the proposal's arithmetic reads differently against it.

- `corporation_count = 8` (`src/world/corporation_generation.hpp:26`) — the player plus 7 named rivals. **Ben ruled 7 syndicates TOTAL (2026-08-21, NR-493)** — six AI plus the player — so this constant drops to **7** and the carve runs over seven named corps, not eight.
- Background firms are **not** a fixed 40. `generate_background_firms` runs a *measured* stop condition — spawn until real production reaches ~90% of real demand — bounded at 200/body as anti-runaway only (`corporation_generation.cpp:1750`). The recorded working figure is **~80**.
- Every background firm **already runs the full corp_ai scored-utility layer, identical to a rival** (Ben's ruling, 2026-08-11, BL-365 — real background corporations): real buildings, real recipes, real stockpiles, real market orders, picked up by `corp_ai.cpp`'s uniform non-player iteration with **no separate code path**.

So the self-running AI layer the proposal asks for **is built**. This item is not "give corporations autonomy"; it is **"hang ownership on the autonomy that already exists"**. That is the single most important fact about the item — it is what makes a framing change of this reach affordable.

## The move

`corporation_component` does two jobs at once. Split them: the operating job **keeps the name and the code**, and the strategic job moves up into a new `syndicate` entity that holds equity and nothing else.

**Do NOT split the operating entity type.** One `corporation_component` still covers every operating firm, named or background; the syndicate is a *new* type above it, not a fork of it. That is what keeps `corp_ai.cpp`'s uniform iteration intact — the property the whole design leans on. Forking the operating type forks the scorer, and the fork is the expensive part.

## The generation consequence the rename surfaced

**This is new, and it is load-bearing.** Under Ben's original wording the named corps *became* the holders, so nothing needed carving. With "corporation" retained for the operator, that no longer follows — and the question it exposes is real: **today's 8 named corporations own buildings.** A syndicate holds equity and does not operate, so those assets cannot simply travel with it.

The resolution, and it is the natural one: at generation, each of the **7** named corps **splits** into a syndicate plus one or more operating corporations carved from its former holdings, with the syndicate seeded holding a **majority stake** in each. Consequences:

- The operating population goes from ~88 to ~88 — the named corps' assets stay in the world, just under carved operating corporations rather than the named corp directly.
- Every syndicate starts with a portfolio rather than an empty balance sheet, so the mechanic is live from turn one instead of needing an acquisition before it does anything.
- The player's opening position is legible: *you own most of these two firms, and a sliver of that third*.
- Focus coherence survives — a carved corporation inherits its parent's `industrial_focus`, so the specialists premise (`GENERATION_STRATEGY.md`) is untouched.

This lands in **BL-526 (ownership-class derivation)**, which is already the generation-pass item.

## Collision with BL-523 (corp kind axis) — found on merge, 2026-08-21

**BL-523 lands on the same seam and neither item knew about the other** — they were authored in
parallel branches on the same day. Recorded here rather than left for whichever builds second.

BL-523's finding: `corp_ai.cpp` **contains no reference to `is_background` at all**, so a background
filler firm evaluates `military_base` and `hire_unit` on exactly the same terms as a named rival.
Its fix is to make the scorer read a corporation *kind*.

This item's BL-529 adds a **control gate** to that same candidate evaluation. So two designs now
add a gate to `corp_ai.cpp`'s candidate loop, and they are **orthogonal axes, not duplicates**:

|  | background firm | named / carved corp |
|---|---|---|
| **not player-controlled** | kind gate applies (BL-523) | ungated — acts as today |
| **player-controlled** | both gates apply | control gate applies (BL-529) |

Two consequences worth settling before either is built (**NR-500**):

1. **This item weakens `is_background`'s meaning.** BL-524's carve splits named corps into operating
   corporations — and nothing yet says whether a carved corporation is background or named. BL-523's
   axis needs that answer, and this item creates the ambiguity.
2. **The gates should be one mechanism, not two.** Two independently-added filters on the same loop
   is how a candidate evaluation becomes unexplainable — the same argument BL-219 made when it
   retired a second mechanism deciding one field.

## The three genuinely new mechanics

Everything else is reuse.

**1. Equity — an ownership relation.** Which syndicate holds what fraction of which corporation. Nothing like it exists: `corporation_component` has a `balance` and an `assets` list and no relational field at all. Shape in **BL-525 (equity data model)**.

**2. Ownership class — public / private / closed.** Three states, and the middle one is the point:

- **Public** — shares trade openly. The investable surface.
- **Private** — shares exist and change hands **only by negotiation**. A private corporation can refuse to sell you a stake exactly as it can refuse to sell you goods — which is **BL-350 (procurement/contract seam)**'s quote / lead-time / refusal machinery pointed at equity instead of ordnance. Reuse, not a second system.
- **Closed** — no external equity, ever. The designer's lever to put specific firms permanently out of reach.

Two states would make "private" a synonym for "unavailable", which is dead content. Three makes private the **negotiated middle** — and the game already owns the verb for negotiating. Derivation in **BL-526 (ownership-class derivation)**.

**3. Valuation and the profit split.** A corporation needs a price (**BL-527**, corporation valuation) and a way to pay its holders (**BL-528**, dividends and the payout dial).

## What is reuse, and must stay reuse

- **An equity price is a price.** It should go through `resolve_price` — price band, EMA smoothing, the existing order book — not a parallel valuation engine. `MARKETS.md` owns that machinery and should keep owning it.
- **Earnings already exist.** `FINANCE.md`'s per-building profitability is the input; a corporation's value is book assets plus a multiple on smoothed trailing profit.
- **Ownership class is DERIVED, not authored** — the principle BL-219 established when it retired the authored focus-weighting table. The derivation source is to hand: a region whose history produced strong enforceable-promise institutions (`docs/lore/HISTORY.md`'s Charter Age) yields public corporations; a late or statist industrialiser yields private or closed ones — reading the **same BL-218 industrialisation-timing scalar the focus derivation already reads**. One mapping, no new machinery, and a coherent outcome: a late statist industrialiser with closely-held, raw-heavy firms is a recognisable thing.

## The standing-rule question, and the ruling — CONTROL AT MAJORITY (Ben, 2026-08-21)

`.claude/rules/io-standing-rules.md` § Determinism & data model: *"The player's own corp is never auto-acted on strategically."* Corporations that self-run **while the player owns them** puts that rule's **subject** in question.

**Ben's ruling (2026-08-21, resolving NR-491): equity DOES confer operating control above a majority threshold.** This **overturns** the decision taken on his behalf earlier the same day, which had said equity is never a control seam at any fraction. The recommendation is superseded; what follows is the design under his ruling, including an honest account of the three costs the "never" position was defending against — they do not vanish, they become costs to manage.

### The rule, restated

> A corporation has a **controlling holder**: the syndicate holding **> 50%** of its shares, or none if no syndicate is above the line. A corporation whose controlling holder is the player's syndicate **is the player's corp** for the purposes of the standing rule, and is therefore **never auto-acted on strategically**. Every other corporation — minority-held, unheld, or controlled by a rival syndicate — runs itself on its own `corp_ai` scorer exactly as today.

Control is **derived, never stored as an independent flag**. It is a pure function of the equity relation, recomputed rather than cached, so it cannot drift out of agreement with the shares that define it. Two stored copies of one fact is how they diverge (the same argument BL-525 makes for the reverse-lookup index).

### The three costs, and what pays them

**1. Micromanagement.** The "never" position was defending the economic premise: the player must not end up managing an entire economy. Under the ruling the exposure is **bounded by majority stakes held**, not by corporations in the world — hold majorities in three corporations and you have three build queues, not eighty-eight.

That bound is not merely a mitigation; it is the mechanic's central trade-off. **Control costs attention.** A syndicate can spread thin and stay purely financial, or concentrate and take the wheel — and the second choice is genuinely more powerful *and* genuinely more work. That is a better strategic question than either pure alternative, and it is the strongest argument for Ben's ruling over the recommendation.

It does mean the **opening portfolio's shape is now load-bearing**: BL-526's carve seeds each syndicate with majority stakes, so an opening that carves five ways hands the player five build queues on turn one. The carve count must be tuned against attention, not just against portfolio interest. Recorded there.

**2. The scorer's uniform iteration forks.** This cost is **real and is now paid**. `corp_ai.cpp` must skip any corporation whose controlling holder is the player's syndicate — a gate that did not exist before. Constraints on it, all binding:

- The check is **deterministic** and reads the equity relation directly.
- It must **not shift any other corporation's cadence slot**, on the BL-409 precedent — the index is over the sorted corp set, so excluding a corporation from *acting* must not renumber the others.
- Under `corp_ai_params::spectating` the gate has **no subject** and every corporation evaluates, exactly as BL-409 established: the prohibition protects a corp *because a human owns it*, and spectate removes the owner.

Owned by **BL-529 (rival syndicate behaviour)**.

**3. The prohibition's subject.** The "never" position kept the subject readable off the type. Under the ruling it is readable off **one derived predicate** instead — `controlling_holder == player_syndicate` — which is nearly as crisp, provided control stays derived (above) and the threshold stays a single named constant rather than a per-corporation setting.

### What the ruling settles downstream

- **BL-528's open question is answered.** If majority confers *operating* control it certainly confers *financial* policy, so the majority holder sets the payout ratio. The financial-versus-operating carve that item proposed collapses — majority takes both.
- **Minority holding stays purely financial.** Below the line, equity is exactly what the overturned ruling described: a claim on profit and nothing else. So both readings survive, split by the threshold, rather than one replacing the other.

### Newly open, raised BY the ruling (NR-499)

**Control changes hands mid-campaign, and nothing yet says what that feels like.** Cross above 50% and a corporation the scorer was running becomes yours to drive; fall below and it reverts. Unaddressed: whether reversion is immediate or lagged, what happens to a build order in flight, and whether a hostile syndicate can take control *of a corporation the player controls* by buying past them — which is an acquisition contest, and the same relational threshold BL-450 (rivals score stance) needed its own dated grant to cross.

## Why this is not a fourth identity pivot

It reads like one — corporation → governing body → militia → investor — and that reading is wrong in a way worth stating, because the churn concern is real and this item should not be filed under it.

**BL-094 (player-identity pivot) already settled that companies are arm's-length counterparties**, not the player's economic arm; `GLOSSARY.md` § Corporation states it in those words. And BL-094 left one thing explicitly open:

> *"The exact shape of the militia's non-mandate revenue (contract income, requisition, plunder) is left for BL-350 or a later item — this rewrite states only that the mandate is the prototype's funding floor."*

**Equity income is an answer to that open question.** It does not replace the identity; it *funds* it. In the live ancient arc the same holds with the mercenary company in the militia's seat (`ROADMAP.md` § The two arcs — *"BL-094's militia one era earlier, the same shape"*): you are paid to fight, and you put the proceeds into the workshops that arm you.

## The dilemma this creates — why it earns its space

Under the house rule every system justifies itself by feeding **Trade or Conflict** (`io-standing-rules` § Tone). This feeds both, through one tension:

**You buy from corporations you part-own.** Squeeze a supplier on price and you take it back out of your own equity in that supplier. Fatten it and you pay more for your ordnance, but the position appreciates. Neither side of that trade dominates, and both sides are already-built machinery — the order book on one side, the profit split on the other.

That is also the answer to BL-094's replaced design test — *does this change what the militia can FIELD, or what it must ANSWER TO?* Equity changes what you can afford to field, and a stake in a supplier changes whether that supplier can afford to refuse you.

## Children, in dependency order

- **BL-525** — equity data model + serialisation (the foundation; everything else waits on it).
- **BL-526** — ownership class derived from the history ladder, **plus the named-corp → syndicate + carved-corporations split** described above.
- **BL-527** — corporation valuation and the share price.
- **BL-528** — dividends, retained earnings, and the payout dial.
- **BL-529** — **rival syndicate behaviour** — the new strategic behaviour proper, and the one the symmetry rule makes mandatory.
- **BL-530** — the portfolio ledger.

## Open — NOT settled here

- ~~The count~~ — **SETTLED (Ben, 2026-08-21, NR-493): seven syndicates in total, the player one of them.** `corporation_count` drops 8 → 7 and the carve runs over seven named corps. Taken literally from Ben's original "instead we have 7 corporations", against the recommendation to keep 8 as the no-change option.
- **The minor (NR-494).** These items carry a proposed `v0.1.23` that `ROADMAP.md` does not yet name.
- **Does the player's seat become a syndicate, or hold one?** In the live ancient arc the player is a mercenary company (`ROADMAP.md` § The two arcs). A mercenary company that *holds* a syndicate and a mercenary company that *is* one are different games. Not settled here; it belongs to BL-094 (player-identity pivot).

## Authority propagation

**Carried NOW, per Ben's 2026-08-21 instruction** ("work it into design including CLAUDE and README"): `CLAUDE.md` and `README.md` carry the **framing**, marked forward-looking and clearly unlanded — the same shape NR-053 used for the governing-body framing, and in both cases also correcting a stale "governing body" line that BL-094's 2026-08-10 militia rewrite had already superseded. `GLOSSARY.md` carries the **Syndicate** term marked *designed, not built*, on the precedent of its own **Militia** entry (which is marked exactly that way for BL-094) — a term used across seven items with no glossary entry is the drift GLOSSARY exists to prevent.

**Owed ON LANDING, not now** (authority time-slice): `GENERATION_STRATEGY.md` § The economic premise (the tier becomes load-bearing), `CORPORATION_GENERATION.md` (the syndicate carve + ownership class), `MARKETS.md` (equity through `resolve_price`), `FINANCE.md` (dividends as a sixth flow).

items.title: Equity data model — integer shares, an ownership relation, and the save seam
items.summary: The foundation of BL-524 (ownership tier): which syndicate holds what fraction of which corporation. INTEGER share counts, never float fractions — float ownership accumulates error across ticks and the simulation is deterministic by standing rule. Adds an ownership_class enum to corporation_component, a holdings relation on the new syndicate entity, and a DERIVED controlling_holder query (> 50%) that NR-491 needs and that must never become a stored flag, and versions the save format. Every other equity item waits on this one.
items.design:
Foundation item for **BL-524 (ownership tier)**. Nothing else in the equity cluster can start until this lands.

## Integer shares, not float fractions — the load-bearing call

Ownership must be **integer share counts** (`shares_outstanding`, `shares_held`), not `float fraction`.

The reason is the standing rule, not taste: *"The simulation is deterministic"* (`io-standing-rules` § Determinism & data model). A float fraction is mutated every time shares change hands, and repeated add/subtract on a normalised float **accumulates representational error** — so a long campaign can drift a holder's stake, and worse, drift it *differently* on a replay of the same seed once the operation order shifts. Integer share arithmetic is exact and replays byte-identically.

It also makes two things free that the float model makes fiddly: the total is checkable (Σ held == outstanding, a cheap harness assertion), and a partial sale has no rounding question.

Percentages are a **display** concern — computed at render time, never stored.

## Shape

On `corporation_component` (the operating firm):

- `ownership_class` — `{ public, private, closed }`. Set by **BL-526 (syndicate carve + ownership class)**; defaults to `closed` so an ungenerated or legacy corp is inert rather than accidentally tradeable.
- `shares_outstanding` (`uint32_t`) — `0` for a corp no one can hold.

On the new `syndicate_component` (the holder):

- `holdings` — its positions in operating corporations: `vector<equity_holding>` where `equity_holding = { entity_id corporation; uint32_t shares; }`.
- `balance` — its own cash, distinct from any corporation's.

**Held on the holder, not the corporation.** The holder-side list is the one iterated every tick (valuing a portfolio, paying dividends into a balance); the corporation-side question ("who owns me") is rarer and derivable. If profiling later shows the reverse lookup is hot, add a **rebuilt-on-load index**, never a second serialised copy — two stored copies of one fact is how they diverge.

## Controlling holder — derived, never stored

Ben's NR-491 ruling (equity confers operating control above **> 50%**) means something must answer "who controls this corporation". It is a **query over the equity relation, not a field**: `controlling_holder(corporation)` returns the syndicate above the threshold, or none.

Deriving it rather than storing it is the same argument this item already makes against a second serialised copy of the reverse lookup — a stored control flag and the shares that define it are two copies of one fact, and they diverge the first time a partial sale is applied without updating both. The threshold itself is **one named constant**, not a per-corporation setting, so the predicate stays uniform.

Cheap to compute: it needs the corporation's holders, which is the reverse lookup, so if profiling makes control hot it is the **rebuilt-on-load index** above that answers it — still not a stored flag.

## Determinism of iteration

`holdings` must be kept in a **deterministic order** — sorted by `entity_id` on insert. An unordered container keyed by pointer or hash gives a different iteration order between runs, and dividend accumulation into a float `balance` is order-sensitive. This is the same class of bug the project already guards against by iterating the sorted corp set for cadence slots (BL-409).

## Serialisation

New arrays on the flat-binary seam, so this is a **save-format version bump** — the seam TECH_FOUNDATIONS owns, and the reason this item is `M` rather than `S`. Write `shares_outstanding` and `ownership_class` per corporation, then the syndicate array with each one's `holdings` run. A pre-bump save loads with `ownership_class = closed`, `shares_outstanding = 0`, and no syndicates at all — which is exactly today's behaviour, so the upgrade path is inert rather than lossy.

## Verification

A `tools/verify/` headless harness (`equity_conservation.cpp`, on the model of `money_conservation`): shares are **conserved** — for every corporation, Σ held across all syndicates plus unissued == `shares_outstanding`, asserted after N ticks of trading. Conservation harnesses are the project's existing idiom for exactly this class of invariant.

## Not in scope

No trading verb, no valuation, no dividend — those are BL-527/BL-528/BL-529. This item lands the **fact of ownership** and nothing that moves it.

## FILE SCOPE CORRECTED 2026-08-22 (hotspot audit)

Declared `src/world/serialisation.cpp`. **It does not exist, and no item in the backlog creates
it.** There is no whole-world serialiser in this project: the seam is **sectional** — each subsystem
writes its own flat-binary stream (`order_book`, `province`, `history_log`, `procurement`),
each with its own magic and version.

So an equity record's persistence is a **new sectional stream authored by this item**, not an edit
to a central file that was never going to be there. Three other items declare the same phantom path;
NR-537 records the set.

## CORRECTED 2026-08-23 — a world serialiser exists now

The 2026-08-22 note above says `src/world/serialisation.cpp` *"does not exist, and no item in the
backlog creates it"*, and concludes the seam is sectional. **BL-536 landed the same day and makes
half of that wrong.**

`src/world/world_save.{hpp,cpp}` (847 lines) plus `binary_io.hpp` (442) are a **whole-world
snapshot**: a uint8 per enum, length-prefixed strings and containers, ceilings on both to stop a
corrupt length sizing an allocation, and every enum read back through `r_enum` against a named
maximum so an out-of-range byte is **rejected rather than cast**.

**What survives from the old note:** the path `serialisation.cpp` still does not exist, so this
item's file list was right to drop it. **What changes:** an equity record does not need a new
sectional stream of its own — it needs **fields on `corporation_component` that world_save
writes**, which is a much smaller job, and it inherits the range-gated reader for free.

**And a constraint that did not apply yesterday now does:** any enum this item adds is append-only
for real, against a live save format, rather than against a future one.

items.title: The syndicate carve, and public / private / closed DERIVED from the history ladder
items.summary: Two generation jobs. (1) THE CARVE: each of the 7 named corporations (corporation_count drops 8 to 7 per NR-493) splits into a syndicate plus one or more operating corporations carved from its former holdings, the syndicate seeded holding a majority stake in each — so every syndicate starts with a portfolio rather than an empty balance sheet. (2) OWNERSHIP CLASS: assigns each generated corporation its ownership_class from its home region history rather than an authored table — the same principle BL-219 established when it retired the authored focus-weighting table, reading the SAME BL-218 industrialisation-timing scalar the focus derivation already reads. Strong enforceable-promise institutions yield public corporations; late or statist industrialisers yield private or closed ones. One mapping, no new machinery.
items.design:
Requires **BL-525 (equity data model)** for the fields to exist.

## Job 1 — the carve

Today's named corporations own buildings — **seven of them** under Ben's NR-493 ruling, down from eight. A syndicate holds equity and does not operate, so those assets cannot travel with it (see BL-524 § The generation consequence the rename surfaced).

Each named corp therefore **splits**: one syndicate, plus one or more operating corporations carved from its former holdings, with the syndicate seeded holding a **majority stake** in each. A carved corporation **inherits its parent's `industrial_focus`**, so the specialists premise survives untouched. The ~80 background firms are unaffected — they are already operating corporations and simply become available to hold.

How many corporations each named corp carves into is the tuning question: one is simplest and gives a syndicate a single concentrated position; two or three make the opening portfolio a real object with something to trade. **Recommendation: carve on focus boundaries** — a corp holding both mines and refineries carves into an extraction corporation and a processing one — so the split is explicable from the holdings rather than arbitrary.

## Job 2 — ownership class: derived, not authored

**BL-219** already made this argument for `industrial_focus` and won it: an authored weighting table was retired in favour of derivation from the corp's home region history, on the reasoning that *"two mechanisms deciding one field is how that field becomes unexplainable."* Ownership class takes the same treatment for the same reason.

The derivation source is already computed. `docs/lore/HISTORY.md`'s ladder produces, per region, an **institutional strength** signal (the Charter Age's enforceable promise — stage 2) and **BL-218's industrialisation-timing scalar**, which the focus derivation reads today. This item reads the same two, so it is **one more mapping over existing outputs, not new generation machinery**.

## The mapping

- **Strong enforceable-promise institutions + early industrialisation → `public`.** Widely-held ownership needs an institution that makes a claim on a stranger's profit enforceable. Where the ladder produced that, shares can be held at arm's length.
- **Late or statist industrialisation → `private`.** Ownership stays close, transfers by negotiation. This is the **majority** case by design — it is the interesting one, and it is what feeds BL-350's negotiation seam.
- **No enforceable-promise stage, or a state-chartered origin → `closed`.** Out of reach entirely.

The coupling to focus is a **feature, not contamination** — BL-219 made the same point. A late statist industrialiser with closely-held, raw-heavy firms is a recognisable, coherent thing; a player learning to read the map learns both facts from one signal.

## The distribution is the tuning surface

The mapping's thresholds decide **how much of the world is investable**, which is the item's real dial. Too many public corporations and the portfolio is a shopping list; too few and the mechanic is inert.

**Open (Ben's, not settled here): the target public fraction.** The instinct is that `public` should be a **minority** — it is the frictionless case, and friction is where the game is — but the number wants play-testing, not authoring. State it as a named constant in one place so tuning is a data change, the same way `corp_ai_params` holds the trading thresholds.

## Determinism

Derivation consumes **no randomness** — it is a pure function of ladder outputs already fixed upstream. That keeps it out of the RNG stream entirely, so adding it cannot shift any downstream generation draw. Same discipline as the `abundance` post-multiply in tile Pass 6.

## Verification

Extend the existing generation audit harness: assert the class distribution falls in an expected band across N seeds, and that **re-running one seed reproduces every corporation's class and every carve exactly**. A distribution that collapses to one class on some seeds is the failure mode to catch.

items.title: Corporation valuation — a share price through resolve_price, not a parallel engine
items.summary: Gives an operating corporation a price. The design position is that an equity price IS a price and belongs in resolve_price’s existing machinery — price band, EMA smoothing, order book — rather than a parallel valuation engine; book value plus a multiple on smoothed trailing profit is the anchor, with FINANCE.md per-building profitability as the already-existing input. Design-owed on the multiple and on whether the order-book route survives contact.
items.design:
Requires **BL-525 (equity data model)**. `design-owed`: the position below is argued, but two calls need Ben.

## The position — an equity price is a price

`MARKETS.md` already owns price resolution: a **price band**, **EMA smoothing**, and a matched price-time **order book** with preferred-seller routing. A share price wants every one of those properties.

So the design position is: **route equity through `resolve_price`, do not build a valuation engine beside it.** This is the legible-over-clever call the tone rule asks for — a second pricing path that drifts from the first is precisely the locally-clever debt.

## The anchor

A traded price still needs something to be a price *of*. Both inputs already exist:

- **Book value** — the corporation's `balance` plus its `assets` at build cost.
- **Trailing earnings** — `FINANCE.md`'s per-building profitability, already computed per tick and already surfaced.

`anchor = book + k * ema(profit_per_tick)`. The EMA is the same smoothing `resolve_price` already applies to goods, so it is reuse rather than a second smoother with its own time constant.

## The two open calls

**1. What is `k`?** The earnings multiple sets how much a corporation's *prospects* count against its *substance*. High `k` makes the market growth-hungry and volatile; low `k` makes it a book-value shop where nothing interesting happens. It wants a named constant and play-testing, not an authored number — but the *band* it should sit in is a design question, not a tuning one.

**2. Does the order-book route actually survive contact?** Goods clear against population and background demand; shares clear against **syndicate intent only**. A thin book with ~8 possible buyers behaves differently from a goods market with ~80 participants, and it may need a market-maker or a band-clamped floor to avoid a two-order book swinging a corporation's price 10x. This is the risk that makes the item `design-owed` rather than `designed`: the reuse argument is strong, and the failure mode if it is wrong is a nonsense price on a visible surface.

**Recommendation if forced:** ship the anchor first, with the traded price band-clamped tightly around it, and loosen the band only once BL-529 (rival equity behaviour) gives the book real participants. An anchor-only price is boring but never absurd; an unclamped thin book is absurd on its first tick.

## Private and closed corporations

A `private` corporation has **no traded price** — only the anchor, disclosed or not. That is correct and is part of the point: valuing a private corporation is a judgement the player makes with incomplete information, which is what `DISCOVERY.md`'s activity fog is already for. A `closed` corporation needs no valuation at all.

## Not in scope

Dividends (**BL-528**) and who trades (**BL-529**).

items.title: Dividends and retained earnings — the payout dial as the holder’s only lever
items.summary: Splits an operating corporation’s profit between retained earnings (which fund its own corp_ai growth) and dividends (paid pro-rata to the syndicates holding it). Adds a sixth flow to apply_budget’s five. The payout ratio is deliberately the syndicate’s ONLY lever over a corporation — the counterweight that makes BL-524’s no-operating-control ruling a design rather than a restriction. Who sets it is now ANSWERED (Ben, NR-491): the majority holder, since operating control implies financial policy. Below the threshold the ratio is not yours, which is what makes crossing the majority line a real objective.
items.design:
Requires **BL-525 (equity data model)**. `design-owed` on one call, stated below.

## The split

An operating corporation's per-tick profit divides:

- **Retained** — stays in the corporation's `balance`, and is therefore what its own `corp_ai` scorer spends on building, hiring and surveying. This is "growing itself", in Ben's phrase.
- **Distributed** — paid **pro-rata by share count** into each holding syndicate's `balance`.

`FINANCE.md`'s `apply_budget` has five flows (income / expenditure / maintenance / wages / interest). Dividends are a **sixth**, and must run **after** the other five — a corporation distributes what survives its obligations, never ahead of its wage bill. Getting that order wrong lets a corporation pay a dividend it cannot afford and then miss payroll, which would read as a bug in the money loop rather than a policy.

## Why the payout ratio matters more than it looks

**BL-524 ruled that equity confers no operating control.** The payout ratio is therefore the syndicate's **only** lever over a corporation — and that is what makes the ruling a design rather than a restriction. The dial is genuinely strategic:

- **Pay out** — cash now, and the corporation stops growing, so the position stops appreciating.
- **Retain** — no income, but the scorer compounds it, and the anchor under BL-527 rises with the earnings it produces.

That is a real trade with no dominant side, expressed as one number. It also composes with BL-524's central dilemma: a supplier you starve of retained earnings is a supplier that cannot expand to meet your own procurement.

## Who sets it — ANSWERED by Ben's NR-491 ruling (2026-08-21)

**The majority holder sets it.** This was option 2 below, and it stops being a judgement call: if a > 50% stake confers *operating* control, it self-evidently confers *financial* policy. The financial-versus-operating carve proposed below is therefore **unnecessary** — majority takes both, and no line needs drawing between them.

What survives, and matters: **below the threshold the payout ratio is not yours**. A minority holding is exactly what the overturned "never" ruling described — a claim on profit and nothing else. So a minority holder's only real lever is whether to keep holding, which is what makes crossing the majority line a genuine strategic objective rather than a bigger version of the same thing.

The options are kept below as the record of how the call was reached.

## The original open call — who sets it

Three candidates, and the fork is genuine:

1. **The corporation sets it** (its own scorer picks, per its growth appetite). Cleanest, keeps `corp_ai` uniform, but leaves the syndicate with **no lever at all** — which would make BL-524's ruling into exactly the restriction it is meant not to be.
2. **A majority-holding syndicate sets it.** Gives the strategic reason to accumulate past 50%, which the game wants. But it is a control seam, and BL-524 just ruled control out — so it needs an explicit carve: *financial* policy is a holder right, *operating* policy is never one.
3. **The home nation caps it** (a law or charter term). Fits the ancient arc's polities and ties into the policy strand, but it depends on a nation-actor layer that is still forming.

**Recommendation: 2, with the carve stated explicitly.** It is the only one that makes majority ownership *mean* something without reopening the build queue, and the distinction it needs — how profit is split is financial, what gets built is operating — is a line a player will find intuitive. It should be Ben's call, not taken here, because it directly qualifies a ruling already taken on his behalf in BL-524 (NR-491).

## Verification

Extend `money_conservation`: dividends **move** money between balances and never create it. Σ all balances must be unchanged by the distribution step alone. This is the harness idiom the project already has for the money loop, and it is the assertion that catches a pro-rata rounding leak.

items.title: Rival syndicate behaviour — holders that buy, sell and negotiate for corporations
items.summary: THE NEW STRATEGIC BEHAVIOUR, and the item the symmetry rule makes mandatory: rival syndicates must invest as the player does. Adds equity verbs to the corp_command seam (buy/sell shares, open a negotiation for a private stake, set payout), scores them in corp_ai.cpp’s existing deterministic candidate list, and owns the NR-491 CONTROL GATE — corp_ai must skip any corporation the player’s syndicate majority-holds, without shifting any other corp’s cadence slot, capped per evaluation and subject to the solvency gate. Explicitly a widening of the BL-202/BL-203 exception in its established shape, not a new actor class.
items.design:
Requires **BL-525** (the relation), **BL-527** (a price to trade at) and **BL-528** (a reason to hold). This is the *new corporation behaviour* **BL-524 (ownership tier)** exists to enable.

## Why it is mandatory, not optional

`CONCEPT.md` § Symmetrical rules: *"All non-player factions operate under the same ruleset as the player, or a deliberate, defined subset. No hidden AI exceptions."* If the player can buy into a corporation and a rival cannot, the ownership tier is a player-only cheat and the world stops being a contest. **The mechanic is not shippable without this item.**

## It is a widening in the ESTABLISHED shape, not a new actor class

This matters for the standing rule. `io-standing-rules` sanctions a **deterministic scored-utility** layer for background corporations over the `corp_command` seam — build, demolish, survey, road (BL-202/BL-203), plus standing sell orders (BL-293) and hiring (BL-324). Each was admitted as *"one more legal verb on the same deterministic scored-utility layer, not a planner of its own."*

Equity verbs are admitted on identical terms. **Nothing here is a planner**: no multi-turn acquisition strategy, no modelling of another corp's intent, no hidden state. A candidate is scored this tick from present world state, and the highest-scoring legal verb is issued.

## The verbs

On `corp_command`, so the player, the scorer and the MCP word interface all reach them identically:

- `buy_shares(corporation, count)` — `public` only; clears against BL-527's book.
- `sell_shares(corporation, count)`.
- `open_stake_negotiation(corporation, count)` — `private` only; routes into **BL-350 (procurement/contract seam)**'s quote / lead-time / **refusal** machinery. A private corporation refusing to sell a stake is the same object as a supplier refusing to sell ordnance, and should be the same code.
- `set_payout_ratio(corporation, ratio)` — gated on whatever BL-528 settles for who may set it.

**Every one of these must land in `ACTIONS.json`.** The dictionary is *transcribed* from `corp_command.hpp`, not authored, and a stale entry misleads the AI player the way a stale golden misleads a visual check.

## Scoring

Equity candidates join the existing candidate list rather than forming a second pass — that is what keeps the layer one scorer. Utility reads what is already computed: BL-527's anchor against the asking price, BL-528's expected dividend against the corp's own cost of capital, and a **concentration penalty** so a rival syndicate does not sink its whole treasury into one position.

**Cap at one equity action per evaluation**, exactly as BL-324 capped hiring. Uncapped, a syndicate with cash empties the book in a single tick and the market never has a second participant.

## The solvency gate — and why BL-324's ruling does NOT transfer

BL-394/NR-218 settled that for `hire_unit`, *"never on cash" governs AVAILABILITY, not spend*: which roster rows are offered is decided by stockpile and market access alone, while the spend is gated.

**That ruling does not transfer here, and the difference should be stated rather than inherited.** A hire has a non-cash precondition (the goods must exist); a share purchase has **none** — it is a purely financial act. So for equity, cash gates **both** availability and spend: a syndicate cannot see a position it could not fund. Carrying BL-324's asymmetry across would offer rivals positions they can never take, which is noise in the candidate list rather than a widening.

The spend itself is subject to the ordinary reserve floor and must **reserve against later candidates in the same evaluation**, as hiring does.

## The control gate — the fork Ben's NR-491 ruling pays for

> **Coordinate with BL-523 (corp kind axis) before building.** That item adds a *kind* gate to this
> same candidate loop and was authored in a parallel branch the same day; the two are orthogonal
> axes but should land as **one gating mechanism**, not two independently-added filters. See
> BL-524 § Collision with BL-523, and NR-500.


This item owns the cost the "never" recommendation was defending against. `corp_ai.cpp` must **skip any corporation whose `controlling_holder` is the player's syndicate** — a gate on the previously uniform non-player iteration.

Three binding constraints:

1. **Deterministic**, read from the equity relation via BL-525's derived query — never from a cached flag.
2. **It must not shift any other corporation's cadence slot.** BL-409 established that admitting one more corp shifts no rival's slot because the index is over the *sorted corp set*; excluding one from **acting** must preserve that property exactly. Skipping must happen at the act step, not by removing the corporation from the iterated set.
3. **Under `corp_ai_params::spectating` the gate has no subject** and every corporation evaluates — the BL-409 rule verbatim: the prohibition protects a corp *because a human owns it*, and spectate removes the owner.

A rival syndicate's controlled corporations are **not** gated — they are auto-acted on like everything else. The gate's subject is the human, not the fact of control.

## Determinism

The binding constraint, and the whole basis of every grant above. The scorer stays **pure, seeded and replayable**; equity iteration order is fixed by BL-525's sorted `holdings`; ties break on `entity_id`, never on iteration order. Verify with a determinism harness on the `spectator_determinism` model — same seed, same equity state after N ticks, byte-identical.

## Open

**Should a rival syndicate ever take a stake in a corporation ANOTHER syndicate majority-holds?** That is an acquisition contest, and it is the point at which equity stops being a financial layer and becomes a relational one — the same threshold **BL-450 (rivals score stance)** crossed for hostility, which needed its own dated grant. Not assumed here; flag before building it.

items.title: The portfolio ledger — what I hold, what it earns, what it is worth
items.summary: The surface for BL-524 (syndicate tier) — holdings, cost basis, current value, dividend income, and the payout dial. Needs its question_log.json pair (the question it answers, why it earns its space, the item that demanded it) before it is built; that pair is required on every surface and its wording is Ben’s, so the item is design-owed by construction rather than by omission.
items.design:
The player-facing half of **BL-524 (ownership tier)**. `design-owed` **by construction**: `question_log.json` requires every surface to declare the question it answers and why it earns its space, entries marked `drafted` are explicitly *"awaiting Ben's wording and are open questions, not settled prose"*, and this surface has no entry yet.

## The question it should answer

Drafted, for Ben to accept or rewrite: **"What do I own, what is it paying me, and what is it worth now?"**

## Why it earns its space

BL-524 ruled that equity confers no operating control, so a syndicate's entire relationship with a corporation is **financial**. That relationship has no home on any existing surface: the budget ledger shows the five `apply_budget` flows, the Corporation lens shows presence on the map, and neither can show a position. Without this surface the ownership tier is legible only as a number moving in the header — which is the definition of a mechanic that does not earn its space.

## Content

Per holding: corporation, shares held, **cost basis**, current value (BL-527's anchor or traded price), unrealised gain, and trailing dividend income. Cost basis is the one that must be **stored** rather than derived — nothing else in the world remembers what you paid, and without it "is this position working" is unanswerable.

Plus the **payout dial** per holding, wherever BL-528 lands the right to set it.

## Controlled versus financial holdings

Ben's NR-491 ruling splits the portfolio in two, and the surface has to show the split: a **controlled** holding (> 50%) carries a build queue you are answerable for; a **minority** holding is a pure claim on profit. A player who cannot tell at a glance which of their positions they are *running* will neglect one, and the neglected build queue is the expensive kind of surprise.

So the ledger sorts or groups on control, and a controlled row reaches its corporation's management surface. This also makes the attention cost of concentration visible at the moment the player is deciding whether to cross the line — which is where BL-524 says the real trade-off lives.

## Conventions this must obey

- **The toggle rule** — the nav-rail icon toggles the ledger; re-clicking the *active* sub-view tab closes it.
- **A live check, not just a capture** — `visual` requirements on an interactive surface need the app opened and the thing clicked (DELIVERY.md step 4). A dial and a sortable table are interactive by definition, so a green `verifier-visual` run is not sufficient evidence here.
- **`question_log.json` pair is required**, not optional.

## Open

Whether private-corporation holdings show a **value at all**, or only a cost basis and an income line. Showing a confident number for something with no market contradicts BL-527's position that a private valuation is a judgement under incomplete information — and `DISCOVERY.md`'s activity fog is the existing model for showing a stale or absent fact honestly rather than inventing one.

items.title: apply_session_close.js reformats backlog.json and requirements.json wholesale
items.summary: apply_session_close.js writes all three of its targets with JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2). Measured stored indents: backlog.json 1, requirements.json 1, golden_log.json 2 — so two of three are reformatted end-to-end on every run, burying the handful of status flips a session-close commit exists to show. Fix by detecting and preserving each file’s existing indent. Filed from NR-498.
items.design:
Found at session close on 2026-08-21 while checking whether the tool applied to a design session. It did not — nothing was delivered — but reading it surfaced this.

## The defect

`apply_session_close.js` writes all three targets with `JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2)` (lines 40, 61, 81). Measured stored indents:

| File | Stored | Written | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `docs/development/backlog.json` | 1 | 2 | **reformatted** |
| `docs/development/req/requirements.json` | 1 | 2 | **reformatted** |
| `scripts/verify/golden_log.json` | 2 | 2 | ok |

## Why it matters

It buries the change it exists to show. `backlog.json` is ~700 KB across ~490 items; a run that ships three items produces a diff touching every line, so the three status flips become unreviewable — and any accidental edit inside that diff becomes invisible.
