It also fights the ordinary tooling. `backlog_query.js`, `backlog_lint.js` and the hand-append path all round-trip at indent 1, so the next tool to touch the file flips it back and the churn alternates forever.

## Fix

**Detect and preserve each file's existing indent** rather than hardcoding the other number. Three lines, and — unlike simply changing `2` to `1` — it cannot drift again if a store is reformatted for an unrelated reason later. Re-encoding a fixed assumption is what broke it the first time.

## Verification

Run the tool over a no-op session-close (empty `delivered_items`) and assert `git diff --stat` reports **zero changed lines** on all three stores. A tool that rewrites a file it changed nothing in is the whole bug, so that is the assertion that actually catches it.

items.title: Lenses keep the province view — blend every lens across province vertices
Every legend moves beside the minimap, scrollable, in a fixed quarter of its space
items.design:
## Ben, 2026-08-22 (UI session)

> "Anything which needs a legend should use about 1/4 the minimap space with a
> scrollable legend. Pairing this, we can try to keep names shorter, and use
> text wrapping"

Three parts, all one item:

1. **A fixed home.** Legends stop painting free-hand on the canvas and move to
   a reserved region beside the minimap, sized at about a quarter of the
   minimap space. Every lens that needs a legend uses the same region.
2. **Scrollable.** The region does not grow to fit its contents. Forty nations
   scroll; they do not overflow.
3. **Shorter names and wrapping.** Long entries wrap rather than run out of the
   box, and the labels themselves get shortened where they can be.

## This is the fix for NR-503

The Country lens legend currently lists 40 nations in one ungoverned column,
runs past the bottom of the canvas and overprints the tile ledger. It is drawn
as a canvas overlay with no container, which is why nothing clips it and why
text_overflow_floor cannot see it — the text is not clipped, it is overdrawn.
A reserved, scrolling region removes the whole failure class rather than
tuning this one legend.

items.title: Tile selection becomes an accordion, with an available-buildings tab at province grain
items.design:
## Ben, 2026-08-22 (UI session)

> "we should rework tile selection. We should use the accordion for different
> types of view, and bundle the resource view into a dropdown. One new accordion
> tab would be something like an available buildings tab - which shows each
> possible resource's maximum buildings, and how many are currently built. But
> also the maximum capacity for buildings in that province"

## Three tabs, confirmed

Ben picked the set: **Terrain**, **Resources (dropdown)**, **Available
buildings**. Province and Ownership were offered and NOT chosen — do not add
them speculatively.

## The resource view becomes a dropdown

Today it is a carousel — "Iron Ore (1/7)" with prev/next arrows, so reading the
seventh resource costs six presses. It becomes a dropdown, matching
draw_lens_resource_combo, which already does exactly this for the lenses.

## Available buildings — PER PROVINCE THROUGHOUT

Ben ruled the grain explicitly: per province, not per tile with a province
footer. So every number on the tab is a province number:

- per possible resource, the **maximum** buildings the province could carry
- per possible resource, how many are **currently built**
- the province's **overall building capacity**, which is BL-513's ceiling

## The dependency worth naming

That capacity figure is BL-513 (province building limit), which landed complete
on 2026-08-21 — derived from area, infrastructure, habitability and population.
NR-406 flagged it as the first ceiling in the game that MOVES during play, and
NR-421 measured it as inert by orders of magnitude rather than by a near miss.
This tab is the first surface that shows it, so it is also the first thing that
will make either of those facts visible to a player.

items.title: A slight national hue on the base map, the blend stopping at national borders, and the Country lens retired
items.design:
## Ben, 2026-08-22 (UI session)

> "I like the idea of NR-505, we can stop blending across national borders,
> and give a slight hue for each country, replacing the national lens entirely"

Three moves in one sentence, and they only work together.

1. **The blend stops at NATIONAL borders.** BL-514 removed the province-match
   term from the corner blend so land became one continuous field. This puts a
   term back — but a different one, at a coarser grain. Within a nation the
   field stays continuous; between two nations it does not blend at all.
2. **Every tile takes a slight hue from the nation holding it.** Slight is the
   operative word: this is a wash over the terrain colour, not the saturated
   fill the Country lens used. Terrain must stay readable through it.
3. **overlay_mode::country is RETIRED.** Not hidden, not defaulted off —
   removed. The base map now answers "who holds this ground?" so a lens that
   answers only that has nothing left to do.

## Why this is the better answer to NR-505

NR-505 reported that blending Country produced a border gradient in a colour
belonging to neither nation, on the one lens whose whole job is a categorical
boundary. The entry proposed making Country fill uniformly per province. Ben
went further, and the further answer is cleaner: if nationhood is a permanent
property of the ground rather than something you switch a lens on to see, then
the border is a place the blend must not cross — at any grain, under any lens.
The artifact cannot recur, because the mean of two nation colours is never
computed anywhere.

## What to be careful about

- **The hue must not fight the texture.** BL-520 marks take their ink from the
  tile's own drawn fill, so a national wash tints the marks too. That is
  correct and self-consistent, but it means a heavy wash muddies terrain twice.
- **Retiring a lens is a wider edit than it looks.** overlay_mode::country is
  named in the lens bar, canvas_command's cycle, ACTIONS.json, LENSES.md,
  question_log.json, and several verify scripts (province_render.lua and
  lens_legend.lua both drive it by name). The enum's `count` sentinel is what
  the lens cycle takes its modulus from, so removing a member silently
  renumbers every lens after it — check anything that persists a lens index.
- **The Country legend goes with it**, which is the same legend BL-533 just
  re-homed and the one NR-503 was raised about. Retiring the lens closes that
  thread rather than reopening it.

## Ordering

This supersedes the Country half of BL-532. Do not re-tune the categorical
blend first — BL-535 removes the case entirely.

items.title: A campaign can be saved and resumed - the world-snapshot flat-binary serialiser
items.summary: The world-snapshot flat-binary serialiser BL-107 has been blocked on since 2026-07-05. Magic IOSV + version, field-wise writes, derived state rebuilt on load (corp_modifiers re-folded from earned_techs), battles included, and a separate app-envelope section carrying the sim tick, world_params, the generation_report, the app histories and a narrow ui_state slice. Motivated equally by player save/resume and by golden captures that skip the ~30-45 s cold start.
items.design:
## Ben, 2026-08-22 (design call, four questions)

> Mode: build now. Layout: field-wise, padding-immune. Envelope: all four parts.
> Battles: serialise `active_battle` too.

The item BL-107 (save-format magic + version header) has been blocked on since
2026-07-05, named there as "a WORLD-SNAPSHOT flat-binary serialiser... no backlog
item exists for it yet - file one before promoting this". This is that item.

**Two motives, one mechanism.** The player-facing one is ordinary: save a campaign,
resume it. The development one is what raised it - `make_hard_coded_world` costs
~25-38 s and the pre-game warm start another ~6 s, paid on every capture run. A
design pass that iterates on one surface pays that cold start over and over. Loading
a snapshot is ~1 s. (`--verify-all` already amortises generation across the whole
suite in ONE world; what this buys is the *iterative single-script* loop, which is
exactly the design-pass case.)

## The format

Magic `IOSV` + a `world_save_version` uint32, on the convention the three existing
streams already established - `history_log` (`IOHL`), `order_book` (`IOOB`),
`procurement` (`IOPC`). A mismatch is REJECTED, never reinterpreted.

**Field-wise writes, not raw struct blocks** (Ben's call). TECH_FOUNDATIONS says
"tile structs *will be* written and read as raw binary", and raw would have been
faster for the ~50k tiles that dominate the ~17 MB. Field-wise was chosen anyway:
the schema still moves weekly, and a padding-baked layout turns every field addition
into a silent misread caught only if someone remembers the version bump. The three
shipped streams are all field-wise; a fourth that was not would be the odd one out.

## Three buckets, and the second is the one that bites

1. **Serialised.** bodies, tiles, buildings, markets, stockpiles, units, population
   centres (+ `population_centre_tile`, `population_centre_name`), nations,
   `tile_to_nation`, corporations, `corp_body_pools`, convoys, trade routes,
   `history_log`, `provinces`, `battles`, the order book, procurement, the stance
   tables, `earned_techs`, `laws`, `workforce_supply_overrides`,
   `body_last_glimpse_tick`, `belt`, the well-known entities, and every id counter
   including the private `m_next_id` (which needs an accessor - a load that restarts
   id allocation from 1 would collide with every live entity).
2. **Derived - rebuilt on load, never read.** `body_tile_index`, `astar_cost_cache`,
   `body_reach_cost`, `body_market_index` (+ its two stamps), `ai_decisions`,
   `current_day_tick`, and **`corp_modifiers`**. That last one is the trap: it is
   accumulated at tech-earn time and deliberately not hashed, so a save that neither
   writes it nor rebuilds it silently drops every earned buff, and `state_hash`
   would not notice. Already recorded as a change-note on BL-107, 2026-08-19.
3. **The app envelope** - outside `world`, and all four parts are in scope per Ben:
   the sim tick + `world_params`; the `generation_report` in full; the app-owned
   per-tick histories; and a narrow `ui_state` slice (`primary_level`, `active_body`,
   `selected_entity`, `selected_province`, `overlay`, and the three camera
   zoom/pan triples). NOT the whole 632-line `ui_state` - transient panel and paging
   state has no business surviving a load.

**The envelope is a separate stream section from the world snapshot**, so `world/*`
stays SDL- and UI-free and the headless harness can exercise the world half alone.
`src/world/world_save.{hpp,cpp}` writes the world; `src/core/save_game.{hpp,cpp}`
wraps it with the envelope.

## Battles are IN, reversing a standing comment

`world.hpp` says of `battles`: "NOT SERIALISED, deliberately and on precedent...
A save taken mid-battle therefore drops the fight - acceptable while nothing can
save mid-tick, and the thing to revisit first if that changes." Ben's 2026-08-22
call revisits it. `campaign_battle_state` carries `rng_state` and `stream_seed`, so
a restored battle continues on the same stream rather than re-rolling - which is the
only version of this worth having. The sorted (province, attacker, defender) order
is preserved across the trip, since that ordering is what recovers order-independence
from the unordered containers battles are discovered from.

## What this does NOT do

No autosave cadence, no save-slot UI, no compression, no cross-version migration.
BL-107's header is the version guard and rejection is the whole migration story for
the prototype - broader versioning stays deferred until the data model stabilises.

**Authority on landing:** `docs/tech/TECH_FOUNDATIONS.md` § Save model /
Serialisation, whose present claims are written in the future tense specifically
because this did not exist.

items.title: The national budget — a nation allocates its treasury across weighted priorities, and that allocation is what a nation IS
items.summary: The spend side the treasury has never had. A nation holds a weighted allocation over priority lines; each tick it spends its treasury down those lines, and every credit leaves as a DIRECT TRANSFER to a corporation. Answers NATIONS.md Q1 (what is a treasury for) and is the substrate BL-539 (lobbying) shifts.
items.design:
## Why this is the spine item and not a feature

Ben, 2026-08-22, settling NATIONS.md Q1: *"Treasury can be used for things that it is used for in
the real world. Logistics maintenance, Schooling, Military research, Academic research, public
space exploration."*

Before this item a nation's treasury only ever **rose**. Two flows credited it (the extraction levy
and the import tariff) and nothing anywhere debited it, so a nation's balance was a scoreboard with
no game attached. That is the defect NR-398 flagged and this item closes.

It is the spine because three other items hang off it and are meaningless without it. BL-539
(lobbying) shifts **these weights**. BL-542 (the nation scorer) chooses **these weights**. BL-538
names **these lines**. Build this first or build nothing.

## The object

```
struct nation_budget
{
    std::array<float, priority_count> weights;   // normalised, sums to 1.0
    float                             reserve_fraction;  // held back, not spent
};
```

Carried on `nation_component`, beside `treasury`. **Weights, not amounts** — a nation states
what it cares about, and the amounts follow from what it has. That makes a poor nation and a rich
nation with the same character behave recognisably alike, which is what makes political character
legible across a campaign.

## The three rules that keep it honest

**1. Every credit out is a DIRECT TRANSFER to a named corporation.** Ben's Q2 ruling:
*"Payment to corps is direct and not on the market."* So a budget line does not bid, does not
clear, and does not touch `clear_markets`. It debits the treasury and credits a corp balance in
the same float, in the same tick — the same conservation shape the levy and tariff already have
(`law_author_harness` R1, `money_conservation`). A harness row asserts it per line.

This is the rule that stops the budget becoming a second, hidden market. It also means the whole
system inherits the conservation guarantee for free rather than needing a new argument.

**2. Nations save.** Ben, Q2: *"Nations should be able to save up, and so should corps."* So a
nation does **not** spend to zero each tick. `reserve_fraction` is held back, and an underspent
line accumulates rather than evaporating. A treasury that must be emptied every tick would make
saving impossible and would turn every windfall into immediate noise.

**3. Weights are normalised, spending is bounded by the treasury.** A nation cannot allocate what
it does not hold. Where a line's demand exceeds its share, the line is partially filled and says
so — never overdrawn, never silently dropped.

## Determinism

The pass runs once per economy tick, in sorted nation-id order, over lines in a fixed authored
order. Float accumulation is therefore the same sequence every run. It issues only transfers, is
pure over `const world&` plus the two mutations it makes, and consumes no RNG — the same shape the
2026-08-18 grant requires of any nation behaviour (`.claude/rules/io-standing-rules.md`).

## What this item does NOT own

Which lines exist (BL-538). How the weights are chosen (BL-542). How a corporation changes them
(BL-539). This item owns the **object, the pass and the conservation guarantee** — the machinery a
nation spends through, with the weights authored as a flat default until BL-542 lands.

## The check

`nation_budget_harness`: (1) conservation per line — treasury debited equals corp balances
credited, bit-exact, over any tick span; (2) a nation with an empty treasury spends nothing and
errors nowhere; (3) `reserve_fraction` is respected — a nation with weights summing to 1.0 and a
reserve of 0.2 never spends more than 80% of what it holds; (4) two runs of one seed produce
identical treasuries and identical corp credits; (5) with every weight zero the world is
bit-identical to the pre-item build (the inertness rule BL-343 and BL-480 both ship under).

---

> ⟳ **2026-08-23 — the mechanism has landed; the item has not.** `src/world/nation_budget.{hpp,cpp}`
> is in the build and `tools/verify/nation_budget_harness.cpp` is green at 36/36, plain and under
> AddressSanitizer + UBSan. What is still owed is everything that makes it MOVE: nothing produces a
> `budget_claim` (BL-538 owns what a line buys), nothing authors a `nation_budget` (BL-542's nation
> scorer does), nothing calls `run_national_budget` from the economy tick, and the weight vector has
> no serialisation seam because it has no writer yet. The pass is INERT by construction until then —
> a world where no nation authors a budget is bit-identical to the pre-item build, and R2 asserts it.
>
> **Two defects were fixed before it landed**, both found by the Sprint N1 adversarial pass and both
> now guarded by rows that fail against the pre-fix code:
> * a claim carrying a `line` outside the enum was an out-of-bounds write (`budget_priority` is
>   `uint8_t`-backed, so 0..255 are valid values while only 0..8 are valid indices). ASan-confirmed.
>   The gather loop now drops the whole claim, per the untrusted-input-boundary rule.
> * the spend bound was a decremented remainder, which drops the low bits of every pay it subtracts
>   and therefore under-counts. Over 512 generated shapes it overdrew 156 times and drove 26 solvent
>   treasuries NEGATIVE — not cosmetic, because the `treasury > 0` gate then locks that nation out of
>   spending on every following tick. The bound is now a running total of what has been paid.
>
> **Rule 1's conservation claim was NARROWED** rather than the code changed — see NR-546. The pass
> debits exactly what it credits, bit-exactly, for any weights; the world's total credit afterwards is
> exact only where each credit is representable at its destination, because `balance += amount`
> rounds. That is the rounding `apply_budget` has always carried, not a leak.

items.title: The nine priority lines — what a nation actually buys, each mapped to machinery that already exists
items.summary: Names the lines BL-537's budget spends down. Five are Ben's (2026-08-22); four more were proposed at his request and are marked as such. Every line is deliberately mapped onto a system Io already ships, so a line is a new consumer of old machinery rather than a new subsystem.
items.design:
## The rule this item is written under

**A priority line must spend through machinery that already exists.** A line that needs a new
subsystem is not a line, it is a separate item wearing a budget's clothes. This is what keeps a
nine-line budget from being nine unbuilt features.

Each line below names the code it spends through. Where none exists, the line is marked
`[NEEDS A HOST]` and is explicitly out of the first cut.

## Ben's five (2026-08-22, settling NATIONS.md Q1)

**1. Logistics maintenance.** Pays corporations to place and maintain road. Spends through the
shipped `place_road` verb and `road_generation`; the beneficiary is whichever corp does the
work. Load-bearing because of BL-325's ruling 3 — **economic reach IS military reach** — so a
nation funding roads is funding force projection for everyone inside its borders, including
companies it may later regret helping.

**2. Schooling.** Raises the productivity of labour in the nation's own territory. Spends through
the workforce scalar the wage formula already reads (`base_wage`, `wt_scalar`, the habitability
term in `apply_budget`). The beneficiary is every corp employing inside the jurisdiction, which
makes it the one line whose benefit a nation cannot aim.

**3. Military research** and **4. Academic research.** Both spend through `tech_gate` /
`condition_subject::science`. **This is the debit mechanism BL-478 (ancient research spend) is
missing** — NR-387 records that item as design-owed precisely because *"the debit mechanism has no
design"* and that it *"gates the 92-object ancient_tech_ladder.json becoming reachable."* A nation
research budget is that mechanism. The military/academic split is the same machinery reading two
different subsets of the ladder.

**5. Public exploration.** Funds surveys. Spends through `survey_system`, which already has a
paid dispatch with a cost and a duration that scale with body size and distance — the closest fit
of any line, because the mechanism is complete and merely has no funder but the player.

## Proposed at Ben's request (2026-08-22) — four more, ranked by fit

**6. Contracted force.** The nation pays a company to make a fact about the world true. **This is
BL-377's client and its money source**, and it closes the largest open loop in the game: levy →
treasury → contract → the player's income. Historically it is simply how ancient and early-modern
states raised force. Highest value of the four by a distance, and the reason is structural rather
than thematic: BL-377 is the reopened critical-path item for Sprint 16 and currently has no
counterparty with money.

**7. Strategic reserve.** The nation buys goods into a public stockpile — grain against famine,
ordnance against war. Historically the Roman *annona* and the ever-normal granary. Two properties
earn it a place: it is **countercyclical** (a nation buys when prices are low, which puts a floor
under a glut that is an actor's choice rather than an abstraction), and it is the purest form of
Ben's own reverse direction — *"corporations funded directly via taxes."*

**Conservation caution, and its fix.** This is the one line that looks like it must touch the
market, which would break BL-537's rule 1. It does not have to: buy through **BL-350's procurement
seam**, from a named supplier, at a quoted price. That keeps every credit a direct transfer, reuses
a shipped mechanism, and gets a supplier's right of refusal for free.

**8. Public works.** Temples, aqueducts, harbours. Buys standing rather than output. The Era −1
works roster (BL-321) already holds a works table at province grain; MANUAL.md § 5 lists the
campaign-era equivalent as `[OWED]`, so this line has a host **half** built. `[NEEDS A HOST]`
for the campaign grain — out of the first cut, named so the gap is visible.

**9. Charters and monopolies.** The inverse line: the nation **sells** a privilege rather than
buying a service — exclusive operating rights inside its borders, for a fee and an obligation.
This is `docs/lore/HISTORY.md`'s Charter Age arriving in the campaign era rather than staying in
the pre-history, and it is the natural place for BL-540's access dimension to be *bought* rather
than merely earned. Revenue, not spending, so it credits the treasury — the first flow to do so
that is neither a levy nor a tariff.

## First cut

Lines 1–5 (Ben's, all hosted) plus 6 (contracted force, because BL-377 needs it). Lines 7 and 9
follow once BL-350's seam is pointed at a nation. Line 8 waits on a campaign works roster.

items.title: Lobbying — a corporation spends credits to shift a nation’s budget weights, which is the only way a law subject touches law
items.summary: Corp -> nation, the forward half of Ben's 2026-08-22 channel. A corp spends credits to move a nation's priority weights; the shift is bounded, decays, and is visible. Fits the player identity exactly: a mercenary company does not pass a law, it pays someone who does.
items.design:
## Why this fits the player identity rather than straining it

The player is a **law subject, never a legislator** — MANUAL.md § 1.2, SYSTEMS.md § Policy, and
BL-094's rewrite all say so, and the 0 CE refocus did not change it. That has left a real gap since
the pivot: the player has narrow levers that reach force, and **no lever at all on the rules it
operates inside**. "Route around it, price it in, or take work somewhere else" is the whole of the
player's response to law today.

Lobbying is the one mechanism that closes the gap without breaking the identity. **You do not pass
the law. You pay someone who does.** The player stays a subject, and the subject acquires a voice.

## The verb

One new `corp_verb`, appended (the enum is serialised and append-only):

```
lobby,   ///< the corp spends `quantity` credits to move `counterparty`
         ///  (a nation) toward `order` (a priority line).
         ///  Bounded, decaying, visible.
```

It is a legal verb on the existing seam, which means the rival scorer reaches it through
`corp_ai` exactly as it reaches build, hire and place_sell_order — no parallel mechanism, no
second command type.

## The four properties that stop it being a slider

**1. Bounded.** A single spend moves a weight by at most a capped delta, authored in
`economy.lua`. No amount of money buys a nation outright in one tick. This is the difference
between influence and purchase, and it is the property that keeps a rich player from ending the
political layer on turn one.

**2. Decaying.** Influence bleeds back toward the nation's own preferred weights (BL-542's scorer
output) at an authored rate. So lobbying is a **standing cost, not a purchase** — you hold a
nation's attention or you lose it. This is also what gives a poor-but-persistent company a path
against a rich-but-inattentive one.

**3. Diminishing.** The second credit spent on the same line in the same window buys less than the
first. Without this, the optimal play is one enormous spend, and the mechanic collapses to a
threshold check.

**4. Visible.** A lobbied nation's weights are readable, and so is the fact that *someone* has been
lobbying — though not necessarily who, which is a BL-068 competitor-visibility question rather than
a new one. A player who cannot see that a rival has bought the research budget cannot respond, and
an invisible mechanic is indistinguishable from an unimplemented one.

## THE STANDING-RULE QUESTION — flagged, not assumed

A **rival** lobbying to shift a law that binds the player's corp is a *relational action taken
against a corp a human owns*. That is the same class of widening as BL-450 (rivals score stance),
which needed and received an explicit dated grant.

The 2026-08-18 nation grant covers a **nation** acting. It does not obviously cover a **rival
corporation** acting politically against the player, and reading it as though it does would be
exactly the quiet precedent `.claude/rules/io-standing-rules.md` exists to prevent.

**This item must not ship the rival half until that grant is given or refused.** The player half
and the nation-side machinery are unblocked. Raised as NR-517.

## Scale

There are roughly 88 corporations. If every one lobbies every nation every tick, the political
layer is noise. Two bounds: a corp lobbies at most one line per evaluation (the `hire_unit`
precedent, one per tick), and the scorer only values a line it can actually benefit from. The
intent is that most corps never lobby at all, and the ones that do are legible.

## The check

`lobbying_harness`: (1) a bounded spend moves the weight by exactly the capped delta and no
more; (2) with no further spend the weight decays back to the scorer's preference within the
authored window; (3) diminishing returns — two half-spends move the weight less than one whole
spend; (4) conservation: the credits leave the corp and are **consumed**, not transferred (a
lobbying fee is a cost, not a gift to the treasury — unless Ben rules otherwise, flagged);
(5) determinism across two runs of one seed; (6) inertness at zero rates.

## RULED 2026-08-22 (Ben, design register) — the rival half is GRANTED, and the fee is CONSUMED

**Q1: grant it, on the same terms as BL-450.** The blocker this item shipped with is lifted. A
rival corporation may lobby a nation against the player, deterministically, seeded, through the
scored-utility layer, issuing only the legal `lobby` verb — never a planner. Recorded as a dated
widening in `.claude/rules/io-standing-rules.md`, because its subject is a corp a human owns.

What the grant does **not** admit, stated so it is not read wider than it is: a rival **enacting**
law (only a nation can), and influence acquired by any route other than the `lobby` verb.

**Q2: the fee is CONSUMED**, as this item assumed. It is a cost, not a transfer — so the
treasury's inflows stay purely legal (levy, tariff, charter fees), and a nation never profits from
being lobbied. That last part is the real reason: a nation that profited would give BL-542's
scorer an incentive to be corruptible.

**Consequence for the harness:** the conservation row is *"the credits leave the corp and are
consumed"*, not *"arrive somewhere"* — the one flow in the corp↔nation channel that deliberately
does not conserve, and it must say so where a reader would otherwise assume the channel's rule.

items.title: A nation’s stance toward a corporation — graded, multi-dimensional, derived, and the gate on who may operate inside its borders
items.summary: Settles NATIONS.md Q6. Ben, 2026-08-22: 'Nations should have a stance towards corporations, but this is more like a digital spectrum, possibly multiple dimensions, and mostly derived towards who can act internationally in their borders.' Distinct from BL-448's corp-corp stance in all three of those ways.
items.design:
## It is NOT BL-448's stance, and the differences are the design

`src/world/stance.cpp` gives every **corp pair** a directed hostility state and a symmetric
friendship state. Nation → corp is a different object on three axes, and Ben named all three.

| | Corp → corp (BL-448) | Nation → corp (this item) |
|---|---|---|
| Shape | discrete tri-state | **graded**, a spectrum |
| Dimensions | one | **several** |
| Origin | **declared** — a corp opts in | **derived** — nobody declares it |

The last row is the load-bearing one. Hostility is *"a declared state a corp opts into"* (Ben,
2026-08-17), and a rival *"may score and declare it, never acquire it ambiently."* A nation's
stance is the opposite by construction: it is a **read** of what a corporation has actually done
inside the jurisdiction, recomputed from observable facts, never stored as a flag and never
declared by anybody.

That makes it the same kind of object as `standing.cpp`'s coarse power read — derived, honest,
no hidden state — rather than the same kind as `stance.cpp`, despite sharing the word.

## The dimensions — two, deliberately, not "possibly multiple"

Ben said *"possibly multiple dimensions."* Two is the honest first cut, and each must gate
something or it is decoration.

**Access** — *may this corp operate inside our borders?* The dimension Ben named
(*"mostly derived towards who can act internationally in their borders"*). Below a threshold, the
corp cannot place buildings or open new trade in that nation's territory. This is the first time
anything in Io gates `placement_rules` on a political fact rather than a physical one.

**Trust** — *would we contract this corp to act on our behalf?* The dimension **BL-377 needs**: a
mercenary company's client relationship has to ride on something, and inventing a parallel axis for
it when this one exists would be the duplication NATIONS.md Q6 was raised to avoid.

A third dimension is easy to add and should be resisted until one gates something.

## What it is derived FROM

All observable, all already in the world, none of it new state:

- **Domicile.** Is the corp's `home_nation` this nation? A domestic firm starts high on both.
- **Contribution.** Does it pay this nation's extraction levy — i.e. does it extract on tiles the
  nation owns? A firm that pays is a firm that counts.
- **Foreign entanglement.** Its home nation's pair-state with this one, which is where BL-541's
  directional relations feed in. Ben, Q5: nations act *"respecting historical grudges"* — a
  company from a resented nation carries that resentment.
- **Record.** Completed vs failed contracts for this nation (once BL-377 lands).
- **Conduct.** Interdiction (BL-458) inside the jurisdiction, declared hostility toward a domestic
  firm.

Recomputed on a fixed cadence in sorted order, pure, no RNG.

## THE STANDING-RULE QUESTION — same as BL-539

A nation's stance **gating the player's corp** out of a territory is a consequence imposed on a
corp a human owns, arrived at by an actor the player does not control. Whether the 2026-08-18
nation grant reaches that far is a call for Ben, not an assumption for a session. Raised as NR-517
alongside BL-539's half.

The derivation itself is uncontroversial — it is a read of public facts. **The gate is the part
that needs the grant.**

## The check

`nation_stance_harness`: (1) derivation is pure — same world, same values, twice; (2) a domestic
levy-paying corp scores above a foreign non-paying one on Access, on every seed; (3) the gate
actually gates — a corp below threshold is refused placement and the refusal names the reason;
(4) no stored flag: clearing all derived state and recomputing reproduces every value bit-exactly;
(5) inertness — with the gate threshold disabled, placement behaviour is bit-identical to today.

## RESHAPED 2026-08-22 by Ben's NR-520 ruling — sentiment is the substrate

This item's **two dimensions were right and its storage was wrong.** Access and Trust survive
unchanged as concepts, as gates, and as the thing BL-377's client relationship rides on. What
changes is that they are **dimensions of BL-545's sentiment at nation→corp grain**, not a new
per-nation table this item invents.

Everything the design says about *derived, never declared* is now the substrate's guarantee rather
than this item's own promise — which is a strengthening, because the same guarantee then covers
`corp_reputation` and the Era −1 grudges too.

**`requires` BL-545.** Build the substrate, then express these two dimensions on it.

## RULED 2026-08-22 (Ben, design register)

**The rival/player half is GRANTED** — see BL-539's note and the standing rules. A nation's derived
stance may gate the **player's** corp out of a territory.

**TWO dimensions, Access and Trust, generalised to every grain** (Q1 on RELATIONS). Not one, not
per-grain — *"a substrate whose shape varies by grain is not a substrate."* A third must gate
something before it is added.

items.title: Tariffs become directional — nation A’s duty against nation B, seeded from the pre-history as an expression of diplomacy
items.summary: Settles NATIONS.md Q4. Ben, 2026-08-22: 'This should be an emergent consequence of generation, wherein nations gain their tariffs as a directional mode of diplomacy.' Also fixes NR-400 - today no actor can enact a tariff at all, so the whole pass is dead code in a played game.
items.design:
## What changes, precisely

Today `law_effect_kind::import_tariff` resolves as **(author nation, resource) → rate**, charged
to any buyer domiciled outside the author. It is blind to *which* foreigner is buying, so it is a
posture toward the world rather than toward a neighbour.

Ben's ruling makes it directional: **(author nation, TARGET nation, resource) → rate.** A tariff
becomes a statement about a specific relationship — which is what a tariff has always been.

## The record change, and the fork worth naming

Recommended: **the tariff stays a `law` and gains a target.**

```
entity_id target_nation = null_entity;   // null == all_nations, mirroring all_resources
static constexpr int all_nations = ...;  // a blanket tariff is still expressible
```

Why this rather than moving tariffs onto the nation-pair relation: enacting a tariff **is** a
legislative act, and `law` already carries an author, a predicate, a rate and a resource scope.
Moving it out would mean two ways to charge a duty and would break the clean rule that only a
nation can author law. The sentinel mirrors `all_resources` exactly, so a blanket tariff — what
ships today — remains one record.

**The fork, stated rather than decided:** the alternative is that pair-state carries the rate and a
law merely *references* it. That reads better if tariffs later need to change without a legislative
act. It reads worse today, because nothing else in the codebase has a nation-pair table yet and
this item would have to invent one. Recommend the law field; revisit if BL-542 grows a pair table
of its own.

## Seeding from the pre-history

*"An emergent consequence of generation"* — the Era −1 sim (`history_sim.cpp`) already produces
four thousand years of polities campaigning, consolidating and losing ground. What it does not
currently do is hand the campaign a **relational residue**.

The design: at campaign setup, derive an initial directional tariff map from the pre-history's
pair outcomes — who conquered whom, who lost ground to whom, who never touched whom. A nation that
was invaded within living memory levies against its invader; distant strangers levy nothing.

Two properties this must have. It is **deterministic**: same seed, same grudges, same tariff map,
with no RNG in the derivation. And it must be **legible** — a player should be able to read a
tariff and find the war that caused it, which is what makes the pre-history worth simulating
rather than merely summarising.

## This fixes NR-400 as a side effect

NR-400 records that **nothing in `src/` can enact a tariff** — no verb, no UI, no seeding — so
`any_import_tariff_enacted` is permanently false and the entire pass is dead code in play. It
is built, proved, and unreachable.

Generation-seeding makes it reachable on turn one, which is why Ben's answer to Q4 and the
NR-400 defect are the same work. Note the consequence honestly: **this changes every generated
world**, and every golden and price band downstream of a cross-border sale will move. That is a
deliberate one-time re-bless, and it should not be taken while the economy benchmark is red
(NR-278's standing advice).

## The check

Extend `law_harness` / `money_conservation`: (1) a directional tariff charges the targeted
nation's buyers and **no one else** — a third-party foreign buyer pays zero; (2) the
`all_nations` sentinel reproduces today's blanket behaviour bit-exactly; (3) conservation holds
per pair — buyer debited equals target treasury credited; (4) the seeded map is identical across
two runs of one seed; (5) with seeding disabled the world is bit-identical to the pre-item build.

## AMENDED 2026-08-22 — the grudges have a home now

The seeded directional map this item derives from the Era −1 pair outcomes lands in **BL-545's
nation→nation sentiment**, rather than in a table this item invents. A tariff rate is then read
*off* sentiment at enactment, which is what makes it *"an emergent consequence of generation"*
(Ben, Q4) rather than a second seeded artifact that could drift from the first.

Unchanged: the record shape (a `law` gaining `target_nation`), the `all_nations` sentinel, and
the determinism and legibility requirements. **`requires` BL-545.**

## AMENDED 2026-08-22 — the grudges ride the two-dimensional substrate

BL-545's dimension count is settled at **two (Access, Trust) at every grain**, so the seeded
nation→nation residue this item reads is a two-dimensional value rather than a scalar. A tariff
rate reads off it; which dimension it reads off is the small call owed at promotion.

items.title: What a nation wants — niche-fill and conflict avoidance under historical grudges, which is a POSITIONAL objective and not an accumulative one
items.summary: Settles NATIONS.md Q5 and is the first use anyone has made of the 2026-08-18 nation-behaviour grant. Ben, 2026-08-22: 'Nation objectives should be terrestrial diplomacy. Figuring out which economic niche can be well filled, and how to avoid conflict while respecting historical grudges.'
items.design:
## The objective, and why its shape matters more than its terms

A corporation maximises **profit** — an accumulative quantity, unbounded, and the same target for
every corp in the world. That is the right objective for a firm and the wrong one for a country.

Ben's answer gives a nation a **positional** objective instead: a nation does not want to be rich,
it wants to be **needed and unthreatened**. Three terms:

**1. Niche fit.** *"Figuring out which economic niche can be well filled."* How well does this
nation's output profile complement what its neighbours lack? Computable today from
`nation_component::resource_abundance`, the resolved market prices, and the trade actually
crossing its borders. A nation scores well by producing what others need and cannot make — not by
producing the most.

**2. Conflict avoidance.** *"How to avoid conflict."* A negative term on the expected cost of war,
read from pair-state and from force standing near its borders. Note what this implies: a
well-played nation in Io is one that **stays out of fights**, which is unusual for a strategy game
and is a large part of why the layer is worth having. Nations that avoid each other leave the
Conflict pillar to the companies, which is where the player lives.

**3. Grudges as weights, not as goals.** *"Respecting historical grudges."* The Era −1 residue does
not give a nation a target; it **biases** the first two terms. A grudge makes a neighbour's niche
less attractive to complement and a conflict with them less costly to accept. This is what keeps
the pre-history load-bearing in the campaign rather than being scenery.

## "Terrestrial"

Ben's word. Nations are **local** actors: their horizon is their neighbours and their own ground,
never the whole world and never off it. A nation does not have a global strategy, and the scorer
must not be given a global view — which is also what keeps it cheap over ~43 nations.

## The constraints are the grant

This is the **first use anyone has made of the 2026-08-18 nation-behaviour grant** (ruling 4 of
NR-331, `.claude/rules/io-standing-rules.md`). The grant's terms are not decoration and this item
lives inside them:

- **Pure, seeded, deterministic, replayable.** No wall-clock, no unseeded RNG, no iteration-order
  dependence. Sorted nation order, fixed term order, fixed float sequence.
- **A scored-utility layer issuing only legal verbs.** It emits budget weights (BL-537) and, later,
  tariff enactments (BL-541). It does not plan, does not look ahead, and does not maintain goals
  across ticks beyond the state the world already holds.
- **Never a planner.** The line the grant draws, and the one worth re-reading before every
  extension.
- **Nothing that varies the generated world.** `docs/lore/HISTORY.md` is authority for what the
  ladder produces; this scorer reads its residue and never re-rolls it.

## Cadence

The same staggered-slot shape `corp_ai` uses, for the same reason: ~43 nations evaluated on a
rotation rather than all at once. **The slot index must be over the sorted nation set**, so that
adding a nation shifts nobody else's slot — the property `spectator_determinism` asserts for
corps and the one most easily broken by accident.

## The check

`nation_scorer_harness`: (1) determinism — two runs of one seed produce identical weights on
every nation, every tick; (2) a nation with a complementary neighbour scores niche-fill above one
with an identical neighbour, measured rather than asserted; (3) grudge bias is directional — the
term differs between A→B and B→A where the pre-history differs; (4) locality — a change on the
far side of the map does not move a nation's weights; (5) cadence — adding one nation shifts no
other nation's evaluation slot.

---

> ⟳ **2026-08-23 — the scorer has landed; the VERB has not.** `src/world/nation_ai.{hpp,cpp}` is in
> the build and `tools/verify/nation_scorer_harness.cpp` is green at 60/60, plain and under
> AddressSanitizer + UBSan, both TUs warning-clean at `-Wall -Wextra`. It is the **first use anyone
> has made of the 2026-08-18 nation-behaviour grant**, and it stays inside the grant's terms: pure,
> seeded, deterministic, a scored-utility layer that emits weights and never plans.
>
> The three terms are built in the fixed order the item names — **niche fit** read as output SHARES
> (so a nation never scores by producing the most), **conflict avoidance** as a negative term on
> expected war cost, and **grudges** biasing the first two multiplicatively per-neighbour while
> contributing to no line of their own. Cadence is `corp_ai`'s staggered slot keyed on the index
> into the **sorted** nation set. Every constant is in `nation_ai_params`.
>
> **It returns weights and writes nothing, and nothing calls it**, so a world runs bit-identical to
> the build before it. What is owed is the wiring: `run_national_budget` still takes its budgets as
> a parameter because nothing authors them into `nation_component`, and a persistent field ahead of
> its author would be state with no writer and a serialisation seam owed for nothing.
>
> **Two design substitutions, both flagged rather than absorbed** (NR-553), both isolated to one
> function so replacing them moves nothing else. The **grudge has no data source** — no campaign-era
> nation-pair state reaches `world`, so it is derived from contested border length plus
> `expansionism` posture until BL-541 lands. And **nations hold no stance**, so reading force
> standing across a border required bridging corp-grain `stance` to a nation-grain input — the first
> place in the codebase that does, and arguably BL-540's to own.

items.title: The value anchor — a unit’s equipment costs about twice its wage at BASE prices, calibrated once at authoring time
items.summary: Settles NATIONS.md Q3. Ben, 2026-08-22: 'the equipment needed to sustain a unit costs about 2x their salary for that year', clarified same session: 'let's divorce wages from goods somewhat. My 1/2 figure can use base prices. We don't have to rederive wages every tick.' So the anchor is an AUTHORING-TIME calibration against the authored base_price table, not a runtime coupling.
items.design:
## The problem Ben named

*"We don't have a stable way to consider how valuable things are right now."* That is exactly
right, and it is why NR-382's levy-rate question could not be answered on its own terms. `1.0
cr/unit` is not a number anyone can reason about, because nothing in the game says what a credit
is worth relative to anything a player cares about.

An anchor fixes that. Not by pricing everything, but by fixing **one ratio between two quantities
the player already understands** and arguing every other price against it.

## The anchor

**A unit's equipment costs about twice its wage.**

Both halves already exist in `scripts/economy.lua` § `unit_upkeep`, both at zero, both charged
per head per tick:

    credits_per_head = 0.0                                    -- the wage
    goods_per_head   = { ordnance = 0.0, food_rations = 0.0 } -- the equipment

An economy tick is one quarter (`sim_loop::econ_tick_days` = 90, `k_ticks_per_year` = 4), and
both halves are per head per tick — so the annual factor appears on **both sides of the ratio and
cancels**. Ben's "for that year" needs no calendar arithmetic anywhere:

    sum over r of ( goods_per_head[r] x base_price[r] )  ~=  2 x credits_per_head

## AT BASE PRICES, AND ONCE — Ben's clarification, 2026-08-22

*"Let's divorce wages from goods somewhat. My 1/2 figure can use base prices. We don't have to
rederive wages every tick."*

Three things follow, and they make this item much smaller than its first draft.

**1. `base_price`, never the resolved market price.** `base_price` is an **authored table** in
`scripts/world_gen.lua` — ordnance 43.0, food_rations 6.0, steel 8.0, machinery 22.0 — and it is
**seed-invariant**. (Deposit *rarity* carries a small seeded jitter; the base-price table does not.)
So the anchor is stated against a stable constant, and it means the same thing in every generated
world.

This is what dissolves the first draft's main worry. That version proposed resolving the prices the
live game would resolve, which would have made the ratio drift with local scarcity and made the
same authored rates mean different things on different bodies.

**2. It is an authoring-time calibration, not a runtime coupling.** Nothing recomputes anything per
tick. The pass charges the authored rates exactly as `run_unit_upkeep` already does; the anchor is
the **argument for what those rates should be**, applied once when they are set, and re-checked only
when the base-price table or the roster moves.

**3. "Divorce somewhat" — a band, not an equality.** The wage is authored independently (see
BL-544) and the goods draw is sized against it. The relationship is a **calibration band with a
tolerance**, not an identity the code enforces. A class whose equipment is unusually cheap or dear
should be able to sit outside the band deliberately, and say so in a comment.

## Worked illustration — not the authored numbers

Purely to show the calculation is a single line. Suppose a wage of `credits_per_head = 5.0`:

    equipment budget = 2 x 5.0 = 10.0 cr / head / tick, at base prices
    ordnance      0.15 x 43.0 = 6.45
    food_rations  0.60 x  6.0 = 3.60
                                -----
                                10.05   -- inside any sensible band

**The wage itself is not this item's to set** — BL-544 (unit wage reference) owns what a soldier's
pay is anchored to. This item owns the equipment side and the ratio between them.

## What it unblocks, in three places

**1. The unit upkeep rate.** MILITARY.md § What is absent: *"No upkeep rate... every authored rate
is `0.0`, so a standing force still costs credits once, at hire, and nothing thereafter. Turning
it on is an `economy.lua` edit, not a code change."* This is the edit, and it now has a reason
behind it rather than a guess.

**2. The levy rate (NR-382).** With the anchor in place a levy stops being `1.0 cr/unit` and
becomes a legible statement: *this nation's levy income funds N units per year.* That is a number
Ben can rule on, and it is the form the question should have been asked in.

Recall why the placeholder had to go: enacted at 1.0, it moved net-worth finals from 78K-499K to
-3.6M..-5.2M, with **30/30 corps insolvent on all five benchmark seeds**.

**3. Ordnance gets a consumer with a size.** BL-457 added ordnance as the roster's first terminal
military good *because* BL-454's upkeep would consume it. At rate zero it never has. The anchor
sizes that draw, which is the first real demand signal the military half of the economy has ever
put into the market.

## Sequencing, and one warning

Do **not** set the levy rate in the same change as the upkeep rate. Turning on upkeep moves every
corp's cost base; setting the levy moves it again; doing both at once makes the benchmark
uninterpretable. Land the anchor and upkeep first, re-measure, **then** rule on the levy.

## The check

`value_anchor.cpp`, reading the authored tables — no world generation and no market resolution
needed, which makes it one of the cheapest harnesses in the suite:

1. The band holds for every roster class at the authored rates, against `world_gen.lua`'s
   `base_price`, within a stated tolerance.
2. It FAILS when a rate or a base price is perturbed — a check that cannot fail is not a check.
   This is the row that earns the harness, because it is what catches a base-price edit silently
   invalidating the calibration.
3. At all-zero rates the world is bit-identical to the pre-item build.
4. The derived "units funded per year" figure for the seeded levy is reported, so NR-382 can be
   answered against a number rather than a feeling.

---

> ⟳ **2026-08-23 — the CHECK has landed; no rate has been authored.** `tools/verify/value_anchor.cpp`
> is registered in the `verifier-headless` skill and green at 22/22. It authors nothing: it reads
> `economy.lua`'s `unit_upkeep`, `world_gen.lua`'s `base_price` and `recipes.lua`'s baskets out of the
> Lua text and states the identity Ben's figure implies, at base prices and at authoring time — both
> of his narrowings. **Picking the rates is still Ben's.**
>
> Three things the Sprint N1 adversarial pass changed about it, each now verified in both directions:
> * **R3 is a BRANCH, not an assertion.** The first cut hard-asserted the shipped rates were zero, so
>   it would have gone RED on the one day the harness exists for — the reviewer authored its own
>   solved fixture into `economy.lua` and got exit 1 with the anchor satisfied and all 19 rows in
>   band. It now asks which state the content is in and asserts the invariant belonging to it.
> * **the anchor is scale-invariant, and the harness says so.** All 33 base prices ×10 leaves every
>   ratio bit-identical, because the anchor is a ratio. That was a silent false green; it is now an
>   asserted property, paired with the row that DOES bind an absolute price — ordnance's markup over
>   its own recipe basket against the five Advanced-Fabrication peers `recipes.lua` id 27 names
>   (1.415–1.443, ordnance 1.433). Tripling steel alone drops it out.
> * **the perturbation sizes are derived from `k_tolerance`**, not picked, and each RED row is paired
>   with a GREEN one just inside the band, so widening the band moves both together.
>
> **The finding still stands and is still the interesting part:** the wage half is power-scaled and
> the goods half is flat, so the anchor BOUNDS `credits_per_head_per_power` — at the demonstration
> fixture, ≤ 0.00654 over the roster's 0..420 power span. A flat goods table cannot follow a
> power-scaled wage.

items.title: What anchors a soldier’s wage — the gap BL-543 opens by divorcing the wage from the goods
items.summary: BL-543 sizes a unit's EQUIPMENT against its wage. Nothing sizes the wage. Ben's 'divorce wages from goods somewhat' (2026-08-22) makes credits_per_head an independently authored number, so it needs its own reference - and the obvious candidate is the civilian wage the game already pays.
items.design:
## The gap, stated plainly

BL-543's anchor is a **ratio**: equipment costs about twice the wage. A ratio fixes one quantity
only if the other is known, and `unit_upkeep.credits_per_head` is currently `0.0` with nothing
arguing for any other value.

Ben's clarification is what opens this. While the wage and the goods were a single locked
identity, either one could have been treated as the free variable. *"Divorce wages from goods
somewhat"* makes the wage an **independently authored number**, which is the right call — and it
means the wage now needs a reference of its own.

Filed `design-owed` deliberately: the reference is a real call, not an obvious one.

## The obvious candidate, and why it is not obvious

Io already pays a wage every tick — the **civilian** one. `scripts/economy.lua` authors
`base_wage` per building type, currently **6.0 to 15.0** per unit workforce per tick, and
`apply_budget` scales it by workforce contention and by mean habitability.

So the natural reference is: **a soldier costs some multiple of a worker.** That gives the wage the
same property the equipment ratio has — it is a statement about two things a player already
understands, rather than a number from nowhere.

What makes it non-obvious is that the two are not the same kind of quantity. `base_wage` is per
unit *workforce*; `credits_per_head` is per *head* in a unit. Whether one head of a Levy Spear is
one unit of workforce is a modelling question nobody has answered, and answering it is most of this
item.

## Three candidate references

1. **A multiple of civilian wage.** Soldier = k x worker, k authored. Simplest, and it couples the
   military cost base to the economy automatically — schooling or habitability changes move both.
2. **A multiple of hire cost.** `hire_axis_cost` is 5.0 (`unit_roster.hpp`). Anchors upkeep to
   what raising the unit cost, which is the comparison BL-454's own comment reaches for:
   *"against `hire_*` above, which is what it costs to raise one."*
3. **Authored per class from the roster's `power_mod`.** Consistent with NR-322's ruling that
   unit quality is DERIVED from `power_mod` rather than authored separately.

**Recommendation: 1, with the per-class spread from 3.** A soldier's pay tracking a worker's pay is
the relationship that stays true as the rest of the economy moves, and `power_mod` gives the
spread between a levy and a regiment without a second authored table.

## Why it matters beyond tidiness

Get the wage wrong and BL-543's ratio faithfully propagates the error into the goods draw, which
then propagates into ordnance demand — the first real demand signal the military half of the
economy puts into the market. The ratio is only as good as the quantity it is a ratio *of*.

## The check

Extend `value_anchor.cpp`: the authored `credits_per_head` sits within a stated band of the
chosen reference for every roster class, and the check fails when it does not.

items.title: Sentiment is the substrate — one continuous, directed, derived quantity under every relational read in the game
items.summary: Ben's ruling on NR-520, 2026-08-22: sentiment is the substrate. Four things that were separately designed collapse into one - CONCEPT.md's never-built sentiment, BL-540's nation->corp dimensions, corp_reputation, and the Era -1 grudges BL-541 reads. Stance stays the discrete DECLARED layer above it.
items.design:
## The ruling

Ben, 2026-08-22, settling NR-520: **sentiment is the substrate.**

RELATIONS.md put all four relational quantities in one table and made visible what none of them
individually showed: **three designs were converging on the same continuous derived quantity and
none knew about the other two.** CONCEPT.md's sentiment (designed since the concept doc, never
built), BL-540's nation→corp Access/Trust (designed 2026-08-22 without reference to it), and
`corp_reputation` (already a continuous per-pair float moved by conduct).

This item is the convergence, taken deliberately rather than discovered later.

## What sentiment IS

**One directed, continuous, derived value from an observer to a subject**, where an actor is a
corporation or a nation.

- **Directed.** A→B is not B→A. Every existing use already needs this: reputation is keyed
  (buyer, supplier); a nation reads a corp and never the reverse; a grudge is asymmetric by
  nature.
- **Continuous.** A float, not a state. Bands are a *presentation* choice (the BL-262 standing
  precedent), never the storage.
- **Derived from conduct, never declared.** This is the line that separates it from stance, and it
  is not negotiable — see the invariant below.

The grains it must cover on day one, because they already exist in some form:

| Observer → subject | Today | After |
|---|---|---|
| corp → corp | `corp_reputation` (buyer→supplier) | a sentiment view (BL-546) |
| nation → corp | BL-540's Access / Trust | sentiment dimensions |
| nation → nation | Era −1 grudges, read by BL-541 | seeded sentiment |

## THE INVARIANT — sentiment must never become hostility on its own

Ben ruled on 2026-08-17 that **hostility is a declared state a corp opts into**, and that a rival
*"may score and declare it, never acquire it ambiently."* That ruling stands and this item must not
quietly overturn it.

So: **sentiment informs a declaration; it never makes one.** A scorer may read sentiment and choose
to `declare_hostile`; no threshold anywhere may flip a stance table by itself. The two layers stay
separate on purpose:

    stance      DECLARED, discrete    — an act, always attributable to an actor
    sentiment   DERIVED,  continuous  — a reading, attributable to conduct

A harness row asserts it directly: driving sentiment to any value, in either direction, mutates no
stance table.

## What it dissolves

**BL-391's deadlock falls out for free.** The reputation floor is unrecoverable because the only
two writers are contract completion and cancellation, so the recovery path is a cycle with no
entry. A continuous quantity that **decays toward neutral** has no permanent floor by construction:
a burned relationship heals with time, "wait" becomes a legitimate strategic move, and the fix is a
property of the substrate rather than a special case bolted onto procurement.

**BL-541's grudges get a home.** *"Tariffs as an emergent consequence of generation"* (Ben, Q4)
needs somewhere for the Era −1 residue to live between generation and the campaign. Seeded
nation→nation sentiment is that place, and it means a tariff is readable back to the war that
caused it.

**CONCEPT.md's oldest unbuilt promise gets a home.** § Sentiment-based diplomacy has said
*"Designed, not built — no sentiment layer exists in code"* since the concept doc. This is the
layer.

## Dimensions — one open call, deliberately not taken here

BL-540 proposed two (**Access**, **Trust**), each gating something. Reputation is effectively one
(*will you deal with me*). CONCEPT.md describes a single value shaped by several factors.

Ben's ruling settles the **architecture**, not the dimension count. This item assumes **the BL-540
pair, generalised** — Access and Trust at every grain — and flags it: a third dimension must gate
something before it is added, and collapsing to one would make Access and Trust inexpressible
separately, which BL-540 needs. Raised as NR-522.

## Contributing factors

CONCEPT.md names three — trade history, territorial conflict, ideological alignment. All three are
computable from state Io already holds: convoys and matched trades, `corp_hostile_pairs` plus
battle outcomes, and `nation_component::politics`. Add the two the existing uses need: contract
completion/cancellation (reputation's current writers) and levy contribution (BL-540's own list).

Authored weights in `economy.lua`, so tuning is a data change.

## Determinism

Recomputed on a fixed cadence over a sorted actor list, factors summed in a fixed order, decay
applied as one multiply. Pure, seeded, no RNG — the 2026-08-18 grant's terms, which this sits
inside because a nation is one of the observers.

**Cadence caution, the one most easily broken:** the slot index must be over the **sorted actor
set**, so adding an actor shifts nobody else's slot. That is the property
`spectator_determinism` asserts for corps and the one BL-542 carries the same warning about.

## The check

`sentiment_harness`: (1) the stance invariant — driving sentiment to any extreme mutates no
stance table, in either direction; (2) decay — an unmaintained value returns to neutral within the
authored window, and **there is no floor a value cannot leave**, which is BL-391's defect asserted
as its own row; (3) directedness — A→B and B→A move independently; (4) determinism across two runs
of one seed; (5) seeded nation→nation sentiment is identical across two generations of one seed;
(6) inertness — with all factor weights zero, the world is bit-identical to the pre-item build.

## RULED 2026-08-22 (Ben, design register) — two dimensions, and the factor list is WIDE

**Dimensions: two — Access and Trust — at every grain.** NR-522 closed. Access gates operating
rights inside a jurisdiction; Trust is what a contract client reads. A third dimension must gate
something before it is added.

**Decay is anchored, not authored as a bare rate**, and Ben widened the question while answering
it: *"Certain actions might make a rival wary, such as buying a background firm that they wanted.
There are tonnes of realistic ways to affect sentiment."*

That is a ruling about **factors**, not only about decay, and it changes this item's scope in one
specific way: the factor list must be **open-ended and cheap to extend**, because the design intent
is that many ordinary actions move sentiment. Two consequences:

1. **A factor is authored data, not a code branch.** Weights live in `economy.lua` and a new
   factor is a table row. Anything else makes "tonnes of realistic ways" unaffordable.
2. **Acquisition is a named factor from the start.** Ben's own example — *buying a background firm
   a rival wanted* — is the BL-524 syndicate tier's equity purchase and BL-371's acquisitions.
   Sentiment is where an acquisition's *political* cost lands, and nothing else in the design has
   a place for it.

The rate itself takes BL-543's treatment: expressed against something the player already
understands, not a number typed once.

## ABSORBED FROM BL-345 AND BL-158 (2026-08-22 triage)

Two older items were designing this same substrate and are retired into it. What they carried that
this item did not is taken up here rather than lost.

### From BL-345 — the acceptance rule, which is the better half of it

> **A stub nothing reads is indistinguishable from no stub.**

BL-345's stated failure mode for a data-model minor: shipping serialisable records no code path
consults, declaring the model positioned, and discovering later that the shape was wrong *because
nothing ever exercised it*. Its answer was to make **the consumer the acceptance criterion**, not a
follow-on.

**That rule now binds this item.** Sentiment does not land as storage plus a harness; it lands with
a consumer that changes observable behaviour. **BL-541 (directional tariffs) is the natural one** —
it reads nation→nation sentiment and turns it into a rate — and BL-540's Access gate is the second.

What does **not** transfer is BL-345's shape: it proposed a **symmetric** per-pair scalar, and Ben's
2026-08-22 ruling is **directed**. That contradiction is the reason it is retired rather than merged.

### From BL-158 — which got here first, on 2026-08-02

BL-158's settlement proposed, three weeks before this item existed:

> **`sentiment`** — a fixed-point scalar per **ordered pair**, one bounded range, no sub-axes.
> *Trust/fear/respect decomposition is a v0.3.0 question; one axis proves the storage.*

It argued **against** the symmetric model for exactly the reason Ben later ruled on — *"a symmetric
scalar cannot express 'A resents B, B is indifferent', which is the ordinary case"* — and cited
BL-225's directional seizure cost as the evidence.

**So NR-520 undercounted.** It recorded three designs converging on one continuous derived quantity;
there were **four**, and the earliest was already correct about the direction question. This item
keeps its ruling (two dimensions, Access and Trust) and takes BL-158's determinism rule verbatim,
because it is sharper than anything written since:

> At 43 nations an N×N table is ~1,850 ordered pairs — trivial to store, which is what makes the
> **walk rule load-bearing rather than pedantic**: any iteration over pairs is a **sorted walk over
> nation ids**, never over an unordered container, and any aggregate accumulates in fixed point in
> that fixed order.

---

> ⟳ **2026-08-23 — the substrate has landed; nothing emits into it.** `src/world/sentiment.{hpp,cpp}`
> is in the build with its flat-binary round trip, and `tools/verify/sentiment_harness.cpp` is green at
> 41/41, plain and under AddressSanitizer + UBSan. What is owed is the emitters — no completed
> contract, trade, cancellation or use of force calls `apply_sentiment_events` yet — and BL-546's
> migration of `corp_reputation` onto it.
>
> **The stance invariant is enforced by CONSTRUCTION, not by a test**, which is stronger than the item
> asked for: `sentiment.cpp` includes no world header and every signature takes only
> `sentiment_table&`, so it has no reach to a stance table at all. The harness asserts it anyway — a
> structural argument nobody checks is one refactor away from being false.
>
> **One harness row was rebuilt** after the Sprint N1 adversarial pass: R6's order-independence rows
> ran on a stream with exactly one event per ordered pair, so nothing ever accumulated and the
> canonicalising `std::stable_sort` could be deleted with all 39 rows still passing. They now run on
> a stream with five events per key, driven to the saturation limit so the fold is order-sensitive by
> two whole points rather than by a low bit. Verified by mutation: without the sort, three rows fail.

items.title: Procurement reputation becomes a view of sentiment rather than a second store — and it is on the serialisation seam, so the migration is the work
items.summary: The corp->corp half of BL-545's ruling. w.corp_reputation is already a continuous directed float moved by conduct - it IS sentiment at buyer->supplier grain, under a different name and in a different table. Filed separately because it is the one relational quantity that IS serialised, so migrating it is a save-format change rather than a rename.
items.design:
## Why this is its own item

`world::corp_reputation` is a `std::map<std::pair<entity_id,entity_id>, float>` — a **directed,
continuous value between two corporations, moved by conduct.** That is BL-545's definition of
sentiment, arrived at independently by BL-350 and living in its own table under its own name.

Under Ben's NR-520 ruling it becomes a **view of sentiment**, not a second store.

It is filed apart from BL-545 for one reason: **it is the only relational quantity that is
serialised.** `procurement.cpp` writes it into the procurement stream behind
`procurement_version`, and that seam gates on strict version equality — so this is a save-format
change, not a rename.

*(That gate costs nothing today. NR-399's amendment establishes there is no game save/load path at
all: neither `read_procurement` nor `read_history_log` has a caller anywhere in `src/`. The
migration should still be written as though saves exist, because BL-107 will make them exist.)*

## What changes and what must not

**Changes:** the store. Reputation stops being its own map and becomes a read of the (buyer,
supplier) sentiment value on the Trust dimension.

**Must not change:** the two writers' *meaning*. Contract completion raises it and cancellation
lowers it, at the rates `economy.lua` already authors. Those become sentiment factors with the
same weights, so procurement behaviour is unchanged on landing — the migration is a substrate swap,
not a balance change, and a harness row proves it.

**Gains, for free, from the substrate:** decay toward neutral, which is the BL-391 deadlock fix.
Land BL-391 *through* this item rather than beside it.

## The one thing to watch

`request_quote`'s refusal reads a floor. Once the value decays, the floor stops being permanent —
which is the point — but every consumer that treated "below the floor" as terminal must be
re-read. There is exactly one today (`corp_command.cpp`'s quote path), so the sweep is small; it
will not stay small once BL-377's contract seam reads the same axis.

## The check

Extend the procurement harness: (1) with decay disabled, every procurement outcome is
**bit-identical** to the pre-migration build across the benchmark seeds — the migration changes no
behaviour on its own; (2) with decay enabled, a corp driven below the floor recovers within the
authored window, which is BL-391's defect asserted as a passing row; (3) the version bump reads and
writes a round trip; (4) reputation and sentiment never disagree, because there is only one store.

---

> ⟳ **2026-08-23 — landed, and BL-391 landed through it.** `world::corp_reputation` is **gone as a
> store**; every read is a view of the (buyer, supplier) **Trust** value on BL-545's substrate.
> Deleting the field rather than aliasing it is what made the consumer sweep provable — every stale
> reference became a compile error rather than something to grep for. The sweep found exactly one
> floor comparison in the whole tree (`corp_command.cpp`'s quote path) and it now carries a comment
> saying the refusal is a condition of today and not a verdict.
>
> **Two save formats moved with it**, which is why this was its own item: procurement **2 → 3** (the
> trailing reputation block is gone, not re-derived — NR-552 records why keeping a
> compatibility-shaped block was rejected) and the world snapshot **1 → 2** (the pair map carries two
> floats and rejects a null id, a self pair, a non-finite value or a stored-neutral row).
>
> **BL-391 is dissolved in mechanism, not yet in play.** Decay toward exact neutral with row erasure
> means there is no value a supplier relationship cannot leave, so the deadlock has no floor to sit
> on — but the shipped decay rate is zero until `scripts/economy.lua` authors one, and **that number
> is Ben's call**. The harness proves both halves: with decay off every procurement outcome is
> bit-identical to the pre-migration build (constants captured from a binary built before a file was
> touched), and with decay on a corp driven below the floor recovers inside the authored window.
>
> `procurement_harness` 66 PASS, `save_roundtrip` OK with Access and Trust asserted distinct, both
> clean under ASan+UBSan. Seven mutations run, each landing on the row that owns its claim — including
> one that makes the fold assign instead of accumulate, which the pre-existing single-completion
> fixture would have passed.
>
> **One reported finding did NOT survive verification** (NR-551): a claimed layout-sensitive
> determinism violation in spectate. Four clean trees give identical hashes, and the lane's own probe
> re-run moves neither. Nothing to fix.

items.title: Named people holding specific roles — the handles on institutions that currently hold everything
items.summary: Ben, 2026-08-22: 'we might also want to include a system whereby named people get specific roles' - one of two systems he named as having had no attention. docs/PEOPLE.md opens the subject as a PROPOSAL; its § Open questions are the six calls owed before any code. Extends BL-207 (persona counsel packs) rather than inventing a rival, and ships BL-370 (corp leader figure) as its first role.
items.design:
## The claim

Every quantity in Io is held by an institution. A corporation has a balance, a nation has a
treasury, a unit has a strength. **Nobody holds anything.**

That is fine for an economy and becomes a real cost once the game has *relations*. Sentiment
(BL-545) is a directed float between institutions; lobbying (BL-539) is a corporation influencing a
nation. Both are correct and both are abstract in a way that is hard to care about.

**A person is what makes an institutional relation legible. Sentiment is a number; a person is who
holds it.**

## The rule that keeps it from being decoration

**A person exists only where a ROLE exists, and every role must gate or bias something.** A named
figure who only decorates is the `military_points` defect with a face — generated, displayed, read
by nothing. That deletion (2026-08-17) and NR-257's five orphan resources are the precedents.

## What already exists, and must be built ON rather than beside

- **BL-207 (persona counsel packs)** — `designed`, A, parked. Advisory personas seated per corp,
  reading the blackboard, biasing the strategy weight through a bounded transparent nudge, moddable
  in Lua, fully deterministic. **This is already a person-with-a-role, fully designed**, and its
  discipline is the model: counsel *biases scoring, never bypasses validation* — no new verbs, no
  fog access, blackboard reads only.
- **BL-370 (corp leader figure)** — `design-owed`, parked, Ben's own 2026-08-11 ask. **One role,
  and the one to ship first**, because it needs no other system.
- **Name generation is free and already correct.** `tongue.cpp` generates per-culture phoneme
  systems; `city_names.cpp` and `body_names.cpp` coin from them. A person's name is one more draw.
  The standing rule binds absolutely: **never an Earth name, by any route.**

## The proposed shape

A person is **a name, a role, a seat, a tenure, and at most one bias** — the bias expressed as a
`scalar_modifier` (modifier_set.hpp) so it inherits determinism, serialisation and ledger
legibility for free. **One bias, not a trait sheet:** a person with five modifiers is a spreadsheet
with a name.

Five candidate roles, each mapped to shipped machinery: **company head** (BL-370), **counsel**
(BL-207), **commander** (doctrine, which MILITARY.md lists as an all-zero stub), **minister** (which
budget line BL-537 favours), **contact** (the buyer/supplier pair sentiment is already keyed on).

**Minister is the one that changes another system's design** — it gives BL-539's lobbying a target,
makes succession a political event, and gives BL-542's scorer somewhere for preferences to live.

## Scale is the constraint that decides buildability

~88 corporations and ~43 nations. A person per institution per role is **thousands of people the
player will never look at**.

**Proposed: a cast, not a population.** People are generated only where a role is seated, and seated
sparsely — the player's corp, nations the player has met, units the player commands, suppliers
dealt with. **A person is created when someone would plausibly know their name**, which makes
BL-089's activity fog the natural gate and costs nothing to generate.

## Mortality

Tenure is what makes a person more than a label; a person who never leaves is a permanent modifier
wearing a name. Proposed: people age on the economy tick, leave deterministically in sorted seat
order, and a successor is drawn with a different bias. **That gives the game change the player did
not cause and cannot prevent**, and succession is the cleanest first event (BL-548).

## What must not happen

No role may **act** — biasing is permitted, deciding is a planner and planners are prohibited. No
Earth names. No bulk generation. **No decoration:** if removing a role's bias changed nothing
measurable, the role should not ship.

## Owed before code

The six § Open questions in `docs/PEOPLE.md`: which roles and in what order; one bias or several;
are people mortal; does the player's own figure carry a bias at all; are people visible to rivals
under BL-068; do people exist in the pre-history.

## RULED 2026-08-22 (Ben, design register) — and the "one bias" proposal is OVERTURNED

**Q1 — all five roles, in the proposed order:** company head, counsel, commander, minister, contact.

**Q2 — SEVERAL biases, not one.** *"People are a real optimisation axis."* This overturns the
proposal outright, and the reasoning behind the proposal — *a person with five modifiers is a
spreadsheet with a name* — is recorded as the concern it was rather than deleted. What replaces it
is that a person is a **build choice**, and the design owes a guard against the spreadsheet failure
that is not "only one modifier": legibility of the *set*, not scarcity of it.

**Q3 — people are MORTAL.** Age and replacement, deterministically. So succession is real, and it
is EVENTS' first family (see BL-548).

**Q4 — the player's figure is CHOSEN AT START**, bias included. So the company head is a build
decision at campaign setup, not a portrait — which makes it a New World wizard concern
(`docs/ui/STARTUP.md`) as well as a generation one.

**Q5 — banded like everything else** (BL-068). You learn who a rival's people are as you learn the
rest of them. No special case.

**Q6 — a few exist in the pre-history**: only the figures whose deeds the campaign world still
remembers. `history_log` already records deeds with nobody to attribute them to; this gives the
memorable ones a name and leaves the rest institutional.

### The sequencing consequence

**PEOPLE now gates EVENTS.** Ben chose *personal* as the first event family, and that family
depends on this item. What was the fourth-ranked family by machinery is first by ruling, so this
item moves ahead of BL-548 rather than beside it.

items.title: An event system — things that happen TO the player, seeded so they stay deterministic
items.summary: Ben, 2026-08-22: 'we also want to begin including random events.' docs/EVENTS.md opens it as a PROPOSAL. The meta layer already supplies two thirds of an event (predicate + effect); only the TRIGGER is new.
