It is also the consumer collapse_strain has been waiting for, which turns an unwired vocabulary entry into a working mechanic rather than adding a sixth.
items.design:
## The interesting problem is the word "random"

**Io is deterministic and that is non-negotiable.** A truly random event is prohibited. So the
system either breaks the invariant or does not exist — **except that the game already solved this
exact problem once, and the solution is a ruling.**

Ben, 2026-08-13, BL-315 ruling 4 on battle resolution: the resolver draws from a **seeded stream
folded from the battle's own identity**, so the same save replayed produces the same battle, while
the player — who cannot see the seed — faces a genuinely uncertain fight.

> **Uncertain to the player, deterministic to the engine.**

That transfers wholesale. An event is drawn from a stream folded from `(world_seed, tick,
scope_id)`. It needs no new argument, only the discipline of never reaching for a wall clock.

## The meta layer already supplies two thirds

An event is **a trigger, a predicate, and an effect**:

| Part | Supplied by | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Predicate — when is it eligible | `condition_set` (BL-342) | shipped, 9 subjects |
| Effect — what it does | `modifier_set` (BL-479) | shipped, 6 subjects |
| **Trigger — does it fire this tick** | — | **the only new part** |

That is the whole cost, and it is exactly the meta layer's promise: *a new rule family costs an
enumerator, not a subsystem.*

**And it supplies the consumer `collapse_strain` has been waiting for.** That subject is wired to
nothing — one of five vocabulary-only entries NR-524 raises — and BL-477 says *"each era has a
collapse state to avoid, and that's what defines meta."* **Events are how strain manifests.**

## Four families, ranked by existing machinery

1. **Environmental** — bad season, flood, seam running thin. Reads generated terrain and deposits;
   lands on `extraction_rate`, **the one wired modifier subject.** Cheapest, and the natural cut.
2. **Economic** — glut, shortage, supplier failure. Riskiest to balance; the economy is the most
   tuned part of the game.
3. **Political** — this family is **already half-built and does not know it**. BL-537 (budget),
   BL-539 (lobbying) and BL-541 (tariffs) all produce discrete dateable changes a player should be
   told about. **An event is the notification layer those systems are missing**, and that half is
   arguably not "random" at all.
4. **Personal** — succession, death, defection. Depends on BL-547.

## An event that is not surfaced did not happen

BL-458 (interdiction) shipped **silent** (NR-407) — it works, and nothing tells the player their
convoy was taken. That is the strongest available argument for the rule this system adopts outright:
**an event lands with its message, in the same change.** Io already has the surface (the comms
dock), so this costs a channel, not a system.

## What must not happen

- **No event may be unavoidable and unsignalled** — a player must be able to see that a *class* of
  thing can happen, or it reads as the game cheating.
- **No wall clock, no unseeded draw.** Ever.
- **No event may ACT.** An effect moves a scalar or sets a flag. An event that places a building,
  declares hostility or enacts a law is a planner. **It may create the conditions for an actor to
  decide; it may never decide.**
- **No event may be purely negative.** A system that only takes is a tax with a story. Ben's
  interconnectivity ask argues the best events **open a door rather than close one** — a shortage
  that makes a trade route worth building, a succession that makes a nation lobbyable.
- **No event may bypass BL-068's fog.**

## Owed before code

The six § Open questions in `docs/EVENTS.md`. Two decide the system's size: **how often is an
event** (the single number separating texture from chaos), and **do events drive the collapse
metagame or merely express it** (BL-477).

## RULED 2026-08-22 (Ben, design register)

**Q1 — PERSONAL first**, not environmental. Succession, death, defection. **So BL-547 (people)
gates this item**, and the family that was fourth by available machinery is first by ruling.

**Q2 — SEASONAL.** One every few years, so a decade has a shape. An economy tick is a quarter, so
this is single digits of events per decade, not per year.

**Q3 — YES, a bounded choice with priced outcomes.** This is the answer that moves the system
closest to BL-087's quests, and the boundary now needs stating: **an event's choice is priced and
immediate; a quest is a predicate held open over time.** Nothing else separates them.

**Q4 — events EXPRESS the collapse metagame, they do not drive it.** Strain accumulates elsewhere;
events are how the player learns about it. **That bounds this system's size** — it is a
notification and consequence layer, not the metagame's engine, and BL-477 keeps the accumulator.

**Q5 — SYMMETRIC.** Everyone is subject, and watching a rival get hit is content. Harder to
balance and it removes the "difficulty dial pointed at the player" failure entirely.

**Q6 — BL-289 stays GENERATION-SIDE ONLY**, as a pre-history divergence. It does not become a
campaign event.

### The tone ruling, which is the most useful line in the answers

> Ben: **"Events should usually be boring. Occasional high stress chains."**

Two things follow, and neither was in the proposal. **A baseline event should be unremarkable** —
texture, not incident; the system's default register is low. And **events CHAIN**: a high-stress
period is a linked sequence, not one large roll. A chain needs an event to be able to name its
successor and a cooldown that gates the chain rather than each link, which is a shape the flat
authored table above does not yet have.

items.title: Friendship finally permits something — passage through territory, and immunity from interdiction
items.summary: Ben, 2026-08-22 (design register, RELATIONS Q2): friendship permits PASSAGE THROUGH TERRITORY and IMMUNITY FROM INTERDICTION. Until this ruling friendship gated exactly zero - four verbs and a UI column changing a table no behaviour read.
items.design:
## What this closes

BL-448 landed symmetric friendship on 2026-08-19 and left what it permits as *"a later call."*
Hostility went on to gate three things — interdiction, battle engagement, the march queue.
**Friendship gated zero.** `are_friends` had no consumer outside `stance.cpp` and the corporation
panel: an offer/accept handshake, a confirm popup and a UI column, all changing a table nothing
consumed. NR-521 recorded it.

Ben's ruling gives it two consumers, and both are cheap because both read an existing predicate at
an existing site.

## 1. Immunity from interdiction

`supply_system.cpp`'s interception check currently asks one question: has the tile's unit owner
**declared hostility** toward the cargo's owner? The ruling adds a second: **a friend never
intercepts a friend**, whatever else is true.

Order matters and is not arbitrary. `declare_hostile` already **dissolves a friendship row
atomically** (stance.hpp invariant 2), so the two states cannot both hold — which means the
friendship check is not a conflicting predicate, it is a **cheaper early-out** on a pair that
hostility has already been excluded from. Implement it as such, and the invariant is what makes it
safe.

## 2. Passage through territory

The larger half, and it needs a territory model to pass *through*. Two candidate readings, and the
call is owed:

- **Reach-anchor sharing** — a friend's cities and hubs count as supply anchors for your
  `body_reach_field`, so a friendship extends your network rather than merely permitting movement
  on it. Strong, and it lands on machinery that exists.
- **Placement permission** — a friend may site buildings inside your reach envelope where a
  stranger may not. This overlaps BL-540's **Access** dimension at nation grain, and a corp-grain
  version of the same idea should not be invented separately.

**Recommend the first.** It is the one that cannot be confused with BL-540, and it makes friendship
a *logistics* fact — which fits the chain, where logistics is the recurring constraint.

## Why it matters beyond the feature

Friendship becoming real is what makes hostility a **choice** rather than the only stance with
consequences. Before this, declaring hostile was the only stance verb that did anything, so the
stance table read as a war switch with decorative alternatives.

## The check

Extend the interdiction harness: a friendly unit on a convoy's tile does **not** intercept, on
every seed; declaring hostility mid-run dissolves the friendship and interception resumes on the
next tick; and with no friendship rows anywhere the world is bit-identical to the pre-item build.

items.title: A nation can go bankrupt — infrastructure is paid for from tax, and too much debt has major penalties
items.summary: Ben, 2026-08-22 (design register, LOGISTICS Q5): 'Roads do not decay, but nations have to pay tax to support them. If a nation runs into too much debt supporting infrastructure, it can go bankrupt with major penalties. But between these states nothing changes.'
items.design:
## The ruling, and what it rejects

Asked what the network costs to maintain, Ben rejected decay outright and replaced it with a
**fiscal** cost carrying a **failure state**:

> *"Roads do not decay, but nations have to pay tax to support them. If a nation runs into too much
> debt supporting infrastructure, it can go bankrupt with major penalties. But between these states
> nothing changes."*

Three things are settled by that sentence and the last clause is the load-bearing one.

**1. Roads are permanent.** No decay pass, no per-tile upkeep state, no gradual degradation of the
network. The reach field stays a pure function of what has been built.

**2. Infrastructure is a standing charge on the treasury**, scaled by the network a nation holds.
This is what BL-538's *logistics maintenance* budget line actually buys — the line had no sink,
and this is the sink.

**3. "Between these states nothing changes" — the cost is BINARY, not graduated.** A solvent
nation's roads behave exactly as they do today. A bankrupt one suffers major penalties. There is
no middle band where a strained nation's network degrades a little, and **that is deliberate**: a
graduated version would be a second decay model wearing a budget's clothes, which is precisely what
the first half of the ruling rejects.

## Why this is worth having

It gives a nation its **first failure state**. Until now a nation could accumulate treasury
forever and nothing happened either way; NR-398 flagged that the balance was *"a scoreboard with no
game attached"*. A nation that can over-extend has a strategy, and a nation that can fail has
stakes.

It is also the nation-grain reading of a mechanic the player already has: CONCEPT.md § Bankruptcy
and seizure names financial collapse as one of two loss vectors, and BL-073's debt interest is the
corp-grain version. **One concept, two actors** — and the corp side is the precedent for how the
spiral should feel.

## What is owed before code

- **What the penalties are.** "Major" is Ben's word and is not a design. Candidates that read on
  existing machinery: the budget's weights are seized to debt service; law enactment is suspended;
  sentiment toward the nation falls across the board (BL-545); contracts it has offered fail
  (BL-377's *failed* terminal state, from the client side).
- **What the charge is proportional to** — road tiles held, tiles weighted by tier, or reach-field
  coverage. Tier-weighted is the honest one, since a highway is not a track.
- **The threshold.** "Too much debt" wants BL-543's treatment: an anchor, not a number.
- **Whether a bankrupt nation recovers**, and how. A permanent state would be the BL-391 deadlock
  at nation grain, and that shape is already known to be a defect.

items.title: Rivals bid for the same contracts — losing a bid is a real outcome
items.summary: Ben, 2026-08-22 (design register, CONTRACTS Q3): rivals compete for the same contracts and 'losing a bid is a real outcome'. Turns an offer from something addressed to the player into something CONTESTED, and forecloses the BL-446 defect before it can repeat.
items.design:
## What changes

BL-377 designs an offer as something a client makes and the player accepts. Under this ruling an
offer is **contested**: rival companies bid for the same work, and the player can lose it.

## Why it is not a nicety

**It forecloses the BL-446 defect before it happens.** Procurement shipped with no UI and no AI
user, so a counterparty mechanism exists that neither a human nor a rival has ever exercised. A
contract seam where only the player bids would be the same defect at a larger scale — and BL-377 is
the player's *income*, so an unexercised version of it is worse than an unexercised buy side.

It also makes reputation bite in a second direction. Today reputation gates whether you may
*request* work. Under bidding it decides whether you *win* it, against someone else's standing —
which is the difference between a floor and a contest.

## The shape

The scorer already ranks candidates by payoff; a bid is one more candidate with a price attached.
What is new is that the **client** chooses among bids, which is a nation-side decision and
therefore reads BL-545's **Trust** dimension — the dimension BL-540 introduced for exactly this.

**A bid is not haggling.** BL-377 excludes multi-round fee negotiation and that exclusion stands: a
bid is a single sealed number, the client picks once, and the loser is told. Iterated negotiation
is a different mechanic and is not in this item.

## Determinism

Bid resolution is a deterministic argmax over a sorted bidder set with an explicit tie-break —
never first-come by iteration order. The same seed must produce the same winner.

## What is owed

Whether a losing bid costs anything (a wasted evaluation, or a reputation cost for chronic
underbidding); whether the player sees rival bids or only the outcome — BL-068 says the latter;
and whether a client may refuse **all** bids, which is what stops an underbid from always winning.

## FILE SCOPE CORRECTED 2026-08-22 (hotspot audit)

Declared `src/world/contracts.cpp`, **which does not exist** — inherited from BL-377, whose own
declaration of that path is the defect that had it marked complete for ten days. The shipped
contract machinery is `src/world/procurement.{hpp,cpp}`.

This item `requires` BL-377, so the true position is: **the file this item bids into has not been
written yet.** That is a sequencing fact the file list was hiding rather than showing.

items.title: Io has two clocks and the word "tick" means both — rename them apart
items.summary: Ben, 2026-08-22 (design register, cross-cutting Q3): rename one in code - econ_tick vs day_tick - so the ambiguity cannot be read. A DAY TICK is one in-game day (the survey system counts these); an ECONOMY TICK is 90 of them. Both readings in the corpus are correct about different clocks, which is why this is a naming defect rather than a behavioural one.
items.design:
## The collision

`sim_loop` advances a **day tick** (`m_day_tick`) and, every `econ_tick_days` = 30 × 3 = **90**
of them, an **economy tick** (`m_econ_tick`). So `k_ticks_per_year` is 4.

Both of these are true and they contradict each other if you read "tick" as one word:

- `survey_system.hpp`: *"reveals the body region-by-region over sim ticks (**one tick = one day**)"*
- `budget_system.hpp`: *"an economy tick is **one quarter** (k_ticks_per_year = 4)"*

**Nothing is behaviourally wrong.** Every comment is correct about the clock it means. What is wrong
is that a reader — and this project's own documents — cannot tell which clock a bare "tick" is.

## Why it stopped being cosmetic

It cost a session a detour on 2026-08-22, deriving BL-543's value anchor, because *"twice their
salary for that year"* needs to know how many ticks a year is. It happened to cancel there — both
halves of the ratio are per-head-per-tick, so the factor of 4 disappears — **but the next annualised
quantity may not be so lucky**, and BL-550 (national insolvency) and BL-464 (logistic points, a
per-tick rate) are both about to add more.

## The scope, measured rather than estimated

**28 references across 13 source files:**

    src/core/sim_loop.{hpp,cpp}      the definition and the boundary test
    src/core/app.{hpp,cpp}           the advance call
    src/core/session_history.cpp
    src/core/verify_api.cpp
    src/world/logistics.{hpp,cpp}    econ_tick_days_world — the mirrored constant
    src/ui/time_panel.cpp            the quarter countdown
    src/ui/interp.{hpp,cpp}          the interpolation fraction
    src/ui/body_surface_canvas.cpp   convoy progress within a tick
    src/main.cpp

## The rename

`econ_tick_days` → **`days_per_econ_tick`**, and every bare `tick` in a comment gains its
qualifier. The two accessors read `day_tick()` and `econ_tick()` already, which is the pattern to
propagate rather than invent.

**Note the mirrored constant.** `logistics.hpp` carries `econ_tick_days_world` — a restatement of
`sim_loop::econ_tick_days`, because `world/*` must not depend on `core/*` and the headless
harnesses link the world layer alone. **Both must move together**, and the stepped-clock harness
already asserts they agree, so the check for this rename exists.

## Also: GLOSSARY.md defines neither term

Whatever the code does, both belong in the canonical vocabulary. That half is free and should land
with the rename rather than after it.

## Why this was filed rather than done in the session that found it

No build tree and no compiler check available in that session — a 28-site cross-file rename with no
compile is the shape of change that ships a typo. Filed with the scope measured so the doing is
mechanical.

items.title: Four files hand-roll the same byte primitives, and the shared version now exists
items.summary: history_log.cpp, procurement.cpp and sentiment.cpp each carry their own private read_u32/write_u32/read_f32 helpers over reinterpret_cast. BL-536 landed binary_io.hpp on 2026-08-22 as the shared set, with bounds constants and a checked r_enum the three copies do not have. Consolidate the three onto it.
items.design:
## What is duplicated

`src/world/history_log.cpp`, `src/world/procurement.cpp` and `src/world/sentiment.cpp` each open with
the same private helpers — `write_u32`, `write_f32`, `read_u32`, `read_f32` — over
`out.write(reinterpret_cast<const char*>(&v), sizeof v)`. Three copies of one idiom, each written
by a different session following the one before it.

**The fourth copy is the shared one.** `src/world/binary_io.hpp` (BL-536, merged 2026-08-22) is the
same primitives, done once, plus what the three copies do not have:

- `max_field_bytes` and `max_count` as named constants, rather than each stream inventing its own
  (`history_log_max_entries`, `procurement_max_records`, `sentiment_max_records`);
- `r_enum`, which reads a `uint8_t` and **rejects an out-of-range byte rather than casting it** —
  the property that matters most now that thirty enums cross a versioned byte stream (NR-545);
- `w_str` / `r_str` with a length bound, which each copy re-derives.

## Why it is a C and not higher

**Nothing is broken.** All three bound their counts, all three round-trip, and their harnesses pass.
This is duplication rather than a defect, and it was correct at the time each copy was written:
`sentiment.cpp` says in its own comment that it follows *"history_log / procurement exactly"*, which
was the convention until `binary_io.hpp` landed a day later.

What makes it worth an item rather than nothing: **the next person to add a stream will copy the
nearest one**, and there are three wrong nearest ones and one right one. The cost of leaving it is
that the checked `r_enum` never reaches the older streams.

## The work

Replace the private helpers in the three files with `binary_io.hpp`'s. **The byte layout must not
change** — this is a refactor behind three version gates that all still read the same bytes, so
every format version stays where it is and each harness's round-trip row is the proof. Where a
stream's own maximum differs from `max_count`, keep the stream's — a per-stream bound is a
deliberate statement about that stream, not an accident.

One judgement to make while doing it: whether `procurement.cpp`'s and `sentiment.cpp`'s enum reads
should move to `r_enum`. They should — that is most of the value — but it is a **behaviour** change
at the rejection boundary (a byte that was silently cast is now refused), so it lands with a row
asserting the rejection and a note in the item report.

## Found

2026-08-23, integrating Sprint N1's sentiment slice: the slice was written before `binary_io.hpp`
existed and could not have used it. Recorded as NR-549.

items.title: history_conquest_gap measures an Era -1 the game never runs — six divergences from the app's own invocation
A nation's credits arrive from nowhere — the player cannot see who funded them, on which line, or whether the line was rationed
items.summary: BL-537 makes a nation's treasury pay a NAMED corporation directly. Today that lands as an unexplained balance increase. This surfaces the transfer at its two natural homes - a Balance Ledger row group and a comms message - and carries the ONE field that changes a decision: fill_fraction.
items.design:
## The question it answers

> **Who is paying me, on what, and will they keep paying?**

## Why it earns its space

BL-537 is the first flow in the game that puts credits into a corporation's balance **from outside
the market**. `apply_budget`'s five flows are all consequences of the player's own operations;
this one is a consequence of somebody else's decision. Without a surface it is the worst kind of
number — one that moves for reasons the player cannot inspect, on a ledger whose whole promise is
that every credit is accounted.

And it is the player's income under the mercenary framing. `docs/economy/CONTRACTS.md` names the
loop — levy → treasury → contract → the player's income — and this is the leg where the money
arrives.

## What to show, and the one field that matters

`nation_budget_result` and `budget_line_result` already carry everything (`nation_budget.hpp`):
per line, the **share** allotted, the **demand** against it, what was **paid**, and
`fill_fraction` with a `rationed` flag.

**`fill_fraction` is the decision-changing field and the reason this is not a receipt.** A line
paid in full and a line paid at 0.4 look identical in a balance; they predict opposite futures. A
rationed line means other corporations are claiming the same money, so next tick's payment shrinks
unless the player's claim grows. A full line means headroom. That single number turns a passive
receipt into a read on competition the player cannot get any other way — rival internals are
private under BL-068, and this is one of the few legitimate windows onto rival activity.

Minimum row: **nation · line · credits · fill**. Nothing else is required.

## Where it goes — two existing surfaces, no new panel

- **Balance Ledger**, as a row group beside the existing five flows. It is a money flow and that
  is the ledger's subject; a separate panel would split the answer to "where did my money come
  from" across two places.
- **Comms dock**, one message when a transfer lands. `docs/EVENTS.md` adopts BL-458's rule
  outright — *an event lands with its message, in the same change* — and names the political
  family as the one that is **already half-built and does not know it**: BL-537, BL-539 and BL-541
  all produce dateable changes with no notification layer. This is the first of them to get one.

## The visibility line, stated once

The player sees **the transfer they received**. They do **not** see the nation's weight vector,
any other corporation's payment, or the line's full claimant list. `fill_fraction` is the honest
aggregate — it says *how contested* without saying *by whom*, which is exactly the resolution
BL-068 permits for a rival's internals. BL-558 owns what a nation reveals about itself.

## Not in this item

A history of past transfers (that is a ledger-history question, and BL-211's shape), and any
projection of next tick's payment. The fill fraction is the input to that judgement; making the
judgement for the player is the thing this game consistently declines to do.

items.title: Sentiment informs a declaration and may never make one — so if the player cannot see it, it informs nothing
items.summary: BL-545 landed a directed, continuous, two-dimensional value and BL-546 gave it its first emitter. Nothing renders it. Because the substrate's invariant forbids it from ever acting on its own, a surface is not decoration here - it is the mechanism's ONLY output.
items.design:
## The question it answers

> **How does this actor feel about me, and which way is it moving?**

## Why it earns its space — the argument is unusually strong

RELATIONS.md's non-negotiable invariant, preserving Ben's 2026-08-17 ruling:

> **sentiment informs a declaration and may never make one** — no threshold flips a stance table
> by itself.

Read that as a UI requirement and it says something sharp: **the player is the only thing sentiment
can act through.** Every other quantity in the game has a mechanical consumer that reads it whether
anyone looks or not. This one, by design, has none. An unrendered sentiment table is not a system
with a missing view; it is a system with **no output at all** — the `military_points` defect that
`docs/PEOPLE.md` names, arrived at from the opposite direction.

## What to show

**Both dimensions, separately.** Access and Trust move independently by construction (`sentiment.cpp`
decays each on its own rate) and they mean different things: Access is *may I operate here*, Trust
is *will you deal with me*. Collapsing them to one bar would throw away the property the substrate
was built to have.

**The band, not the float.** `band_of` already exists in `sentiment.hpp` with authored edges
(`band_edge_near`, `band_edge_far`) and is documented as presentation-only. Use it. A player
reasoning about "hostile / wary / neutral / warm" is reasoning correctly; one reading -47.3 is
reading noise.

**Direction of travel, and this is the part a level cannot give.** Sentiment DECAYS toward neutral
— that is BL-391's fix — so a value at −40 that is recovering and one at −40 that is falling are
opposite situations and identical numbers. The readable is the trend. Cheapest honest form: the
band plus an arrow, derived from the last stored value rather than from a new history buffer.

**Directed, and shown as such.** A row is *observer → subject*. A→B and B→A are different values
and the surface must never average them: RELATIONS.md keeps hostility directed precisely so *a corp
can be at war and not know it*.

## Where it goes

Beside stance, not apart from it — the **Corporation panel's stance column** is settled (it is one
of only four `settled` entries in `question_log.json`) and sentiment is the layer underneath the
same relation. Two layers of one thing in one column: what they have *declared*, and what the
numbers *say*. The Selection element carries the same pair for a selected corp or nation.

## The visibility line

The player sees sentiment **they hold** and sentiment **held toward them**. Third-party pairs are
private — a rival's feelings about another rival are exactly the "internals" BL-068 protects, and
exposing them would make the map a solved graph. This also keeps the surface bounded: two rows per
known actor, not N².

## Not in this item

The emitters. BL-546 gives the substrate contract completion and cancellation; trade, force and
lobbying events are BL-539/BL-540's. A surface over two factors is still the whole surface — the
rows do not change when more factors land.

items.title: A supplier declines to quote and says nothing — the player sees a dead end where the code now knows a wait
items.summary: BL-391's second surviving demand, and the one BL-546 did not close. request_quote declines below reputation_floor and returns a bare rejection. Now that the value DECAYS the refusal is temporary, and the surface should say so - which turns a dead end into a wait, and a deadlock into a cost.
items.design:
## The question it answers

> **Why won't they deal with me, and when will they?**

## Why it earns its space

BL-391 called the reputation floor a deadlock. BL-546 dissolved the *mechanism* — a quantity that
decays to exact neutral has no permanent floor — but the **player-facing** half of that item is
untouched and BL-391's own text still owes it: *the floor and current standing must be visible*.

The defect is sharper now than before the fix. `corp_command.cpp`'s quote path returns
`rejected_reputation` and the player sees a refusal with no cause and no horizon. Before BL-546 that
was merely opaque; **now it is actively misleading**, because the refusal has an expiry the engine
can compute and the player cannot see. A recoverable situation rendered as a permanent one is worse
than an unexplained one — the player writes the supplier off.

## What to show

Three numbers and one derived one:

- **current standing** — the Trust value toward this supplier, as a band (BL-556's read);
- **the floor** — `reputation_floor`, authored in `economy.lua`, the line being failed;
- **what put it there** — the last factor that moved it, which the substrate already knows;
- **when it clears** — ticks until decay carries the value above the floor. Pure arithmetic on the
  authored rate and the current value, no new state: `sentiment.hpp` documents the decay as a rate
  precisely so it stays computable without a `pow`.

That last one is the item. It converts "they refuse" into "they refuse for eleven more quarters",
which is a **cost the player can price against** an alternative supplier — the difference between a
wall and a trade-off, and the difference between a system that punishes and a system that plays.

## Where it goes

Where the refusal already surfaces: the Selection element's procurement path, next to the quote
that was declined. It is an explanation of a specific rejection, not a standing panel, so it wants
no nav slot.

## The honest edge case

If the authored decay rate is **zero** — which is what ships today until Ben sets it — the answer
to "when will they" is *never*, and the surface must say that rather than compute a divide-by-zero
or quietly omit the line. A surface that reads "never" at rate zero is also the clearest possible
prompt that the rate wants authoring, which is BL-391's remaining open call.

## Pairs with

**BL-390**, which BL-391 names as its partner. This item is the read; BL-390 is the standing model
behind it.

items.title: A nation acts and the player can only see the consequences — what it DID should be readable, what it WANTS should not
items.summary: After BL-537 and BL-542 a nation holds a treasury, funds corporations, enacts law and carries an objective. Selecting one shows a name and a territory. This makes the nation a readable actor, and draws the line between its ACTIONS (public) and its WEIGHTS (private) in the same place BL-068 draws it for rival corps.
items.design:
## The question it answers

> **What kind of nation is this, and what has it been doing?**

## Why it earns its space

A nation is now an actor. It holds a treasury (BL-480's levy, the D4 tariff), it spends on weighted
priority lines (BL-537), it authors law — and after BL-542 it has an objective of its own. Selecting
one still shows a name and a border.

That matters most for the item nobody has built yet: **BL-539's lobbying**. Paying a nation to shift
its budget or its law is a decision the player cannot possibly make well against a nation they
cannot read. A lever with no dial is a slot machine, and lobbying is the player's first reach on law.
This item is the dial.

## THE LINE, and it is the design

> **A nation's ACTIONS are public. Its WEIGHTS are private.**

This is BL-068's rule — *rival buildings visible, internals private, markets public* — carried up a
grain, and it should be stated in NATIONS.md as such.

**Public, because they are observable in the fiction:** what the treasury holds, which corporations
it has paid and on which lines, which laws it has enacted, its tariff and levy rates, its declared
relations. Every one of these is a fact a company operating inside a country would simply know.

**Private, because it is the nation's reasoning:** `nation_budget::weights`, the reserve fraction,
and every term of the BL-542 scorer — niche fit, conflict avoidance, the grudge bias.

The split is not squeamishness, it is what makes the surface *interesting*. A player who is handed
the weight vector reads an answer; a player who is handed **four quarters of transfers** infers one,
and can be wrong. Inference from public conduct is the same game the market already asks the player
to play against rival corps, which is the strongest argument that it fits here: the mechanic already
exists and this extends it to a new actor rather than inventing a second epistemology.

## What to show

A Selection element card for a nation: **treasury** and its direction; **what it funded recently**,
as line + payee + credits (the public half of BL-555's data); **laws in force**, which
`condition_set` + effect already describe as data; **rates** (levy, tariff); **relations** it has
declared. Plus the sentiment pair from BL-556 if the observer is the player.

## Not in this item

Any projection of what the nation will do next, and any surfacing of the scorer. If the player wants
to know what a nation wants, they should have to watch it.

items.title: A stagnant-lid homeworld clears every viability clause and generates with one tectonic plate
items.summary: Bug, Ben 2026-08-22: 'Single Tectonic plate in some seeds.' Traced: run_continents derives plate_count from pl.mobile_lid and yields 1 on a stagnant lid, then EARLY-RETURNS before Voronoi assignment, boundary detection and orogeny - so height_bias stays all-zero and the body reaches tile Pass 1 with no continental signal. It reaches the HOMEWORLD because homeworld_viability's fourteen clauses never test mobile_lid. The stagnant-lid body case is designed and fine; the stagnant-lid homeworld case is not. RULED 2026-08-22: option (a), the gate clause, reusing s.mobile_lid rather than a re-derived theta band. Measure acceptance before and after via planetology_sweep C1.
items.design:
## Ben, 2026-08-22 (bug report)

> "Single Tectonic plate in some seeds."

## The mechanism, traced rather than guessed

`run_continents` (continents.cpp:64) derives plate count as a **consequence** of
planetology, never an independent roll:

```
plate_count = pl.mobile_lid ? clamp(lround(4 + theta * 3), 4, 10) : 1
```

With `plate_count == 1` it pushes one history line ("Interior locked into a single
stagnant plate.") and **early-returns at line 86** — before Voronoi assignment,
before boundary detection, before the orogeny pass. `height_bias` stays all-zero
across every tile and `plate_id` is uniformly 0.

So the body reaches tile Pass 1 with **no continental signal at all**. Terrain then
reflects only the noise bands: no ranges, no rifts, no collision zones. Planetology
has already halved the metals on the same flag (copper 1.25x metal -> 0.18x at
line 1464; rare earth 0.9 -> 0.15 at 1471), so the economy thins out with the relief.

## Why it reaches the HOMEWORLD, which is the actual bug

`homeworld_viability` (planetology.cpp:253) is a fourteen-clause gate — archetype,
civilisation, O2 floor and ceiling, hydrology, water fraction, temperature, arable
share, escape velocity, primary fuel, iron. **`mobile_lid` is not one of them.**

`mobile_lid_at` needs `theta` in [0.55, 2.2] with `mass >= 0.45` and water present.
The viability gate constrains mass and water indirectly, but it never constrains
`theta` at all. A cradle that draws a cold or a very hot interior therefore passes
every clause and arrives with one plate.

This is the line between variety and bug. The Continent lens **already has a legend
line for the stagnant case** ("Stagnant lid: one immobile plate.", body_surface_canvas.cpp:826),
so an ordinary body drawing a stagnant lid is designed content. What was never
designed is the case where it happens to the **one world the campaign is played on**,
whose relief, ranges and copper the whole economy reads.

## The decision, which is Ben's

**(a) Add a mobile-lid clause to `homeworld_viability`** and pay the extra rerolls.
Smallest change; one line in the file that already owns the rejection histogram. It
is a **gate**, not a clamp — reject and redraw, never reshape an outcome — so it
stays on the right side of BL-167's ruling.

**(b) Leave the gate and accept a flat homeworld** as a legible starting condition,
which is exactly what BL-192 (generation affordance guarantees) chose for the
highway tier at 37%.

**(c) Narrow the `radiogenic` / `world_size` preference bands** so `theta` lands in
the mobile window more often. This is the retune, and it is the option BL-192
explicitly rejected as "clamping with extra steps" — it silently changes every other
property those bands drive.

**Recommendation: (a)**, and MEASURE FIRST per the BL-167 pattern. Before the clause
is added, `tools/verify/planetology_sweep.cpp`'s C1 census should report the current
stagnant-lid rate among **passing** homeworlds, and afterwards the acceptance cost.
Both are numbers the sweep already knows how to produce; neither should be a guess.

## Not to be confused with

BL-538 (start viability) may or may not be the same bug under a different reading —
see that item, which is filed design-owed for exactly that reason.

---

## RULED by Ben, 2026-08-22 (elicitation form)

**(a) — add a mobile-lid clause to `homeworld_viability`.** Reject and redraw; pay
the rerolls.

The clause goes in beside the other fourteen, in the same style — a `bool` test
returning `{ false, "<reason>" }` so the sweep's rejection histogram picks it up for
free. The natural form is the same predicate `mobile_lid_at` already computes rather
than a re-derived theta band, so the gate and the flag cannot drift apart:

    if (!s.mobile_lid)  return { false, "stagnant lid" };

**Why this is a gate and not a clamp**, which is the whole reason it clears BL-167:
nothing about the drawn world is reshaped. The draw is rejected and the next attempt
runs, exactly as the existing fourteen clauses do. `resolve_preferences` already
folds the attempt index into the draw, so the search stays a pure function of
(preferences, seed) and `attempts` reports the cost honestly.

**Measure the acceptance cost, do not estimate it.** `tools/verify/planetology_sweep.cpp`'s
C1 census is the instrument and it already reports per-clause rejection rates. Run it
before and after. Two numbers matter: the stagnant-lid rate among currently-*passing*
homeworlds (how often the bug actually bites), and the new acceptance rate (what the
clause costs). The comment at planetology.cpp:290 puts real acceptance at 60-85% and
`max_attempts` at 512, so there is headroom — but that should be confirmed, not
assumed, because the C1 census exists precisely because one clause (heat) turned out
to be the single largest source of rejection once measured.

**Watch for interaction with the `world_size` preference.** `mobile_lid_at` also tests
`mass >= 0.45`, and the `world_size` band bottoms out at 0.66 — so mass is not the
binding term and the clause will reject on theta. A player leaning `world_size` low
combined with a cold `radiogenic` draw is the combination most likely to spend
attempts; if the sweep shows that lean hitting the cap, that is a preference-band
question and a separate decision.

items.title: Some campaign starts are not viable, and nothing defines or measures what viable means
items.summary: Bug, Ben 2026-08-22: 'Starts which are not viable.' Filed design-owed rather than guessed at: the sentence has two readings (the WORLD generates unplayable, or the player CORP opens with no path) that lead to different files and different fixes. What both need first is a predicate and a measured rate, in the BL-167 shape - name the test, sweep it, then choose gate / design-around / retune. RULED 2026-08-22: BOTH readings in scope. Reading 1 largely discharged by BL-559; reading 2 is now the centre. Still design-owed on the PREDICATE, which is the part that must not be guessed.
items.design:
## Ben, 2026-08-22 (bug report)

> "Starts which are not viable."

Filed **design-owed rather than guessed at**, because the sentence has two readings
and they land in different files with different fixes. Both are cheap to answer and
expensive to assume.

## Reading 1 — the WORLD generates unplayable

The homeworld itself is the problem. That reading is largely **BL-559**'s (a
stagnant lid clearing every viability clause, giving one plate and no relief), plus
whatever else `homeworld_viability`'s fourteen clauses fail to catch. The gate
exists and works; the question is what is missing from it.

## Reading 2 — the player's OPENING POSITION has no path

The world is fine and the corp is not. `place_starting_assets`
(corporation_generation.cpp:509) clusters a corp's holdings around a seed tile, and
the result can be a corp with no workable deposit in reach, no market access, or no
capital to build its way out of either.

**BL-192 (generation affordance guarantees) already settled the neighbouring case**
and supplies the precedent. Its subject was the opening processing facility, present
on ~25% of seeds; its ruling was *remove the dependency, do not guarantee the
affordance* — the player does not need to OWN a processor at t=0, they need to be
able to reach one, and construction exists. But BL-192 also named, in its own words,
the one thing it did not do, and it is exactly this item:

> "whether a fresh campaign has the capital and sited opportunity to build one early
> — that is worth measuring, and it is a different question with a much cheaper
> answer than reshaping world generation."

So reading 2 is a measurement BL-192 deferred, not new ground.

## What is needed before either reading can be built

A **definition** and a **measurement**, in the BL-167 shape — the same order that
settled BL-192:

1. **Name the predicate.** Candidates, none of them chosen: workable deposits within
   N tiles of the seed cluster; a market centre within reach; a positive
   `estimate_prospective_profit` on the best buildable site; a positive runway over
   K ticks at the opening balance.
2. **Measure the rate** across a seed sweep, and report which clause fails — the
   `planetology_sweep` C1 histogram is the model.
3. **Then choose** gate / design-around / retune, with the number in hand.

Note one measurement already in the file that bears on step 1: NR-443 recorded that
**`starting_capital` is zero on every generated corp**, which is why
`econ_bankruptcy`'s -5x rule degenerates to a trigger at -0.0. If "viable" is to
include a capital term, that zero is the first thing to look at.

## Open, and un-guessed

- Which reading did Ben mean? (Or both — they are not exclusive.)
- What is the predicate?

---

## RULED by Ben, 2026-08-22 (elicitation form)

**BOTH readings are in scope.** Ben selected the player's opening position *and* the
world generating unplayable. They are not exclusive and the item covers both.

What that settles and what it leaves:

- **Reading 1 (the world)** is largely discharged by **BL-559**, now ruled: the
  stagnant-lid homeworld gets a viability clause. What remains under this item is
  whether any *other* unplayable-world case exists that the fifteen clauses still
  miss — a question the `planetology_sweep` C1 histogram can answer directly, since
  it reports which clause rejects and therefore also what never gets tested.
- **Reading 2 (the opening position)** is untouched and is now the item's centre of
  gravity. It is the measurement BL-192 named and deferred in its own words.

**Still design-owed, and deliberately so: the predicate.** The reading is settled;
what "viable" *means* is not, and it should not be guessed. The candidates named
above stand — reachable deposits within N tiles, a market centre in reach, a positive
`estimate_prospective_profit` on the best buildable site, a positive runway over K
ticks. The zero `starting_capital` on every generated corp (NR-443) is the first
thing to look at if the predicate carries a capital term, because it makes any
multiple-of-starting-capital rule degenerate.

Order of work is unchanged: name the predicate, sweep the rate, then choose gate /
design-around / retune with the number in hand.

items.title: The generated world is surprisingly under-industrialised - too few worked tiles
items.summary: Bug, Ben 2026-08-22: 'Surprising lack of industrialisation (need more worked tiles...)'. Contradicts GENERATION_STRATEGY's saturated-base premise directly. generate_background_firms stops on whichever of two bounds fires first - a MEASURED production/demand ratio at target_ratio 0.90, or the anti-runaway max_firms_per_body 200 - and the file's own measurement seam (measure_production_ratio et al, added 2026-08-20) exists to answer which. Run that first: the lever is different for each answer. Report built TILES per body, not firms. RULED 2026-08-22: raise max_firms_per_body directly rather than measuring first. Caveat carried into the design: the two bounds are in SERIES, so if the 0.90 ratio is what stops the loop the cap raise is inert - which makes reporting which bound fired part of landing the change, not a preliminary.
items.design:
## Ben, 2026-08-22 (bug report)

> "Surprising lack of industrialisation (need more worked tiles, and these should
> not be filled on the default lens)"

The second clause is **BL-562** — the two are one thought and are split only because
they land in different layers. See that item for why the fill matters *because* of
this one.

## Why this is a bug and not a preference

`GENERATION_STRATEGY.md`'s economic premise is a **saturated, earth-like base** whose
broad industry real background corporations own and run (BL-365), with the player and
the major AI arriving as **specialist** space-interested corporations. A world that
reads as sparsely worked contradicts the premise outright: it makes the player the
first industrialist rather than a specialist entering a full economy, which is a
different game from the one the docs describe.

## Where the count is actually decided

`generate_background_firms` (corporation_generation.cpp:1687) stops on whichever of
**two bounds** fires first:

| Bound | Constant | Line | Kind |
|---|---|---|---|
| basket-weighted `production_ratio(production, demand) >= target_ratio` | `0.90f` | 1718 | the MEASURED stop |
| `firms_this_body < max_firms_per_body` | `200` | 1750 | "anti-runaway only" |
| `iter < max_iterations_per_body` | `3 * max_firms_per_body` | 1753 | slack for placement misses |

**Which one actually fires is the whole question**, and the file already says so. A
measurement seam was added on 2026-08-20 (lines 1956+) for precisely this —
`measure_body_demand`, `measure_body_production`, `measure_production_ratio` expose
the **shipped** arithmetic so a harness can ask without re-implementing it (the
comment names the hand-mirrored-table drift this project has hit four times).

**Run that seam before touching a constant.** The fix is different for each answer:

- **The ratio stops it.** The world has 90% of its demand covered and simply has
  fewer, larger firms than expected. The lever is `target_ratio`; raising it toward
  or past 1.0 is a one-constant change with a measurable consequence.
- **The firm cap stops it.** 200 is binding and the ratio never gets there. Raising
  the cap is the change — and the comment at line 1722 records that it was already
  raised once, from 40.
- **Neither** — `max_iterations_per_body` exhausts on placement misses. Then the bug
  is in siting (`place_starting_assets`), not in the stop condition at all, and no
  amount of raising either bound will help.

## The number to report is TILES, not firms

Each firm places a **small cluster** of holdings, so firm count and worked-tile count
are not the same variable and moving the first does not linearly move the second.
Whatever lever moves, the measurement to report is **built tiles per body** — and per
nation, since NR-461 already measured settlement density per nation and refuted a
sprint premise on it.

## What is NOT holding it down

BL-513's per-province building ceiling. NR-421 measured it as **inert by orders of
magnitude, not by a near miss**, and NR-509 saw it stated on screen the day BL-534
shipped: one province reading capacity 0 / 103 over a geology supporting 24 slots.
So the province cap is four times clear of anything geology can support, and
re-pinning `k_province_buildings_per_sustain_unit` is a separate decision already
recorded — not this one.

## Open

How much more is enough? "More worked tiles" sets a direction, not a target. The
honest form is to measure the current built-tiles-per-body figure first and have Ben
name a target against a real number rather than against prose (Rule 0b).

---

## RULED by Ben, 2026-08-22 (elicitation form)

**Raise `max_firms_per_body` (corporation_generation.cpp:1750).** Ben chose the
lever directly over running the measurement seam first.

**One caveat, stated once and then built to.** The two bounds are in series, not in
parallel: the loop runs `for (iter < max_iterations_per_body && firms_this_body <
max_firms_per_body)` and breaks early when `production_ratio >= target_ratio`
(0.90f). So if the **ratio** is what currently stops the loop, raising the cap changes
nothing at all — the loop was never reaching it. Raising the cap only adds firms in
the case where the cap is the binding bound.

That makes one check unavoidable rather than optional, and it is cheap: **report which
bound fired, before and after.** Not as a preliminary study — as part of landing the
change, since it is the only thing that distinguishes "the lever worked" from "the
lever was inert". The seam for it already exists (`measure_production_ratio`, added
2026-08-20) and needs no new harness scaffolding.

**Raise `max_iterations_per_body` with it.** It is defined as `3 * max_firms_per_body`
(line 1753), so it scales automatically — but confirm the 3x slack still absorbs
placement misses at the higher count. Placement gets *harder* as the body fills, so
the miss rate is not constant across the run and the multiplier that was generous at
200 may not be at 400.

**Report tiles, not firms.** Unchanged and still the point: each firm places a small
cluster, so the number that answers Ben's complaint is **built tiles per body**, and
per nation. A firm count that doubles may not double worked tiles.

**Expect the generation cost to move.** `generate_background_firms` runs inside the
~25-38 s world build; more firms means more `place_starting_assets` calls and more
recipe assignment. If the cost becomes noticeable this collides with BL-320 (Era 1
sim perf) and with BL-536's motive for the save format in the first place.

items.title: A built tile keeps its terrain on the default lens - the owner plate stops filling the hex
items.summary: Bug, Ben 2026-08-22, the second half of the industrialisation note: worked tiles 'should not be filled on the default lens'. Today built_plate_colour swaps a built hex WHOLESALE for a deep machine grey or the owner's identity colour, and three further channels are suppressed behind !built gates - texture, relief and the landform glyph. Defensible at today's building density; at BL-561's density it inverts, and the map goes grey exactly where the economy is. On overlay_mode::none the tile keeps terrain, texture and relief, and the building MARKER carries ownership. RULED 2026-08-22: marker PLUS a thin 1px owner-coloured border, so ownership survives at the zoom where a marker does not. Carries a named tension with BL-514, which deleted the province edge stroke to make land one continuous field.
items.design:
## Ben, 2026-08-22 (bug report)

> "Surprising lack of industrialisation (need more worked tiles, **and these should
> not be filled on the default lens**)"

One thought with BL-561, split because it lands in `src/ui/` rather than
`src/world/`. It stands on its own, but the *reason it is now urgent* is that one.

## What happens today

A built tile is swapped **wholesale** for a plate. `built_plate_colour`
(body_surface_canvas.cpp:214-225) returns a deep machine grey, or the owner's
identity colour when the tile has an owner, and its comment states the intent
plainly: "deliberately outside the terrain hues so a built tile never [reads as
terrain]".

That fill then suppresses **three further channels** on the same hex, each gated on
`!built`:

| Channel | Line | The reason given |
|---|---|---|
| substrate/cover texture (BL-520) | 2352 | the hex is swapped wholesale for its owner plate |
| elevation relief | 2090 | "the elevation matters when SITING, and a built tile has already been sited" |
| landform glyph (BL-231/232) | 2721 | a built hex "already carries an enlarged silhouette plus a corp emblem tag" |

Every one of those was a defensible call **at the current building density**.

## Why it inverts

At BL-561's density it stops being defensible: the more industrialised the world,
the more of the map is machine grey, and the terrain the player is reading the map
*for* disappears exactly where the economy is. The fill is only a problem because
there are about to be many more of these tiles — which is why Ben stated it in the
same breath as the density.

## The change

On `overlay_mode::none` the tile **keeps its terrain fill, its texture and its
relief**, and ownership is carried by the **marker** — the building silhouette plus
corp emblem already drawn at line 2636 — rather than by the ground.

The plate treatment is **not deleted**. It belongs to the lenses whose question
*is* ownership (Corporation), where a categorical fill is the right answer and the
density argument does not apply.

## Care needed

- **The three `!built` gates move together or not at all.** Un-suppressing the fill
  while leaving texture and relief suppressed yields a tile that is terrain-coloured
  but flat and untextured — worse than either end state.
- **Marker contrast.** `contrast_ink` picks ink against the *finished* fill. Against
  terrain rather than a known grey plate, the silhouette needs re-checking across the
  substrate range; `icy` (200, 224, 236) is the worst case at the light end and
  `volcanic` (135, 55, 28) at the dark.
- **Hit-testing does not change.** Line 3229's "a built tile resolves to its BUILDING
  across the whole hex, not just inside [the marker]" is a *selection* rule, not a
  rendering one, and should survive untouched.
- **The landform glyph gate is BL-565's too.** That item retires the mountain glyph
  in favour of relief; if relief becomes a mountain's only channel, then a built
  mountain tile losing relief here is a real loss. The two items meet at line 2090.

## Verification

`visual`, and it needs a **live check** — a scripted capture proves the fill changed;
only opening the app and looking proves the map still reads.

---

## RULED by Ben, 2026-08-22 (elicitation form)

**Marker plus a thin owner-coloured border.** The hex keeps terrain, texture and
relief; ownership is carried by the building marker *and* a 1 px identity stroke on
the tile edge.

**Why the stroke earns its place:** a marker shrinks with zoom, and the Planetary
canvas is routinely read at a zoom where a silhouette is a few pixels. The border
keeps ownership scannable at that range without a fill, which is the property the
machine-grey plate was actually providing and the marker alone would not replace.

**The tension to hold, named rather than discovered later.** BL-514 removed the
province edge stroke *entirely* — not dialled to alpha 0, deliberately deleted,
because "land is one continuous field". This puts a per-tile stroke back on land. The
two are reconcilable and the distinction is the argument: BL-514 removed a **partition**
line (an edge between two pieces of ground that are the same kind of thing), and this
adds an **ownership** line (an edge between worked and unworked ground). But it means
the stroke must be visibly *not* a province border — so it should follow the built
tile's own outline only, never run along unbuilt neighbours, and it should not be
mistaken for BL-535's national border, which is also about to become a hard edge.

**Colour source:** the corp identity colour already resolved for `owner_col`, the same
value `built_plate_colour` takes today. Unowned/background-firm tiles need a decision
— either the same stroke in a neutral, or no stroke, and the second is probably right
so that the player's own holdings read as the marked ones.

**Re-check contrast on the extremes.** The stroke sits on terrain now, not on a known
grey. `icy` (200, 224, 236) is the worst case at the light end and `volcanic`
(135, 55, 28) at the dark; a mid-saturation identity colour can vanish against either.

All three `!built` gates still move together — that constraint is unchanged.

items.title: A province can span two nations - the province fill has no notion of who owns the ground
items.summary: Bug, Ben 2026-08-22: 'Provinces cross country boundaries'. Confirmed as an ABSENCE: province.cpp's bw.owner is the region index, and the whole 936-line file has no nation term. RULED 2026-08-22: CO-GENERATE the two partitions rather than constrain the fill - provinces are grown to FIT national borders, so a province edge and a national border are the same kind of line by construction. This dissolves the frontier-fragmentation question (offcuts never exist, so no merge pass). The conquest half of Ben's ruling is split to BL-567. Requirement is headless: no province holds tiles of two nations.
items.design:
## Ben, 2026-08-22 (bug report)

> "Provinces cross country boundaries, and country boundaries should not diffuse
> together"

**The second half is already filed** — BL-535 (national hue replaces the Country
lens) carries Ben's ruling that the corner blend stops at national borders, designed
2026-08-22 and not yet built. It is not duplicated here. The two are complementary:
BL-535 stops the **colour** crossing the border; this stops the **partition**
crossing it.

## Confirmed, and it is an absence rather than a mistake

`province.cpp`'s multi-source flood fill (line 189 onward) claims tiles into
`bw.owner` — where `owner` is the **region index**, not a nation. Line 113 is
explicit: `tile -> region index (+1; 0 = unclaimed)`. Grepping the whole 936-line
file for a nation, country or owner-polity term returns nothing.

The fill's cost function reads terrain and boundaries — its own comment at line 231
says "boundaries win" of the gentle-and-broken-country case — and it **never reads
which nation holds the tile**. So nothing stops a region growing straight across a
national border, and on some seeds it does.

## Why this matters beyond tidiness

The province is no longer a rendering convenience; it is a **load-bearing unit**:

- the grain of **BL-513**'s per-province building ceiling,
- the grain of **BL-534**'s available-buildings table, which is per province throughout by Ben's explicit ruling,
- the grain of the Era -1 sim's territory movement — history_sim.cpp's own comment: *TERRITORY MOVES AT PROVINCE GRANULARITY, NEVER TILE*,
- the render unit under **BL-511**.

A province held by two nations at once has no defined answer to "whose ceiling is
this", "who levies here", or "who loses it when the border moves" (**BL-518**, war
redraws borders — which is the item this breaks hardest).

## The fix: a constraint on the fill, not a post-pass repair

A candidate tile whose nation differs from its seed region's is **not claimable** by
that region. That keeps the fill's shape — still multi-source, still
boundary-respecting — and makes the national border a **hard edge** alongside the
terrain ones it already respects.

Two consequences to expect and to check rather than to be surprised by:

1. **More, smaller provinces near borders.** Nations that interlock will fragment
   their frontier regions. Whether that is acceptable, or wants a minimum-size merge
   pass, is worth looking at on a real map before deciding.
2. **The unclaimed-pocket pass will have more work.** Lines 534-560 handle tiles left
   over ("now they are pockets rather than open country") and lines 646-679 reassign
   them to the best neighbouring region. **That reassignment needs the same nation
   constraint** or it will quietly undo the fix on exactly the frontier tiles the fix
   was for.

## Determinism

The fill is seeded and order-stable today and must stay so. The constraint is a
**rejection inside an existing walk**, adding no new randomness and no new ordering —
the cheap shape. A `headless` check asserting no province contains tiles of two
nations is the requirement, and it is a one-pass scan over `w.provinces`.

---

## RULED by Ben, 2026-08-22 (elicitation form)

Ben's answer went past all three options, and dissolved the question rather than
picking from it:

> "Generate provinces alongside national borders, and have it be impossible to
> conquer a tile without also controlling the province"

Two rulings. **The first is this item.** The second is a forward constraint on a
system that does not exist yet and is filed as **BL-567 (the province is the unit of
conquest)** — see NR-560 for why it was split rather than carried here.

## Co-generation, not a constraint on an existing walk

The item as filed proposed rejecting cross-nation candidates inside the existing
fill. That is the weaker answer and Ben's is better: the two partitions are
**produced together**, so a province edge and a national border are the same kind of
line **by construction** rather than by a rule that forbids one crossing the other.

The practical difference is where the national boundary enters. Under a rejection
rule it enters as a veto at claim time, and the fill's cost function still knows
nothing about it — so region shapes are decided by terrain and then trimmed. Under
co-generation the boundary is an input to the partition, and the regions are grown
to *fit* it.

**This also dissolves the fragmentation question the form asked.** A rejection rule
fragments frontiers because regions grow across the border and then get cut. Regions
grown to fit the border do not need cutting, so there is no scatter of one- and
two-tile offcuts to merge away. That is why the minimum-size merge pass is not part
of this ruling: it was a repair for damage the weaker design would have caused.

## What this touches

Nation territory is assigned by **Pass 2 (territory expansion)** of nation
generation — Voronoi BFS over the tile map (NATION_GENERATION.md), landing in
`nation_component::tiles`, documented as "populated by Pass 2 and **stable
thereafter**". The province fill (province.cpp:189+) runs as its own multi-source
flood fill with no nation term anywhere in its 936 lines.

Co-generation means those two stop being independent. The cheapest honest form,
and the one to design against first: **the province fill takes the national
assignment as a hard input** — seeds are placed per nation, and a region's frontier
is the national border wherever it reaches one, with the terrain cost function
operating only *within* a nation's territory. That is co-generation in effect
(borders shape provinces) without inverting the pass order, which would be a far
larger change to a pipeline whose sequence other passes depend on.

Whether provinces should also feed **back** into where national borders fall — true
mutual co-generation — is a bigger question and is not needed to satisfy the ruling.
Flagged, not assumed.

## Determinism

Unchanged as a requirement and easier to hold than the rejection design: the fill
stays seeded and order-stable, and taking a per-nation input adds no randomness and
no new ordering. `w.provinces` remains generation output, outside `state_hash`, with
its determinism checked by `determinism_harness` field-for-field across two
generations. **Do not let this change disturb that** — BL-467 folds a province id
into a battle seed, so a silent partition regression moves battle outcomes.

## The requirement

`headless`, one pass: **no province contains tiles belonging to two nations.** A scan
over `w.provinces` cross-referenced against `nation_component::tiles`. It should fail
on today's build, which is what makes it worth writing first.

items.title: Province and tile selection become one element, deposits behind the top-right dropdown
items.summary: Ben 2026-08-22: 'Province and tile selection elements can be bundled into one. Keep the drop down at the top right schema pattern, so for the different tile deposits, we can use only one accordion tab.' Two of the three statements are already shipped by BL-534 (the accordion, and deposits behind a dropdown in ONE Resources tab) and this CONFIRMS that pattern as the schema. What is new is bundling province and tile into one element - which reads against BL-534's own record, where Province was offered as a fourth tab and explicitly NOT picked. Design-owed on that point, and on whether BL-473 folds in. RULED 2026-08-22: Province becomes a FOURTH TAB, reversing BL-534s same-day ruling - defensible because the Available buildings tab is already per-province throughout. Ownership declined a second time; treat as settled. Open: whether BL-473 becomes this tabs body.
items.design:
## Ben, 2026-08-22 (bug report)

> "Province and tile selection elements can be bundled into one. Keep the drop down
> at the top right schema pattern, so for the different tile deposits, we can use
> only one accordion tab"

Three statements. Two of them are already half-built, and the third is the item.

## Statements 2 and 3 are shipped — this CONFIRMS them

**BL-534** landed the same day (commit e855163). It turned the Selection band's
centre column from a **one-page-per-deposited-resource carousel** — "Iron Ore (1/7)"
behind prev/next arrows, so reading the seventh deposit cost six presses — into a
three-view accordion: **Terrain**, **Resources**, **Available buildings**. The
resource choice moved *inside* the Resources view as a dropdown, matching
`draw_lens_resource_combo`, which already does exactly this for the lenses.

So "one accordion tab for the different tile deposits, chosen from a dropdown" is
the shape that shipped. What this item adds is the **ruling that the
dropdown-at-top-right is the schema pattern to keep** — reusable, not a one-off for
resources.

## Statement 1 is the new work, and it revisits a ruling

Province and tile selection are **still two elements** and Ben wants one.

**BL-473** (province in selection, open, v0.1.17) proposed the earlier answer: the
Selection band renders the locality cell and the tile preview outlines the province.
That is province *shown alongside* tile. Ben is asking for something stronger — one
element, with province and tile as **views of the same selection** rather than two
panels.

That reads directly against BL-534's own record. Province was **offered as a fourth
tab and not picked**, and the commit is explicit that the array of three "is the
ruling rather than a starting point". So this is Ben revisiting that call — and the
accordion is now the mechanism to revisit it *with*: a Province view sitting
alongside Terrain / Resources / Available buildings, rather than a separate element
beside the band.

## Open, and to settle before promotion

- Does **BL-473 fold into** this item, or does its locality-cell + province-outline
  treatment survive as the Province view's *content*?
- Is **Ownership** back on the table too? It was offered alongside Province and
  declined in the same breath.
- Is the province view a **tab**, or is it the accordion's always-visible header —
  i.e. does selecting a tile select its province, with the tile as the detail?

## The one constraint the implementation must not break

BL-534's commit recorded it, and it is the sort of thing a follow-up quietly undoes:

> `tile_metrics` still builds **one** page list and the two views filter it.
> Splitting it into two builders was the obvious move and the wrong one: the
> full-canvas fold charts the same pages **by index**, so a second builder is how the
> two would come to disagree about what page N is.

Adding a Province view means adding to that one list, not authoring a second.

---

## RULED by Ben, 2026-08-22 (elicitation form)

**Province becomes a fourth tab**, alongside Terrain / Resources / Available
buildings.

This reverses BL-534's ruling of the same day, where Province was offered and not
picked — which is Ben's to reverse, and the reason is visible in what shipped: the
Available buildings tab is *already* per-province throughout, so the accordion had
province content in it before it had a province tab. A fourth tab regularises that
rather than introducing something new.

**The implementation constraint is unchanged and is the thing to get right.**
`tile_metrics` builds **one** page list and the views filter it. A Province view is a
fourth filter over that same list, never a second builder — because the full-canvas
fold charts the same pages **by index**, and a second builder is how the two come to
disagree about what page N is. BL-534's commit recorded this; it applies verbatim here.

**Ownership was not selected**, so it does not get a tab. It was offered twice now and
declined twice; treat that as settled rather than as pending.

**BL-473 (province in selection) is not resolved by this**, and the relationship needs
one call before promotion: its locality-cell + tile-preview-outline treatment is
*content*, and this item supplies the *home*. The most likely reading is that BL-473
becomes the Province tab's body and the two land together — but that is an inference,
not a ruling, and it is the one thing still open here.

items.title: Mountains read as elevated ground, not as a glyph
items.summary: Bug, Ben 2026-08-22: 'Mountains need to blend in as visibly elevated, rather than glyphs.' Both channels already exist and the balance between them is wrong. landform_relief shades warm-above / cool-below by relief_amount (mountain +0.22) and deliberately holds magnitudes small; BL-231/232 draw peaked-teeth glyphs and bridged spans for the four dramatic landforms. The ruling reverses the weighting FOR MOUNTAINS: raise the relief so a range reads as raised ground from the fill alone, retire the mountain glyph and its spans, keep canyon/crater/rift which sink or pit and which relief serves far less well. RULED 2026-08-22: mountain +0.22 -> +0.45, highland +0.12 -> +0.25, other five untouched; mountain retired from the dramatic-landform set entirely, glyph and BL-232 spans both. Must land with or after BL-562, since relief is suppressed on built tiles and the glyph was the only other channel.
items.design:
## Ben, 2026-08-22 (bug report)

> "Mountains need to blend in as visibly elevated, rather than glyphs."

Both channels already exist. The balance between them is what is wrong.

## The relief channel — deliberately quiet

`landform_relief` (hex_render.cpp) blends the tile's base colour toward a warm
highlight above or a cool shadow below, by `relief_amount`:

| Landform | Amount |
|---|---|
| mountain | +0.22 |
| highland | +0.12 |
| plains | 0.00 |
| crater | -0.08 |
| valley | -0.10 |
| rift | -0.14 |
| canyon | -0.16 |

The comment states the intent — *"Warm sun above, cool shadow below — the convention
that makes a shaded map read as topography rather than as two arbitrary tints"* —
and then holds it back on purpose: **"Magnitudes stay small on purpose."** Highlight
is (255, 248, 225), shadow (18, 24, 40).

## The glyph channel — BL-231 and BL-232

body_surface_canvas.cpp:2698+. Only the four **dramatic** landforms draw — mountain,
canyon, crater, rift — each measured at <=1.5% of land tiles, each carrying a
movement cost of x1.3 or worse, "so this is the set where an invisible surprise is
expensive". Mountain draws **peaked teeth** (icons.cpp:614, :741).

BL-232 then added **bridging**: a tile with a same-landform cardinal neighbour draws
this tile's half of each shared **edge** instead of its centred glyph, so a run of
three mountains reads as one range. Measured: **71% of mountain tiles** have such a
neighbour, modal run length 2-3.

## The ruling, and what it changes

For mountains the weighting reverses: **relief carries it, and the glyph stops being
the thing you notice.**

1. **Raise mountain (and highland) relief** well past the current small magnitudes,
   so a range is legible as raised ground at a glance from the terrain fill alone.
   The exact figures are a tuning pass against a live map, not a number to pick here
   (Rule 0b — the current values are tabled above so Ben can name a target against
   them).
2. **Retire the mountain glyph and its spans.** Keep canyon, crater and rift: those
   sink or pit rather than rise, and relief serves them far less well — canyon is
   only -0.16, and crater never spans at all ("a basin is a blob, not a line").

## Two things to be careful of

- **BL-231's original argument does not evaporate.** The glyph existed because a
  x1.3+ movement cost that is invisible is expensive. Relief has to actually *carry*
  that legibility, not merely replace the marker. This is a `visual` requirement and
  it needs a **live check** — a scripted capture proves it renders; only looking at
  it proves it reads.
- **Relief is suppressed on built tiles.** body_surface_canvas.cpp:2090 gates the
  elevation pass on `!built`, reasoning that "the elevation matters when SITING, and
  a built tile has already been sited". If relief becomes a mountain's **only**
  channel, a built mountain tile loses the fact entirely. **BL-562** un-suppresses
  exactly that gate; the two items meet at that line and should be sequenced
  together.

## Propagation

`docs/ui/ICONS.md` is the source-of-truth catalogue for the `ui::icons` vocabulary
and carries the mountain silhouette's shape, meaning and usage. Retiring a glyph is a
change to that vocabulary, so ICONS.md moves as part of landing this — not after.

---

## RULED by Ben, 2026-08-22 (elicitation form)

**Relief roughly doubles, and the mountain glyph is retired entirely.**

| Landform | Now | Ruled |
|---|---|---|
| mountain | +0.22 | **+0.45** |
| highland | +0.12 | **+0.25** |

The other five entries in `relief_amount` are untouched: plains 0.00, crater -0.08,
valley -0.10, rift -0.14, canyon -0.16. Only the two that *rise* move, which is
consistent with the ruling — the complaint was that elevation did not read, not that
depressions did not.

**Mountain leaves the dramatic-landform set entirely.** No centred peaked teeth, no
BL-232 bridged spans. Canyon, crater and rift stay exactly as they are. Relief carries
mountains alone from here.

**The consequence to accept knowingly.** BL-231 admitted the four dramatic landforms
because each carries a movement cost of x1.3 or worse and "this is the set where an
invisible surprise is expensive". Retiring mountain removes the marker from ~1.5% of
land tiles that still carry that cost. The +0.45 relief is now the *only* thing
telling a player that ground is expensive to cross, which is precisely why this needs
a live look and not just a capture — a scripted PNG proves the shading changed; only
opening the app proves the cost is legible.

**The BL-562 interaction is now load-bearing, not incidental.** Relief is suppressed
on built tiles (body_surface_canvas.cpp:2090, gated `!built`). With the glyph gone, a
built mountain tile under today's code would carry **no** elevation signal whatsoever.
BL-540 un-suppresses that gate. **These two items should land together, or BL-562
first** — landing BL-565 alone makes built mountains strictly worse than they are now.

**Propagation is part of landing, not after it.** `docs/ui/ICONS.md` is the source of
truth for the `ui::icons` vocabulary and documents the mountain silhouette's shape,
meaning and usage; `icons.cpp` carries it at :614 and :741, and `landform_spans`
(:700) must stop returning true for mountain. Retiring a glyph is a change to the
vocabulary, so ICONS.md moves in the same commit.

items.title: Legends live inside the minimap box, the minimap runs to the screen edge, and the full width hosts the lens dropdown
items.summary: Ben 2026-08-22: 'Lens legends need to be contained within the minimap space (which we can fill to the border of the screen). This means that we can use the full minimap for dropdown selection.' Revises BL-533, which landed the same day and put the legend in the right chrome column ABOVE the minimap (pinned_panel_rect), not inside it. Three composing moves: drop the minimap's 8px bottom chrome_margin, draw the legend clipped INSIDE the minimap box, and give the freed chrome width to the lens selectors. The selection_band_height coupling and NR-503's overdraw failure are the two traps.
items.design:
## Ben, 2026-08-22 (bug report)

> "Lens legends need to be contained within the minimap space (which we can fill to
> the border of the screen). This means that we can use the full minimap for dropdown
> selection."

## This revises BL-533, which landed the same day

BL-533 (commit 3932eea) acted on Ben's earlier ruling that a legend should take
"about 1/4 the minimap space with a scrollable legend". It moved every legend off the
canvas and into the **right chrome column** — `pinned_panel_rect`, pinned below the
time panel and growing *down toward* the minimap. So the legend today sits **above**
the minimap and **outside** it. Ben is now asking for it **inside** the minimap's own
box.

## Current measurements, so the target is stated against real numbers (Rule 0b)

At 1920x1080:

| Quantity | Derivation | Value |
|---|---|---|
| `minimap_width` | `max(0.28 * min(disp.x, disp.y), 336)` | **336 px** (the floor binds) |
| `minimap_height` | `minimap_width * 0.75` | **252 px** |
| `minimap_rect` right edge | flush to screen edge (BL-312) | `disp.x` |
| `minimap_rect` bottom | `chrome_margin` off the screen bottom | **8 px gap** |
| `right_chrome_width` | `= minimap_width` | 336 px |
| `shell_margin` | | 8 px |
| legend's present home | `pinned_panel_rect` — full chrome width, height left between the time panel and the minimap's top edge | |

## Three moves, and they compose

1. **The minimap fills to the screen border.** Its right edge already does; the
   bottom `chrome_margin` goes.
2. **The legend is contained within that space** — drawn inside the minimap box
   rather than in a panel above it, scrollable, still collapsed until asked for
   (BL-533's *behaviour*, in a new *home*).
3. **The freed chrome above becomes dropdown room** — "we can use the full minimap
   for dropdown selection", i.e. the lens bar's selectors get the whole width instead
   of a strip.

## Two traps, both already paid for once

**The `selection_band_height` coupling.** foldout_column.cpp defines
`selection_band_height = minimap_height + chrome_margin`, and its comment says why:
*"Top edge flush with the minimap's: the minimap floats `chrome_margin` off the
bottom, the strip does not, so the strip is exactly that much taller."* Removing the
minimap's bottom margin **breaks that identity**. The bottom strip's top edge must
still land exactly on the minimap's top edge, so the arithmetic moves with it — this
is the easiest thing in the item to get silently wrong.
